[S11] SECTION 02 | Relationships | How entities point to each other — and where the foreign key lives | 02
[S12] Relationships | EF Core · Relationships | In the database a relationship is just a | foreign key column | . In C#, a matching column name is | not enough | — EF Core needs more to see the relationship. | 1 | In the database | Employees | TABLE | PK | Id | Name | Age | FK | DepartmentId | Departments | TABLE | PK | Id | DeptName | Employees.DepartmentId | references | Departments.Id | 2 | In C# — only a scalar FK | public | class | Employee | { | public | int | Id | { | get | ; | set | ; } | public | string | Name | { | get | ; | set | ; } | public | int | Age | { | get | ; | set | ; } | public | int | DepartmentId | { | get | ; | set | ; } | // just an int | } | public | class | Department | { | public | int | Id | { | get | ; | set | ; } | public | string | DeptName | { | get | ; | set | ; } | } | ❌ No navigation property → EF Core | does not map a relationship | . | DepartmentId | is just a normal column — no FK constraint.
[S13] EF Core · Relationships | Navigation Properties | A | navigation property | points to another entity. Add one, and EF Core | discovers the relationship | and creates the FK constraint for you. | 1 | Reference navigation  (the “one”) | public | class | Employee | { | public | int | Id | { | get | ; | set | ; } | public | string | Name | { | get | ; | set | ; } | public | int | Age | { | get | ; | set | ; } | public | int | DepartmentId | { | get | ; | set | ; } | // FK | public | Department | Department | { | get | ; | set | ; } | // navigation | } | 2 | Collection navigation  (the “many”) | public | class | Department | { | public | int | Id | { | get | ; | set | ; } | public | string | DeptName | { | get | ; | set | ; } | public | ICollection | < | Employee | > | Employees | { | get | ; | set | ; } | = | new | List | < | Employee | >(); | // navigation | } | ✅ Now EF Core sees a | One-to-Many | : | Employees.DepartmentId | → | Departments.Id | with a real FOREIGN KEY constraint.
[S14] Relationships — Overview | EF Core · Relationships | A | relationship | connects two entities through a foreign key. EF Core supports three kinds. | Relationship | Example | Navigation properties | One-to-Many | Category → Products | Collection on one side, reference on the other | One-to-One | User → UserProfile | Reference on both sides | Many-to-Many | Student ↔ Course | Collection on both sides | Principal | The "one" side — the entity whose | PK | is referenced. e.g. | Category | Dependent | The side that holds the | FK | column. e.g. | Product.CategoryId | Navigation property | A property that points to another entity: | Category | or | ICollection<Product>
[S15] Principal & Dependent | EF Core · Relationships | The | FK always lives on the dependent side | . One Category has many Products — so each Product row stores its | CategoryId | . | Category | PRINCIPAL | PK | Id | Name | NAV | Products  (collection) | Product | DEPENDENT | PK | Id | Name | FK | CategoryId | NAV | Category  (reference) | 1 | * | Product.CategoryId | references Category.Id | 💡 Navigation properties are | objects | ( | Category | , | ICollection<Product> | ); the FK property is a | scalar value | ( | int CategoryId | ). You can have both — and usually should.
[S16] One-to-One | EF Core · Relationships | Employee | Department | Manage | 1                                              1 | An Employee | manages | a Department, and a Department | must | be managed by an Employee | By Convention | Data Annotation | Fluent APIs
[S17] One-to-One | EF Core · Relationships | By Convention : | Foreign Key Must Named As : | <NameOfNavigationProperty>Id | <NameOfNavigationProperty><NameOfPrimaryKey> | <TypeOfNavigationProperty>Id | <TypeOfNavigationProperty><NameOfPrimaryKey> | Foreign key property And Both Side Navigation Property is Required In One To One Relationship
[S18] One-to-One | EF Core · Relationships | Data Annotation | Use [ForeignKey] Attribute | if needed | (when FK name | does not | follow EF Core convention rules ) | Fluent APIs | Use Fluent API when the foreign key property name does not follow EF Core convention rules, when a navigation property is missing, or when you need custom foreign key constraints.
[S19] Delete Behavior — What Happens to Dependents? | EF Core ·Delete Behavior | When a | principal | is deleted, | OnDelete() | decides what happens to its dependents. | DeleteBehavior | Effect on dependents | Notes | Cascade | Deleted too | Default for | required | FKs ( | int CategoryId | ) | ClientSetNull | FK set to NULL on | tracked | entities only | Default for | optional | FKs ( | int? ManagerId | ) | SetNull | FK set to NULL (also in the database) | FK must be nullable | Restrict | Delete is blocked while dependents exist | Safe choice for important data | NoAction | Nothing — the database decides | Usually fails with an FK error | // can't delete a Category that still has Products | builder. | HasOne | (p => p. | Category | ) | . | WithMany | (c => c. | Products | ) | . | OnDelete | ( | DeleteBehavior | . | Restrict | );

[S22] One-to-Many | EF Core · Relationships | Employee | Department | Works | M                               1 | An Employee Must | Works in a | Department, and a Department | Must has many | Employees | By Convention | Data Annotation | Fluent APIs

You delete a Category — by default what happens to its Products? | A | They are deleted too (Cascade) | B | Their CategoryId becomes NULL | C | The delete is blocked | D | Nothing happens

Hossam Mostafa
Session 03
Online Learning Platform
Session 03 Assignment: Many-to-Many, Self-Referencing, CRUD, Bulk Operations & Seeding
This is an online learning platform where instructors publish courses and students enroll in them.
Instructors
Each instructor has a full name, an email address, a short bio (optional) and the date they joined the platform.
An instructor can publish many courses, but every course is published by exactly one instructor.
Categories
A category has a name and an optional description.
Categories form a tree: a category may have a parent category (for example Programming → Backend → ASP.NET). A top-level category has no parent.
A category can have any number of sub-categories, but each sub-category has exactly one parent.
Every course belongs to exactly one category.
Courses
A course has a title, an optional description, a price, a level (Beginner, Intermediate or Advanced) and a flag that shows whether it is published.
The published date is recorded only when the course gets published, so it is empty for unpublished courses.
Students and Enrollments
A student has a full name, an email address and a date of birth.
A student can enroll in many courses, and a course can have many students.
Each enrollment records the enrollment date, the progress percentage, a status (Active, Completed or Dropped) and an optional final grade, which is given only when the course is completed.
A student can enroll in the same course only once.
Business rules
Only published courses accept enrollments.
Progress must be between 0 and 100. An enrollment is Completed when its progress reaches 100.
A category that still has sub-categories cannot be deleted.
Task:
Build a Console Application using EF Core (Code-First) with SQL Server as the database provider.
Part 01: Model and Database
Create the entity classes and enums from the case study.
Configure every entity with the Fluent API, each in its own configuration class (IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>): required properties, maximum lengths, decimal precision for money and grade, the composite key of the join entity, and every relationship with an explicit foreign key.
The self-referencing relationship of Category must use a delete behavior that prevents deleting a parent that still has sub-categories.
Create the database with Migrations: one migration for the model and a separate one for the seed data.
Part 02: Seeding
With HasData (inside the configuration classes): at least 5 categories forming 3 levels, 3 instructors and 6 courses. Mix published and unpublished courses, and spread them across instructors, categories and levels.
From code in Program.cs: at least 5 students and 8 enrollments that cover all three statuses. Seed only when the table is empty, so running the app twice does not duplicate data.
Part 03: Operations
Write each operation as its own method, call them from Main in order, and print readable results. Work with foreign key properties and queries on the DbSets directly. Loading related data (Include, lazy loading) is not part of this assignment. A missing row or invalid input must print a friendly message, not crash the app.
Create
Add an instructor: Insert a new instructor and print the generated Id.
Add a course: Insert a course for an existing instructor and an existing category. Check that both exist first, otherwise print a message.
Add several students: Insert three students using one AddRange and one SaveChanges. Print their generated Ids.
Enroll a student: The student and the course must exist, the course must be published, and the student must not be enrolled already. Otherwise print why the enrollment was refused.
Read
Find a course: Get a course by Id using Find, then by title using FirstOrDefault. Print "not found" when the result is null.
Filter courses: Courses priced between two values, ordered by price descending. Print only the title, level and price.
Sub-categories: Print the direct sub-categories of a given category, then print the top-level categories.
Course roster: Print how many students are enrolled in a course, then their names. Do it without joins: get the student Ids from the enrollments first, then get the students with Contains.
Update
Change a price: Load a course, change its price, and save.
Update progress: Find the enrollment by its composite key and set the new progress. At 100 set the status to Completed. Reject values outside 0–100.
Publish a course: Set the published flag and the published date.
Delete
Unenroll: Delete an enrollment using its composite key.
Delete a category: First try to remove a category that still has sub-categories and catch the DbUpdateException, then print its message. After that, write a safe version that checks for sub-categories before deleting.
Delete a course: Delete a course that has enrollments. Print the number of its enrollments before and after, and explain in a comment why they were removed.
Bulk operations
Bulk price raise: In a single statement, without loading the entities, raise the price of all published courses of a given level by 10%. Print the number of affected rows.
Bulk delete: In a single statement, delete all enrollments whose status is Dropped. Print the number of affected rows.

Use | Attach | / | Update | or load it tracked."}, {"label": "Slide 33", "t": 33, "text": "SECTION 04 | Seeding Data | Starting the database with the records your app needs | 04"}, {"label": "Slide 34", "t": 34, "text": "Seeding Data — Three Approaches | EF Core · Seeding Data | Seeding | fills the database with essential records: lookup values, an admin user, default settings. | Approach | When it runs | Best for | HasData() | With migrations ( | Update-Database | ) | Static lookup data with fixed keys | Custom code at startup | Every time the app starts | Dynamic data — admin user, hashed passwords | External files (JSON / CSV) | At startup | Large datasets, data that changes often"}, {"label": "Slide 35", "t": 35, "text": "HasData() — Seeding with Migrations | EF Core · Seeding Data | protected | override | void | OnModelCreating | ( | ModelBuilder | modelBuilder) | { | modelBuilder. | Entity | < | Category | >(). | HasData | ( | new | Category | { | Id | = | 1 | , | Name | = | \"Electronics\" | }, | new | Category | { | Id | = | 2 | , | Name | = | \"Clothing\" | }, | new | Category | { | Id | = | 3 | , | Name | = | \"Books\" | }); | modelBuilder. | Entity | < | Product | >(). | HasData | ( | new | Product | { | Id | = | 1 | , | Name | = | \"Laptop\" | , | Price | = | 999.99m | , | CategoryId | = | 1 | }, | new | Product | { | Id | = | 2 | , | Name | = | \"T-Shirt\" | , | Price | = | 19.99m | , | CategoryId | = | 2 | }); | } | Rules | 1 | You | must | set the primary key ( | Id | ) yourself | 2 | Use | FK values | ( | CategoryId = 1 | ), not navigation objects | 3 | The data is written into the | migration file | 4 | Changing seed data → | new migration"}, {"label": "Slide 36", "t": 36, "text": "Seeding at Application Startup | EF Core · Seeding Data | For | dynamic data | — like an admin user with a hashed password — run your own code when the app starts. Always check first so you don't insert duplicates. | // Program.cs | using | var | context = | new | AppDbContext | (); | context. | Database | . | Migrate | (); | // apply pending migrations | if | (!context. | Users | . | Any | (u => u. | Role | == | \"Admin\" | )) | { | context. | Users | . | Add | ( | new | User | { | Username | = | \"admin\" | , | Email | = | \"admin@company.com\" | , | PasswordHash | = | HashPassword | ( | \"Admin123!\" | ), | Role | = | \"Admin\" | }); | context. | SaveChanges | (); | } | Migrate() | Applies pending migrations — safe for production. | EnsureCreated() | Creates the DB | without | migrations — demos & tests only. Don't mix it with migrations."}, {"label": "Slide 37", "t": 37, "text": "Seeding from a JSON File | EF Core · Seeding Data | Big datasets clutter your code. Keep them in a | JSON file | and load it at startup — you can update the data without recompiling. | // Data/SeedData/categories.json | [ | { \"Name\": \"Electronics\" }, | { \"Name\": \"Clothing\" } | ] | ⚠️ Check | AnyAsync() | first — otherwise the data is inserted again on | every | restart. | public | static | async | Task | SeedAsync | ( | AppDbContext | context) | { | if | ( | await | context. | Categories | . | AnyAsync | ()) | return | ; | var | path = | Path | . | Combine | ( | \"Data\" | , | \"SeedData\" | , | \"categories.json\" | ); | var | json = | await | File | . | ReadAllTextAsync | (path); | var | categories = | JsonSerializer | . | Deserialize | < | List | < | Category | >>(json); | context. | Categories | . | AddRange | (categories!); | await | context. | SaveChangesAsync | (); | }"}, {"label": "Slide 38", "t": 38, "text": "Quick Check | · Seeding Data | EF Core · Seeding Data | Q1 / 2 | Which is required when seeding with | HasData() | ? | A | Navigation properties must be set | B | The primary key value must be specified | C | The table must be empty | D | EnsureCreated() | must be called"}, {"label": "Slide 39", "t": 39, "text": "Quick Check | · Seeding Data | EF Core · Seeding Data | Q1 / 2 | Which is required when seeding with | HasData() | ? | A | Navigation properties must be set | B | The primary key value must be specified | ✓ Correct | C | The table must be empty | D | EnsureCreated() | must be called | 💡 | HasData() | compares seed rows between migrations by key, so every row needs an explicit | PK | value."}, {"label": "Slide 40", "t": 40, "text": "Quick Check | · Seeding Data | EF Core · Seeding Data | Q2 / 2 | You need to seed an admin user with a hashed password. Hossam Mostafa
Session 04
[P01] EF Core
ASP.Net Course
            
National Bank Management System
Session 04 Assignment: Eager Loading & Interactive Menu
The National Bank Group has asked you to build the data layer for their new Bank 
Management System. Branches across the country need a single, reliable system that tracks 
branches, managers, customers (individuals and businesses), bank accounts (including joint 
accounts shared by multiple customers), and every transaction that moves money in or out 
of those accounts.
Your job is not to build the UI or the ASP.NET API. Your job is to build the EF Core Code-First 
data layer that a future team will plug into.
Resources
●
The ER diagram below is the source of truth for the structure.
●
The case study document is the source of truth for the business rules.
Task:
Build a Console Application using EF Core (Code-First) with SQL Server as the database 
provider.
1
[P02] Part 01: Model and Database
●
Translate the ER diagram into C# entity classes.
●
Configure the relationships correctly using the Fluent API (and/or Data Annotations).
●
Use Migrations to generate the database.
Part 02: Seeding
●
After finishing the database creation, seed at least two tables (Branch and Manager) 
with initial data.
Part 03: Interactive Menu
Build a menu with the following options and keep showing it until the user chooses Exit.
●
1) Add a new Customer: Prompt the user for the full name, national ID, date of birth, 
email, phone, address, and customer type (Individual / Business). Validate the inputs.
●
2) Open a new Account for a Customer: Prompt for the account number, account type, 
branch code, customer Id, and ownership role (Primary / CoHolder). You must verify that 
the branch and the customer exist before creating the account.
●
3) Update Account Status: Prompt for the account number and the customer Id, then 
toggle the account status.
●
4) Remove an Account from a Customer: Prompt for the account number and the 
customer Id, then delete the CustomerAccount.
●
5) List all Customers (with accounts): Load each customer’s CustomerAccount rows 
and the account behind each one, and print a tidy formatted list.
●
0) Exit: Break out of the loop and close the connection.
Menu-loop quality requirements:
●
Invalid input (for example letters where a number is expected) must not crash the app. 
Show a friendly error and ask again.
●
After each operation, pause with "Press any key to return to the menu..." before 
redrawing the menu, so the output is readable.
Part 04: Sample Expected Outputs
Initial screen:
2
[P03] Option 1: Add Customer
Option 2: Open Account
Option 3: Update Account Status
3
[P04] Option 4: Remove an Account from a Customer
Option 5: List customers
4

Deep graphs with | several collections | can explode in size — see | AsSplitQuery() | in the next section.

[S19] LINQ Joins — Overview | EF Core · LINQ Joins | Joins | combine two sequences on a | matching key | . They work in memory ( | IEnumerable | ) and in EF Core ( | IQueryable | → SQL). | Inner Join | Only elements that match on | both | sides | Group Join | Each left element with a | collection | of its matches | Left Outer Join | All | left elements, matched or not | 💡 | .NET 10 / EF Core 10 | adds | LeftJoin() | and | RightJoin() | operators — outer joins without the old | GroupJoin + SelectMany + DefaultIfEmpty | pattern. | In EF Core, prefer | navigation properties | + | Include() | / | Select() | when they exist. Write manual joins when there's no navigation between the two sets.
[S20] Inner Join | EF Core · LINQ Joins | Returns only elements whose key exists in | both | sequences — same as SQL | INNER JOIN | . | 1 | Query syntax | var | result = | from | order | in | orders | join | customer | in | customers | on | order. | CustomerId | equals | customer. | Id | select | new | { | customer. | Name | , | order. | Product | , | order. | Total | }; | 2 | Method syntax | var | result = orders. | Join | ( | customers, | order    => order. | CustomerId | , | // outer key | customer => customer. | Id | , | // inner key | (order, customer) => | new | { | customer. | Name | , | order. | Product | , | order. | Total | }); | ⚠️ Query syntax compares keys with the keyword | equals | — writing | == | there is a compile error.
[S21] Group Join | EF Core · LINQ Joins | Pairs each outer element with a | collection | of matching inner elements — e.g. | each customer with all of their orders | . | 1 | Query syntax | var | result = | from | customer | in | customers | join | order | in | orders | on | customer. | Id | equals | order. | CustomerId | into | customerOrders | select | new | { | customer. | Name | , | Orders | = customerOrders | }; | 2 | Method syntax | var | result = customers. | GroupJoin | ( | orders, | customer => customer. | Id | , | order    => order. | CustomerId | , | (customer, customerOrders) => | new | { | customer. | Name | , | Orders | = customerOrders | }); | 💡 A customer with no orders gets an | empty collection — not null | . [S22] Left Outer Join — LeftJoin() (.NET 10+) | EF Core · LINQ Joins | Keeps | every | left element. When there's no match, the right side is | null | . | var | result = customers. | LeftJoin | ( | orders, | customer => customer. | Id | , | order    => order. | CustomerId | , | (customer, order) => | new | { | customer. | Name | , | Product | = order?. | Product | ?? | "No Orders" | , | Total | = order?. | Total | ?? | 0 | }); | // EF Core 10 translates it to a SQL LEFT JOIN | 💡 | RightJoin() | exists too — it keeps every | right | element. | Method syntax only — there's no query-syntax keyword for it. | ⚠️ The right side can be | null | — always use | ?. | and | ?? | .

You'll see this in most existing code. | 1 | Query syntax | var | result = | from | customer | in | customers | join | order | in | orders | on | customer. | Id | equals | order. | CustomerId | into | customerOrders | from | order | in | customerOrders. | DefaultIfEmpty | () | select | new | { | customer. | Name | , | Product | = order?. | Product | ?? | "No Orders" | , | Total | = order?. | Total | ?? | 0 | }; | 2 | Method syntax | var | result = customers | . | GroupJoin | (orders, | c => c. | Id | , | o => o. | CustomerId | , | (c, ords) => | new | { c, ords }) | . | SelectMany | ( | x => x.ords. | DefaultIfEmpty | (), | (x, order) => | new | { | x.c. | Name | , | Product | = order?. | Product | ?? | "No Orders" | });

[S01] SESSION 01 | ASP.NET Core MVC | Model View Controller — Actions, Middleware, Routing, Binding & Validation | .NET Track
[S02] Agenda | MVC · Session 01 | 01 | MVC | Model · View · Controller | 02 | Actions | Action Results | 03 | Middleware | The request pipeline | 04 | Routing | URL → Controller / Action | 05 | Model Binding | Request data → parameters
[S03] SECTION 01 | MVC | Model · View · Controller and how a request flows through them | 01
[S04] What is MVC? | MVC · Model View Controller | MVC | is a design pattern that splits the app into | 3 parts | , each with | one job | — this is called | Separation of Concerns | . | M | Model | The | data | and its rules. Classes like | Product | , validation, business logic. | V | View | The | UI | the user sees. | .cshtml | files = HTML + C# (Razor). | C | Controller | The | brain | . Receives the request, uses the Model, picks a View. | Change the UI → touch only the | View | . Change a rule → touch only the | Model | . Each part is easier to read, test and change.
[S05] How a request flows in MVC | MVC · Model View Controller | Browser | GET /Products | → | Routing | finds the action | → | Controller | Products.Index() | → | Model | gets products | → | View | Index.cshtml | → | HTML | back to browser | The | Controller | never builds HTML itself. | It passes the | Model | to the | View | , and the View turns it into HTML.
[S06] Project Structure & Conventions | MVC · Model View Controller | Route.MvcSession01/ | ├── Controllers/ | │   └── ProductsController.cs | ├── Models/ | │   └── Product.cs | ├── Views/ | │   ├── Products/ | │   │   └── Index.cshtml | │   └── Shared/ | │       └── _Layout.cshtml | ├── wwwroot/     ← css, js, images | └── Program.cs   ← services + pipeline | Convention | Example | Name ends with | Controller | ProductsController | Inherits | Controller | gives | View() | , | Json() | … | Views folder = controller name | Views/Products/ | View file = action name | Index.cshtml | Not found? → look in | Views/Shared/

[S17] SECTION 02 | Actions | Action methods and the results they send back | 02
[S18] Actions | MVC · Actions | An | action | is a | public method | in a controller that handles a request and returns an | Action Result | . | public | class | ProductsController : Controller | { | // GET /Products/Details/2 | public | IActionResult | Details | ( | int | id) | { | var | product = _store.GetById(id); | if | (product | is | null | ) | return | NotFound | (); | // 404 | return | View | (product); | // 200 + HTML | } | [NonAction] | // NOT reachable by URL | public | void | Helper | () { } | } | Must be | public | Can't be | static | or generic | [NonAction] | hides a public method | [HttpGet] | / | [HttpPost] | choose the HTTP verb
[S19] Action Results | MVC · Actions | Helper method | Result type | Sends back | View(model) | ViewResult | HTML from a | .cshtml | view | PartialView() | PartialViewResult | Part of a page (no layout) | Content("text") | ContentResult | Plain text | Json(obj) | JsonResult | JSON data | RedirectToAction("Index") | RedirectToActionResult | 302 → another action | Redirect(url) | RedirectResult | 302 → any URL | NotFound() | · | BadRequest() | · | Ok() | 404 · 400 · 200 | A status code | StatusCode(418) | StatusCodeResult | Any status code | File(bytes, type, name) | FileResult | A file download
[S20] IActionResult — One Action, Many Results | MVC · Actions | Every result type implements | IActionResult | , so an action that returns | IActionResult | can send back | any | of them. | 1 | Specific type | // can ONLY return JSON | public | JsonResult | GetProduct | () | => Json( | new | { Id = | 1 | , Name = | "Laptop" | }); | Use when the action | always | returns the same thing. | 2 | IActionResult | public | IActionResult | Product | ( | int | id) | { | if | (id > | 100 | ) | return | NotFound(); | if | (id == | 42 | ) | return | RedirectToAction( | "Index" | ); | return | Json | ( | new | { Id = id }); | } | Use when the result | depends on a condition | .

[S31] SECTION 03 | Middleware | The request pipeline — Use, Run, Map and why order matters | 03
[S32] Middleware & the Request Pipeline | MVC · Middleware | Middleware | = a piece of code in the | pipeline | . Every request passes through the middlewares | in order | . | Request | from browser | Exception | Handler | Static | Files | Routing | Authorization | Endpoint | Controller action | Response | to browser | ⟶ Request goes down the pipeline, in order | Response comes back up in reverse order ⟵ | Each middleware can: | work before | → | call the next | → | work after | … or | stop | (short-circuit) and answer right away.
[S33] Use · Run · Map | MVC · Middleware | Method | What it does | Calls next? | app.Use(...) | Runs code before & after the next middleware | Yes — | await next() | app.Run(...) | Terminal middleware — ends the pipeline | No | app.Map("/path", ...) | Branches the pipeline for a URL path | Its own branch
[S34] Order Matters | MVC · Middleware | var | app = builder.Build(); | app.UseExceptionHandler( | "/Home/Error" | ); | // 1 | app.UseStaticFiles(); | // 2 | app.UseRouting(); | // 3 | app.UseAuthorization(); | // 4 | app.MapControllerRoute( | // 5 | name: | "default" | , | pattern: | "{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}" | ); | app.Run(); | ExceptionHandler first | → catches errors from everything after it. | StaticFiles before Routing | → | site.css | is served without reaching MVC. | ⚠️ | Authorization after Routing | → it needs to know which endpoint was chosen.

[S45] SECTION 04 | Routing | Mapping URLs to controllers and actions | 04
[S46] Routing | MVC · Routing | Routing | maps an incoming | URL | to a | controller | and an | action | . | {controller=Home} | / | {action=Index} | / | {id?} | {controller=Home} | Route parameter. Default | Home | if missing. | {action=Index} | Route parameter. Default | Index | if missing. | {id?} | ? | = optional. Bound to an | id | parameter.

Hossam Mostafa
Session 02
1. Introduction
The Gym Management System stores the core data of a gym: members, trainers, membership plans , member subscriptions, and training sessions.
2. Features
Member Management: Full CRUD operations.
Trainer Management: Full CRUD operations.
Session Management : Full CRUD operations.
Plans Management: View All Plans , Update and Deactivate(SoftDelete).
Membership Management : Assign plans to members.
Dashboard : analytics and reports.
Identity Management : Login and Sign Out 
3. Technology stack
Backend: ASP.NET Core MVC
ORM: Entity Framework Core
Database: Microsoft SQL Server
Frontend: Razor Views + Bootstrap , Custom CSS
Tools & Libraries: AutoMapper → For object-to-object mapping between ViewModels and Entities.
4. Entities and Their Details
Member
       Represents a registered Gym member
Properties:
Id → Unique identifier for the member.
Name → Full name of the member.
Email → Contact email address.
Phone → Contact phone number.
DateOfBirth → Member’s date of birth.
Gender → Gender of the member.
Address → Structured address containing: (Building # , Street , City)
JoinDate → Date when the member joined the gym.
Photo → Profile picture of the member
Relationships:
● Each Member subscribes to one or more Plans .
Trainer
Represents a gym trainer responsible for guiding members and conducting sessions.
Properties:
Id → Unique identifier for the trainer.
Name → Full name of the trainer.
Email → Contact email address.
Phone → Contact phone number.
DateOfBirth → Trainer’s date of birth.
Gender → Gender of the trainer.
Address → Structured address containing: (Building # , Street , City)
HireDate →  Date the trainer was hired.
Speciality →  Areas of expertise (e.g., strength training, yoga, nutrition).
Relationships:
● A Trainer can conduct many Sessions.
Plan
Represents a gym membership or training plan offered to members.
Properties:
Id → Unique identifier for the plan.
Name → Name of the plan (e.g., Basic Plan, Premium Plan).
Description → Detailed description of what the plan includes.
DurationDays → Duration of the plan in days (e.g., 30).
Price → Cost of the plan.
IsActive → Indicates whether the plan is currently active.
Relationships:
● A Plan can be assigned to many Members.
Session
Represents a scheduled gym session conducted by a trainer for members.
Properties:
Id → Unique identifier for the session.
Description → Details about the session content.
Capacity → Maximum number of members allowed.
StartDate → Date and time when the session begins.
EndDate → Date and time when the session ends.
Relationships:
● Each Session is conducted by one Trainer.
5. ER Diagram 
6. Business Rules
Member Management
Email and phone must be unique and Valid
Egyptian phone validation: (010|011|012|015)XXXXXXXX
Join Date Will Be Calculated Automatically
Trainer Management
Email and phone must be unique and Valid
Cannot delete trainers with future sessions
Must have one specialty assigned
Hire Date Will Be Calculated Automatically
Session Management
Capacity limited to 1-25 participants (enforced by database constraint)
End date must be after start date
Cannot update/deactivate plans with active memberships
Plans can be activated/deactivated
Membership
A member cannot have more than one Active membership at the same time.
Only active plans can be assigned
When a membership is created, its EndDate is automatically calculated based on the plan duration.
Membership status is computed: "Active" if EndDate > Now, else "Expired"
7. Entities Configurations
Name For Member and Trainer : Varchar With Max Length 50
Email For Member and Trainer : Varchar With Max Length 100 With Valid Format Of Email And Unique
Phone For Member and Trainer : Varchar With Max Length 11 With Valid Format Of Egyptian Phone Number And Unique
JoinDate For Member : Join Date is automatically set to the insertion date
HireDate For Trainer : Default Value Insertion Date
Plan Duration Days : Must be From 1 To 365 Days 
Session Capacity : From 1 To 25
Session End Date : must be after start date
Membership Start : Date Default Value Insertion Date
8. MVC Components
HomeController
Index() - Landing page with gym features and statistics
MemberController
Handles all member-related operations through web pages:
Index() - Displays member listing page
Create() - Shows member registration form
CreateMember() - Processes form submission
MemberDetails(int id) - Displays member profile page
HealthRecordDetails(int id) - Shows health record page
MemberEdit(int id) - Displays edit form
MemberEdit() - Processes update
Delete(int id) - Shows deletion confirmation page
DeleteConfirmed(int id) - Processes deletion
TrainerController
Manages trainer operations through web interface:
Index() - Trainer listing page
Create() - Show trainer registration form
CreateTrainer() - Form submission handler
Details(int id) - Trainer profile page
Edit(int id) - Edit form display
Edit() - Update handler
Delete(int id) - Shows Deletion confirmation page
DeleteConfirmed(int id) - Processes Deletion
SessionController
Handles training session management:
Index() - Session calendar/list page
Create() - New session form with trainer/category dropdowns
Create() - Session creation handler
Details(int id) - Session details page
Edit(int id) - Session edit form
Edit() - Update handler
Delete(int id) - Shows Deletion confirmation page
DeleteConfirmed(int id) - Processes Deletion
PlanController
Manages membership plans:
Index() - Plans listing page
Details(int id) - Plan details page
Edit(int id) - Plan edit form
Edit(int id) - Update handler
Activate(int id) - Toggle plan active status
MemberPlan Controller
Manages member memberships:
Index() - Memberships listing page
Create() - Show membership registration form
Create() - Form submission handler
Cancel () - Processes Cancellation of membership

It runs only when you ask for the results — this is called | deferred execution | . | Start | _context.Plans | nothing runs | Add a filter | .Where(p => p.IsActive) | nothing runs | Add sorting | .OrderBy(p => p.Price) | nothing runs | Ask for results | .ToList() | ONE SQL query sent | SELECT | [p].[Id], [p].[Name], [p].[Price] … | FROM | [Plans] AS [p] | WHERE | [p].[IsActive] = 1 | ORDER BY | [p].[Price] | The single query EF Core sends at .ToList() | These run the query | .ToList() | / | .ToArray() | foreach | over the query (also in a view) | .Count() | , | .First() | , | .Any() | 💡 After | .ToList() | you hold a | List<Plan> | — data is in memory, so anything after it runs as IEnumerable."}, {"label": "Slide 54", "t": 54, "text": "Common Mistake: Calling ToList() Too Early | MVC · IEnumerable vs IQueryable | ❌ | Too early | var | all = _context.Members. | ToList | (); | var | page = all | . | Where | (m => m.Address.City == | \"Giza\" | ) | . | Take | (10); | Loads | every | member into memory | Where and Take run in C# | Slow and heavy as the gym grows | ✅ | Right order | var | page = _context.Members | . | Where | (m => m.Address.City == | \"Giza\" | ) | . | Take | (10) | . | ToList | (); | SQL does | WHERE | and | TOP(10) | Only 10 rows reach the app | Fast no matter how big the table is | 💡 Rule: | build the whole query first | (Where, OrderBy, Skip, Take), then call | .ToList() | once at the end."}, {"label": "Slide 55", "t": 55, "text": "QUESTIONS? | Thank You | .NET Track"}]

[@00:45|t=45] What Is a View? A View is the Ul part of MVC. It decides how data looks — no business logic, only presentation. ROUTE O View Shows the result to the user. [@02:15|t=135] The Solution Is Razor Razor is a markup syntax that lets you write C# inside HTML. Now you pick what you want — in your own memory. | Query runs | in app memory | Filters are normal C# code | All rows are loaded first | List<Member> | is IEnumerable [S51] Where the Filtering Happens | MVC · IEnumerable vs IQueryable | IQueryable — filter in the database | _context.Members | . | Where | (m => m.Gender == | Gender | .Female) | . | ToList | (); | SQL Server | SELECT … WHERE Gender = 2 | 10,000 members in table | 4,800 rows | Your app (memory) | Gets only female members — ready to use | IEnumerable — filter in memory | _context.Members. | AsEnumerable | () | . | Where | (m => m.Gender == | Gender | .Female) | . | ToList | (); | SQL Server | SELECT … FROM Members | 10,000 members in table | 10,000 rows | Your app (memory) | Loads everyone, then throws 5,200 away | 💡 Same result list, very different cost. With IQueryable the | database does the filtering | and only the needed rows cross the network. | Numbers are an example for a gym with 10,000 members. [S52] IEnumerable vs IQueryable — Side by Side | MVC · IEnumerable vs IQueryable | IEnumerable<T> | IQueryable<T> | Namespace | System.Collections.Generic | System.Linq | Where it runs | App memory (C#) | Database (SQL Server) | Your lambda becomes | Normal C# code that runs | An expression tree EF Core turns into SQL | Rows loaded | All rows, then filtered | Only the rows you asked for | Best for | Small lists already in memory, C# logic SQL can't do | Filtering, sorting and paging big tables | Gym example | A List<Plan> you already loaded | _context.Plans.Where(p => p.IsActive) | 💡 Easy way to remember: | IQueryable asks the database | , | IEnumerable asks your RAM | . [S53] When Does the Query Actually Run? | MVC · IEnumerable vs IQueryable | Building a query does | not | touch the database. It runs only when you ask for the results — this is called | deferred execution | . | Start | _context.Plans | nothing runs | Add a filter | .Where(p => p.IsActive) | nothing runs | Add sorting | .OrderBy(p => p.Price) | nothing runs | Ask for results | .ToList() | ONE SQL query sent | SELECT | [p].[Id], [p].[Name], [p].[Price] … | FROM | [Plans] AS [p] | WHERE | [p].[IsActive] = 1 | ORDER BY | [p].[Price] | The single query EF Core sends at .ToList() | These run the query | .ToList() | / | .ToArray() | foreach | over the query (also in a view) | .Count() | , | .First() | , | .Any() | 💡 After | .ToList() | you hold a | List<Plan> | — data is in memory, so anything after it runs as IEnumerable. [S54] Common Mistake: Calling ToList() Too Early | MVC · IEnumerable vs IQueryable | ❌ | Too early | var | all = _context.Members. | ToList | (); | var | page = all | . | Where | (m => m.Address.City == | "Giza" | ) | . | Take | (10); | Loads | every | member into memory | Where and Take run in C# | Slow and heavy as the gym grows | ✅ | Right order | var | page = _context.Members | . | Where | (m => m.Address.City == | "Giza" | ) | . | Take | (10) | . | ToList | (); | SQL does | WHERE | and | TOP(10) | Only 10 rows reach the app | Fast no matter how big the table is | 💡 Rule: | build the whole query first | (Where, OrderBy, Skip, Take), then call | .ToList() | once at the end. IEnumerable vs IQueryable | 05"}, {"label": "Slide 50", "t": 50, "text": "Two Ways to Work with Data | MVC · IEnumerable vs IQueryable | Both let you write LINQ like | .Where() | and | .OrderBy() | . The difference is | where the work happens | : in SQL Server, or in your app's memory. | 🧾 | IQueryable<T> | System.Linq | An order not yet sent to the kitchen | You can keep changing it. When it's sent, the kitchen (SQL Server) cooks only what you asked for. | Query runs | in the database | Filters become SQL | WHERE | Only matching rows travel to the app | _context.Members | is IQueryable | 🍽️ | IEnumerable<T> | System.Collections.Generic | Food already on your table | Everything was brought out first. Now you pick what you want — in your own memory. | Query runs | in app memory | Filters are normal C# code | All rows are loaded first | List<Member> | is IEnumerable"}, {"label": "Slide 51", "t": 51, "text": "Where the Filtering Happens | MVC · IEnumerable vs IQueryable | IQueryable — filter in the database | _context.Members | . | Where | (m => m.Gender == | Gender | .Female) | . | ToList | (); | SQL Server | SELECT … WHERE Gender = 2 | 10,000 members in table | 4,800 rows | Your app (memory) | Gets only female members — ready to use | IEnumerable — filter in memory | _context.Members. | AsEnumerable | () | . | Where | (m => m.Gender == | Gender | .Female) | . | ToList | (); | SQL Server | SELECT … FROM Members | 10,000 members in table | 10,000 rows | Your app (memory) | Loads everyone, then throws 5,200 away | 💡 Same result list, very different cost. With IQueryable the | database does the filtering | and only the needed rows cross the network. | Numbers are an example for a gym with 10,000 members."}, {"label": "Slide 52", "t": 52, "text": "IEnumerable vs IQueryable — Side by Side | MVC · IEnumerable vs IQueryable | IEnumerable<T> | IQueryable<T> | Namespace | System.Collections.Generic | System.Linq | Where it runs | App memory (C#) | Database (SQL Server) | Your lambda becomes | Normal C# code that runs | An expression tree EF Core turns into SQL | Rows loaded | All rows, then filtered | Only the rows you asked for | Best for | Small lists already in memory, C# logic SQL can't do | Filtering, sorting and paging big tables | Gym example | A List<Plan> you already loaded | _context.Plans.Where(p => p.IsActive) | 💡 Easy way to remember: | IQueryable asks the database | , | IEnumerable asks your RAM | ."}, {"label": "Slide 53", "t": 53, "text": "When Does the Query Actually Run? | MVC · IEnumerable vs IQueryable | Building a query does | not | touch the database. It runs only when you ask for the results — this is called | deferred execution | . | Start | _context.Plans | nothing runs | Add a filter | .Where(p => p.IsActive) | nothing runs | Add sorting | .OrderBy(p => p.Price) | nothing runs | Ask for results | .ToList() | ONE SQL query sent | SELECT | [p].[Id], [p].[Name], [p].[Price] … | FROM | [Plans] AS [p] | WHERE | [p].[IsActive] = 1 | ORDER BY | [p].[Price] | The single query EF Core sends at .ToList() | These run the query | .ToList() | / | .ToArray() | foreach | over the query (also in a view) | .Count() | , | .First() | , | .Any() | 💡 After | .ToList() | you hold a | List<Plan> | — data is in memory, so anything after it runs as IEnumerable."}, {"label": "Slide 54", "t": 54, "text": "Common Mistake: Calling ToList() Too Early | MVC · IEnumerable vs IQueryable | ❌ | Too early | var | all = _context.Members. | ToList | (); | var | page = all | . | Where | (m => m.Address.City == | \"Giza\" | ) | . | Take | (10); | Loads | every | member into memory | Where and Take run in C# | Slow and heavy as the gym grows | ✅ | Right order | var | page = _context.Members | . | Where | (m => m.Address.City == | \"Giza\" | ) | . | Take | (10) | . | ToList | (); | SQL does | WHERE | and | TOP(10) | Only 10 rows reach the app | Fast no matter how big the table is | 💡 Rule: | build the whole query first | (Where, OrderBy, Skip, Take), then call | .ToList() | once at the end."}, {"label": "Slide 55", "t": 55, "text": "QUESTIONS? | Thank You | .NET Track"}]

[@02:05|t=125] What an Action Returns An action returns IActionResuIt — so one action can return a view, a redirect, or an error depending on the situation. 1. Overview
The Library Management System (LMS) is designed to manage books, categories, authors, members, loans, and fines in an efficient and structured way.
It provides:
A structured way to organize books by categories and authors.
Easy registration and tracking of members.
Automated borrowing and returning of books.
Fine calculation for overdue or damaged items.
System Behavior:
The system should allow members to search books by title, author, or category.
When borrowing, the system should assign a due date (e.g., 14 days from loan date).
If the book is returned on time, no fine is applied.
If the book is overdue or damaged, the system should automatically calculate and issue a fine when the book is returned.
If fines remain unpaid, the member’s account status may be set to Suspended.
 
2. Entities & Their Details
2.1 Book ( Represents a book in the library )
Attributes:
 Id  – Unique identifier
Title – Title of the book
Price - the Book Price
 PublicationYear – Year of publication
AvailableCopies – Number of available copies
TotalCopies – Total number of copies in the library
Relationships:
One book → One author
One book → Many loans
One book → One Category (Each book must belong to one category)
2.2 Category ( Represents a category for books )
Attributes:
Id – Unique identifier
Title - Name of the category
Description - Category details
Relationships:
One Category → Many books (Each Book Must Belong To One Category)
2.3 Author ( Represents a writer of one or more books )
Attributes:
Id – Unique identifier
FirstName
LastName
DateOfBirth
Relationships:
One author → Many books (Each Book Must Belong To One Author)
2.4 Member ( Represents a registered library member )
Attributes:
Id – Unique identifier
Name
Email
PhoneNumber
Address
MembershipDate
Status (Active, Suspended)
Relationships:
One member → Many loans (One Member Can Loan Many Books)
2.5 Loan ( Represents a borrowing/returning transaction)
Attributes:
Id – Unique identifier
LoanDate – Date when book was borrowed
Status (Borrowed, Returned, Overdue)
Relationships:
When a member borrows a book, the system should store the following data :
DueDate – Expected return date
ReturnDate –  Actual return date
One Fine → One Loan (if the member exceeds the due date )
2.6 Fine ( Represents the money charged for overdue or damaged books )
Attributes:
Id – Unique identifier
Amount – the fine amount
IssuedDate – Date when fine was issued
PaidDate – Date when fine was paid
Status ( Pending, Paid)
Relationships:
One Fine → One Loan

Route - What's New in C# - Week 1 What's New in C# Versions Week 1: Cleaner Code & Modern Syntax "Write Less, Express More" C# 9 C# 10 C# 11 C# 12 C# 13 C# 14 The C# Evolution: A Quick Timeline C# has evolved dramatically since version 7. Each version focuses on making code shorter , safer , and more expressive . Version .NET Year Theme C# 9 .NET 5 2020 Records, Top-level statements, Pattern matching C# 10 .NET 6 2021 File-scoped namespaces, Global usings C# 11 .NET 7 2022 Raw string literals, List patterns C# 12 .NET 8 2023 Primary constructors, Collection expressions C# 13 .NET 9 2024 params collections, Partial properties, Lock type C# 14 .NET 10 2025 Extension members, Null-conditional assignment, field keyword Today's focus: Syntax features from C# 9–14 that make everyday code cleaner — no new OOP concepts required! 👆 Click to reveal Today's Agenda Section 01 — Project-Level Top-level statements File-scoped namespaces Global & implicit usings Section 02 — Expression-Level Target-typed new() Constant interpolated strings Default lambda parameters Alias any type Null-conditional assignment ?.= Section 03 — Strings & Interpolation Raw string literals """ Improved interpolation $$""" Newlines in interpolation After today you'll recognize old patterns and confidently refactor them to modern C#. No behavior changes — just cleaner code! 👆 Click to reveal Discussion: Old vs. Modern C# Look at these two versions of the same program . What differences do you notice? ❌ Classic C# (Before) using System; using System.Collections.Generic; namespace MyApp { class Program { static void Main ( string [] args) { List < string > names = new List < string >(); names. Add ( "Alice" ); Console . WriteLine (names[ 0 ]); } } } 15 lines ✅ Modern C# (After) List < string > names = new (); names. Add ( "Alice" ); Console . WriteLine (names[ 0 ]); 3 lines — same output! What changed? Each line that disappeared is a modern C# feature doing the work for you: Top-level statements Removed class + Main() File-scoped namespace Removed namespace { } Implicit usings Removed using System; Target-typed new Shorter new() syntax Output (both versions): Alice — Same result, 80% less code! 👆 Click to reveal Top-Level Statements C# 9 Top-level statements let you write code directly in Program.cs — no class , no Main() method, no ceremony. Before (C# 8 and earlier) using System; namespace MyApp { class Program { static void Main ( string [] args) { Console . WriteLine ( "Hello!" ); } } } After (C# 9+) Console . WriteLine ( "Hello!" ); One line instead of 11. The compiler generates the rest. Behind the scenes — What the compiler generates: // The compiler wraps your code in this: internal class Program { static void <Main>$ ( string [] args) { Console . WriteLine ( "Hello!" ); } } Note: You can still access args directly in top-level code — the compiler provides it for you! // args is available automatically if (args. Length > 0 ) Console . WriteLine ( $"Hello, {args[ 0 ]} !" ); else Console . WriteLine ( "Hello, World!" ); Common Mistake: Using top-level statements in more than one file // File1.cs Console . WriteLine ( "Hello" ); // File2.cs Console . WriteLine ( "World" ); // CS8802: Only one compilation unit // can have top-level statements. Rule: Only one file per project can have top-level statements. 👆 Click to reveal File-Scoped Namespaces C# 10 Replace the block-scoped namespace with a simple declaration . Saves one level of indentation across the entire file. Before namespace MyApp.Models { public class Student { public string Name { get ; set ; } public int Age { get ; set ; } } } After namespace MyApp.Models ; public class Student { public string Name { get ; set ; } public int Age { get ; set ; } } Key insight: The semicolon ; after the namespace means "this namespace applies to the entire file ." Limitation: File-scoped namespace allows only one namespace per file . You cannot declare multiple namespaces — if you need that (rare), use the old block syntax. 👆 Click to reveal Global & Implicit Usings C# 10 Global Usings Write global using once , available in every file . // GlobalUsings.cs global using System; global using System.Collections.Generic; global using System.Text; Implicit Usings .NET 6+ automatically adds common usings (hidden in obj/ folder). // Auto-generated for Console apps: global using System; global using System.IO; global using System.Linq; global using System.Collections.Generic; global using System.Threading.Tasks; Where are they hidden? Check obj/Debug/net10.0/YourProject.GlobalUsings.g.cs Best practice: Create a single GlobalUsings.cs file for your project-wide usings. Before vs After — File headers across your project: Before (repeated in every file) // StudentService.cs using System; using System.Linq; using System.Collections.Generic; using MyApp.Models; public class StudentService { ... } // CourseService.cs using System; using System.Linq; using System.Collections.Generic; using MyApp.Models; public class CourseService { ... } After (clean files!) // GlobalUsings.cs (one file) global using MyApp.Models; // StudentService.cs public class StudentService { ... } // CourseService.cs public class CourseService { ... } // No repeated usings! Enable / Disable implicit usings in .csproj: <!-- In your .csproj file --> <PropertyGroup> <!-- Enable (default in .NET 6+) --> <ImplicitUsings> enable </ImplicitUsings> <!-- Disable completely --> <ImplicitUsings> disable </ImplicitUsings> </PropertyGroup> Remove a specific implicit using: <!-- In your .csproj file --> <ItemGroup> <!-- Remove System.Net.Http from implicit usings --> <Using Remove= "System.Net.Http" /> </ItemGroup> 👆 Click to reveal Spot the Bug! Each snippet has one error . Can you find it? Bug #1 // File1.cs Console . WriteLine ( "Hello" ); // File2.cs Console . WriteLine ( "World" ); Hint: How many files can have top-level statements? CS8802: Only ONE file per project can have top-level statements! Hint Show Answer Bug #2 namespace MyApp ; { public class Student { } } Hint: What does the semicolon ; mean for file-scoped namespaces? CS8955: File-scoped namespace uses ; — remove the { } braces! Hint Show Answer Bug #3 namespace MyApp ; public class Helper { global using System.Text; } Hint: Where should global using be placed in a file? CS8915: global using must be at the TOP of the file, before any namespace! Hint Show Answer Bug #4 using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using System.Linq; List < int > nums = new () { 1 , 2 , 3 }; Console . WriteLine (nums. Sum ()); Hint: Are these usings really needed in .NET 6+? IDE0005: These usings are unnecessary — they're already included as implicit usings in .NET 6+. Remove them! Hint Show Answer 👆 Click to reveal next bug Target-Typed new() C# 9 When the compiler already knows the type from the left side, you can omit the type name from new . Before List < string > names = new List < string >(); Dictionary < string , int > scores = new Dictionary < string , int >(); StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder (); After List < string > names = new (); Dictionary < string , int > scores = new (); StringBuilder sb = new (); Works everywhere the type is known: // Field declaration private List < string > _names = new (); // Method parameter with default void Print ( List < string > items = new ()) { } // Return statement List < int > GetNumbers () => new (); Works with constructor parameters too: List < string > names = new ( 10 ); // capacity = 10 HttpClient client = new ( new HttpClientHandler { AllowAutoRedirect = false }); Common Mistake — does NOT work with var : var names = new (); // CS8754: new() type cannot be inferred var sb = new (); // CS8754: same error! // Fix: specify the type on the left side List < string > names = new (); // ✅ 👆 Click to reveal Constant Interpolated Strings C# 10 In C# 10, you can use $"" interpolation with const strings — as long as all parts are also constant . Before (C# 9) const string scheme = "https" ; const string domain = "route.com" ; // ERROR! Can't use $ with const const string url = $"{scheme}://{domain}" ; // Had to use concatenation: const string url = scheme + "://" + domain; After (C# 10+) const string scheme = "https" ; const string domain = "route.com" ; // ✅ Now works! const string url = $"{scheme}://{domain}" ; // Result: "https://route.com" Why it matters: Cleaner code for API endpoints, connection strings, and configuration constants. Common Mistake — all parts must be const : const string baseUrl = "https://api.route.com" ; string version = "v2" ; // NOT const! const string endpoint = $"{baseUrl}/{version}" ; // CS0133: not constant! // Fix: make ALL parts const const string version2 = "v2" ; // ✅ const const string endpoint2 = $"{baseUrl}/{version2}" ; // ✅ works! 👆 Click to reveal Default Lambda Parameters C# 12 Just like methods, lambda expressions can now have default parameter values . Before (C# 11) // No defaults in lambdas! var discount = ( decimal price, decimal rate) => price * rate; // Always need both args: discount( 100m , 0.1m ); // discount(100m); ← ERROR! After (C# 12) // Default values work! var discount = ( decimal price, decimal rate = 0.1m ) => price * rate; // Both work now: discount( 100m , 0.2m ); // 20 discount( 100m ); // 10 Useful for: Callbacks, event handlers, LINQ-style operations with configurable behavior. Same behavior as method defaults: Method default void Log ( string msg, string level = "INFO" ) { Console . WriteLine ( $"[{level}]{msg}" ); } Lambda default (same!) var log = ( string msg, string level = "INFO" ) => Console . WriteLine ( $"[{level}]{msg}" ); Bonus — params works in lambdas too (C# 12): var sum = ( params int [] numbers) => numbers. Sum (); sum( 1 , 2 , 3 ); // 6 sum( 10 , 20 ); // 30 sum(); // 0 👆 Click to reveal Alias Any Type C# 12 The using directive can now create aliases for any type — not just named types. Includes tuples, arrays, and pointers! // Alias a tuple type — much more readable! using Point = ( double X, double Y); using StudentScore = ( string Name, int Score); Point origin = ( 0 , 0 ); Point target = ( 3.5 , 7.2 ); StudentScore best = ( "Alice" , 98 ); Console . WriteLine ( $"Best student: {best.Name}" ); Before (C# 11) — named types only // ✅ Only named types worked using MyList = System.Collections.Generic. List < string >; // ❌ Tuples? NO // using Point = (double X, double Y); // ❌ Arrays? NO // using Matrix = int[][]; After (C# 12) — any type! // ✅ Named types (still works) using MyList = System.Collections.Generic. List < string >; // ✅ Tuples using Point = ( double X, double Y); // ✅ Arrays using Matrix = int [][]; More examples — arrays & nullable types: // Alias for arrays using Row = int []; using Grid = int [][]; // Alias for nullable using OptionalName = string ?; using MaybeInt = int ?; OptionalName nickname = null ; // no warning! Grid board = new int [ 3 ][]; Note: Type aliases are file-scoped by default. To make them available across the project, combine with global using : // GlobalUsings.cs global using Point = ( double X, double Y); // ✅ available everywhere Quick preview: We'll use this more in Week 2 when we explore records and data modeling. For now, just know that using aliases are much more powerful in C# 12. 👆 Click to reveal Null-Conditional Assignment C# 14 You already know ?. for reading through null safely. C# 14 finally lets you use ?. for writing too! ❌ Before (C# 13 and earlier) // The old null-check-then-assign pattern if (order is not null ) { order.Status = "Processed" ; order.UpdatedAt = DateTime .UtcNow; } // Nested? Even more verbose! if (customer is not null ) { if (customer.Address is not null ) { customer.Address.City = "Cairo" ; } } ✅ After (C# 14) // Clean null-conditional assignment order ?. Status = "Processed" ; order ?. UpdatedAt = DateTime .UtcNow; // Chaining works too! customer ?. Address ?. City = "Cairo" ; // Combine with ??= config ?. Settings ??= new Settings (); Key behavior: If the left side is null , the right side never executes — no wasted work, no side effects. Also works with += , -= , and ??= . Also works with +=, -= operators: // Events — safe subscribe/unsubscribe button ?. Click += OnClick; button ?. Click -= OnClick; // Counters logger ?. ErrorCount += 1 ; // Collections order ?. Items ?. Count += quantity; ?. evolution — reading vs writing: C# 6 — Read only // ✅ Safe reading var city = customer ?. Address ?. City; // ❌ Safe writing? NO! // customer?.Address?.City = "Cairo"; C# 14 — Read + Write // ✅ Safe reading (same) var city = customer ?. Address ?. City; // ✅ Safe writing (NEW!) customer ?. Address ?. City = "Cairo" ; 👆 Click to reveal The String Escaping Problem Before C# 11, writing strings with special characters was painful. Especially for JSON, SQL, HTML, and regex patterns. Try writing this JSON as a C# string: // What we WANT: { "name": "Alice", "age": 25 } // What we had to WRITE in C#: string json = "{ \"name\": \"Alice\", \"age\": 25 }" ; // Or with verbatim strings (@): string json = @"{ ""name"": ""Alice"", ""age"": 25 }" ; The pain: Every " needs escaping. Every { in interpolation needs doubling. Multi-line strings lose their formatting. It gets worse with SQL, Regex, and file paths: // SQL string sql = "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = \"Alice\"" ; // Regex — almost unreadable string pattern = "\\d{3}-\\d{3}-\\d{4}" ; // File paths string path = "C:\\Users\\Alice\\Documents\\file.txt" ; 👆 Click to reveal Raw String Literals C# 11 Use three or more quotes """ to create a raw string. No escaping needed! The string contains exactly what you type. Before (escaped mess) string json = @"{ ""name"": ""Alice"", ""age"": 25, ""active"": true }" ; After (clean!) string json = """ { "name": "Alice", "age": 25, "active": true } """ ; Works beautifully with SQL, Regex, and HTML: // SQL — no escaping quotes! string sql = """ SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = "Alice" AND Role = "Admin" """ ; // Regex — backslashes stay as-is! string pattern = """\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}""" ; // HTML — just paste it in! string html = """ <div class="card"> <h1>Hello "World"</h1> </div> """ ; Interpolation with raw strings — use $""" string name = "Alice" ; int age = 25 ; string json = $""" {{ "name": "{name}", "age": {age} }} """ ; // Need literal { } ? Use {{ }} // Need literal {name}? Use $$ with {{name}} 👆 Click to reveal Raw String Interpolation C# 11 Problem: JSON uses { and } , which conflict with interpolation {expression} . Solution: Use $$""" — then interpolation requires {{expression}} (double braces), and single { } are treated as literal text! string name = "Alice" ; int age = 25 ; string json = $$""" { "name": "{{name}}", "age": {{age}}, "generated": "{{DateTime.Now:yyyy-MM-dd}}" } """ ; // Output: // { // "name": "Alice", // "age": 25, // "generated": "2024-12-15" // } Real-world: HTML template with $$""" string title = "Dashboard" ; string user = "Alice" ; string page = $$""" <html> <head><title>{{title}}</title></head> <body> <h1>Welcome, {{user}}</h1> <style> .card { border: 1px solid #ccc; } </style> </body> </html> """ ; Common Mistake — using $ instead of $$ with JSON: // ❌ WRONG: $ treats { as interpolation start string json = $""" { "name": "{name}" } """ ; // CS1733: Expected expression // ✅ FIX: Use $$ so single { } are literal string json = $$""" { "name": "{{name}}" } """ ; // Works! 👆 Click to reveal Newlines in Interpolation C# 11 Before C# 11, interpolation expressions {...} had to be on a single line . Now you can spread them across multiple lines for readability. Before (crammed) int a = 10 , b = 20 , c = 30 ; // Crammed on one line! string msg = $"Result: {(a > b ? a * c : b * c)}" ; // ✅ Works but hard to read on one line After (readable) int a = 10 , b = 20 , c = 30 ; // Multi-line — much more readable! string msg = $"Result: {( a > b ? a * c : b * c )}" ; // ✅ Parentheses needed for ternary inside interpolation Especially useful when combining with ternary operators, LINQ, or method calls inside interpolated strings. Switch expression inside interpolation: int score = 85 ; decimal price = 100m ; string result = $"Discount: {( score switch { >= 90 => price * 0.2m , >= 80 => price * 0.1m , >= 70 => price * 0.05m , _ => 0m } )}" ; // "Discount: 10.0" Note: This works with all interpolated strings — regular $"" , verbatim $@"" , and raw $""" . It's not limited to raw strings! 👆 Click to reveal What We Learned Today Feature Version What It Does Top-level statements C# 9 No class / Main ceremony in Program.cs Target-typed new() C# 9 Less type repetition File-scoped namespaces C# 10 One less indentation level per file Global usings C# 10 Write using once for entire project Implicit usings C# 10 Common namespaces auto-imported Const interpolation C# 10 $"" works with const Raw strings """ C# 11 No more escaping nightmares $$""" interpolation C# 11 JSON + interpolation = easy Newlines in interpolation C# 11 Multi-line expressions inside {} Alias any type C# 12 using aliases for tuples, arrays, etc. Default lambda params C# 12 Lambdas get default values Null-conditional assign C# 14 obj?.Prop = value — safe writes Key takeaway: None of these change program behavior — they only change how we write and read code. The compiler produces the same IL output! 👆 Click to reveal When to Use What? Feature ✅ Use When ❌ Avoid When Top-level statements Console apps, scripts, quick tools Large apps with complex startup File-scoped namespaces Always! Less indentation, no downside Multiple namespaces in one file (rare) Global usings Namespaces used in 5+ files Niche namespaces used once Target-typed new() Type is clear from left side Would make code less readable Raw strings """ JSON, SQL, HTML, regex, paths Simple one-line strings Const interpolation API endpoints, config constants Non-const values or method calls Alias any type Complex tuples, repeated generic types Simple well-known types Default lambda params Callbacks with optional config When a named method is clearer Null-conditional assign Optional updates, event handlers When null means a real error Set your C# version in .csproj: <!-- Use latest C# version --> < PropertyGroup > < LangVersion >latest</ LangVersion > </ PropertyGroup > <!-- Or specify exact version --> < PropertyGroup > < LangVersion >12.0</ LangVersion > </ PropertyGroup > 👆 Click to reveal Next Week: Modern Data Modeling Week 2: Records, Init, Required & More What's Coming Records — data-focused types Init-only setters — safe initialization Required members — compiler-enforced field keyword C# 14 — cleaner auto-properties Primary constructors — less boilerplate Collection expressions — [1, 2, 3] Homework Look at any class you've written in the main sessions. Could it be simpler? We'll connect these features directly to the OOP concepts you're learning. Great work today! 👆 Click to reveal ◀ Previous Next ▶ 1 / 20 📋 Menu 🔴 Laser ⛶ Slide Navigation ×

[S01] Threading | Workshop 05   |   Threads · Thread Pool · Synchronization
[S02] Session Agenda | .NET Track | 01 | Process vs Thread | What a thread really is, and what it costs | 02 | Creating & Controlling Threads | Start · Join · Sleep · passing data in | 03 | Foreground vs Background | The thread that quietly disappears | 04 | Thread Pool | Borrow a thread instead of building one | 05 | Race Conditions & lock | Why count++ is not one operation | 06 | Deadlock | Two threads, two locks, and nobody moves
[S03] Process  vs  Thread | .NET Track | Process | Thread | What it is | A running program | One path of execution inside a process | Memory | Its own private address space | Shares everything with its siblings | Cost to create | Heavy — milliseconds | Light — but still ~1 MB of stack each | Talking to each other | IPC: files, pipes, sockets | Just a shared variable | If one crashes | The others are untouched | The whole process goes down | How many | At least one thread inside it | Never alone — it needs a process | One line to hold on to: | threads share memory. That is the whole reason they are fast, and the whole reason they are dangerous.
[S04] When Threads Help — and When They Hurt | .NET Track | CPU-bound work | Resizing 500 images, hashing, heavy maths | Split across cores and the wall-clock time really drops | Ceiling = the number of cores you actually have | More threads than cores buys you nothing | I/O-bound work | Reading files, calling an API, querying a database | The thread is doing nothing but waiting | Overlap the waiting and the app stays responsive | This is where async/await beats raw threads | The price tag | About 1 MB of stack reserved for every thread | Context switching costs real CPU time | Shared state now needs locking, and locking needs care | A thread is not free — never start one "just in case" | Concurrency | = several things in progress. | Parallelism | = several things running at the same instant. One core gives you the first, never the second.
[S05] Creating a Thread — four ways to start one | .NET Track | Code | // 1 - a method with no parameters | Thread t1 = new Thread(DoWork); | // 2 - a lambda | Thread t2 = new Thread(() => Console.WriteLine("hi")); | // 3 - ParameterizedThreadStart: exactly one object | Thread t3 = new Thread(DoWorkWithData); | t3.Start(42);            // the argument goes here | static void DoWorkWithData(object? data) | { | int n = (int)data!;  // you must cast it back | } | // 4 - a lambda capturing locals (best for many values) | int id = 7; | Thread t4 = new Thread(() => Register(id, "Sara")); | t1.Start();  t2.Start();  t4.Start(); | Watch out for | new Thread(...) does nothing yet — Start() is what asks the OS for a thread | Calling Start() twice throws ThreadStateException | ParameterizedThreadStart takes exactly one object — everything gets cast | A lambda is type-safe and takes as many values as you like — prefer it | Capturing a for-loop variable shares ONE variable across every thread — copy it into a local first
[S06] The Thread Object — what you can read and set | .NET Track | Member | Access | What it gives you | Thread.CurrentThread | static | The thread running this very line | ManagedThreadId | read only | A unique number from the CLR — not the OS id | Name | write once | For you and the debugger only — set it, then leave it alone | IsAlive | read only | True from Start() until the method returns | IsBackground | get / set | Set it BEFORE Start(). See the next slide | Priority | get / set | A hint to the scheduler, nothing more — never a fix | ThreadState | read only | Unstarted → Running → WaitSleepJoin → Stopped | About Priority: | raising it does not make a slow thread fast — it only changes who the OS prefers when both are ready to run. | If your code needs a priority change to work correctly, the real bug is somewhere else.
[S07] Foreground  vs  Background Threads | .NET Track | The process stays alive while ANY foreground thread is still running. Background threads get no such promise. | Foreground  (the default) | Thread t = new Thread(Work); | // t.IsBackground is false | t.Start(); | Console.WriteLine("Main ends here"); | // Main returns... and the app waits | Main ends here | Worker 1 | Worker 2 | Worker 3 | Main finished long ago. The process is still alive only because this thread is. | Background | Thread t = new Thread(Work); | t.IsBackground = true;   // BEFORE Start | t.Start(); | Console.WriteLine("Main ends here"); | // Main returns... and the app dies | Main ends here | The worker is killed mid-sentence. No exception, no finally block, no warning.
[S08] Join and Sleep — making Main wait | .NET Track | Code | static void Work(string name) | { | Thread.Sleep(500);        // pretend to be busy | Console.WriteLine($"{name} done"); | } | Thread[] workers = new Thread[3]; | for (int i = 0; i < workers.Length; i++) | { | int copy = i;             // copy the loop variable! | workers[i] = new Thread(() => Work($"Worker {copy}")); | workers[i].Start(); | } | // wait for every one of them | foreach (Thread w in workers) | { | w.Join(); | } | Console.WriteLine("All workers finished"); | Output | Worker 1 done | Worker 0 done | Worker 2 done | All workers finished | The first three lines come out in any order — that is threading, not a bug | The last line is guaranteed last, because of Join() | Join() blocks the CALLING thread until the other one ends | Sleep(0) gives up the rest of your time slice; Sleep never means "exactly this long"
[S09] Thread Pool — borrow instead of build | .NET Track | Queue the work, forget the thread | using System.Threading; | CountdownEvent done = new CountdownEvent(5); | for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) | { | int copy = i; | ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(state => | { | Console.WriteLine($"item {copy}"); | done.Signal(); | }); | } | done.Wait();      // pool threads are background — | // without this they may never run | Console.WriteLine("all queued work finished"); | new Thread  vs  ThreadPool | Thread | Pool | Who creates it | You | The runtime | Reused after? | No | Yes | Background? | No | Always | Good for | Long work | Short work | Can you Join it? | Yes | No | The pool already has threads warmed up — queuing costs almost nothing | Never block a pool thread for a long time; you are starving everyone else | Task, async/await and Parallel.For all sit on top of this same pool
[S10] Race Condition — count++ is not one operation | .NET Track | The bug | int count = 0; | void Add() | { | for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) | { | count++;      // looks atomic. it is not. | } | } | // two threads, both calling Add() | Expected : 2000000 | Actual   : 1362548   <- different every run | Nothing here is random. The two threads simply overlapped in a different place each time. | What count++ really is | 1 | READ | load count into a register | 2 | ADD | add 1 inside the register | 3 | WRITE | store it back to memory | A reads 100 | B reads 100      <- before A wrote | A writes 101 | B writes 101     <- one increment lost | Three steps means two windows where another thread can cut in.
[S11] lock — one thread at a time | .NET Track | The fix | private static readonly object _gate = new object(); | private static int _count; | void Add() | { | for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) | { | lock (_gate) | { | _count++; | } | } | } | lock (x) { } | is syntax sugar: the compiler emits Monitor.Enter before your code and Monitor.Exit inside a finally — so the lock is released even if the body throws. | What to lock on | YES | a private readonly object, used for nothing else | NO | lock(this) — anyone holding your object can lock it too | NO | lock("key") — strings are interned and shared process-wide | NO | a public field, or typeof(X) | Keep it short: | every line inside a lock is a line the other threads spend waiting.
[S12] lock  ·  Interlocked  ·  Monitor | .NET Track | Tool | Protects | Why you would pick it | The catch | lock (obj) { } | Any block of code | Simple, and you cannot forget to release it | Blocks. No timeout, ever | Interlocked.Increment | One int or long | No blocking at all — a single CPU instruction | Only ++, --, Add, Exchange | Monitor.TryEnter | Any block of code | You can give up after a timeout | You must release it yourself, in a finally | Mutex | Across processes | Works between two running apps | Far slower — it goes through the OS | Start with lock. | Move to Interlocked only when the whole critical section is one counter — then it is both faster and shorter. | Reach for Monitor.TryEnter when waiting forever is not an acceptable outcome, and for Mutex only when two separate processes must agree.
[S13] Deadlock — two threads, two locks, nobody moves | .NET Track | How to write one by accident | // Thread 1 | lock (_lockA) | { | Thread.Sleep(100); | lock (_lockB) { Transfer(); } | } | // Thread 2  — the SAME two locks, reversed | lock (_lockB) | { | Thread.Sleep(100); | lock (_lockA) { Transfer(); } | } | T1 holds A and waits for B.
T2 holds B and waits for A. | Neither will ever let go. The app does not crash — it just stops. | How to avoid it | Always take locks in the SAME order everywhere — this one rule kills most deadlocks | Hold one lock at a time if you possibly can | Never call unknown code (an event, a callback) while holding a lock | Use Monitor.TryEnter with a timeout when you cannot guarantee the order | if (Monitor.TryEnter(_lockB, 500)) | { | try { Transfer(); } | finally { Monitor.Exit(_lockB); } | }
[S14] Which One Do I Actually Use? | .NET Track | Tool | Built for | Pick it when | new Thread(...) | Long-running or blocking work that must not touch the pool | You need Join, a name, or a foreground thread | ThreadPool | Short background jobs, fire and forget | You do not need a result and do not need to wait | Task | Almost everything else | You want a result, exceptions, or continuations | async / await | I/O — files, HTTP, database | The thread would only be sitting there waiting | Parallel.For | The same CPU work over a big collection | Data parallelism, split across cores | Everything below the first row runs on the same thread pool. | Understanding Thread is what makes Task make sense later — but in real code you will reach for Task first. | Rule of thumb: raw threads for control, Task for results, async/await for waiting.
[S15] Thank You | See You Next Session

[P01] Database 
ASP.Net Course
 
​
​
​
​
​
​
            
 
 
Restaurant Management System 
 
A restaurant chain wants to develop a database system to manage its 
operations, including branches, staff, customers, menus, and orders . The 
Restaurant chain operates several branches : 
●​ Each Branch with a unique branch ID, name, address, contact number, and opening 
hours. 
●​ Each branch is managed by a branch manager and has several employees such as 
chefs, waiters, and cashiers. 
●​ Every employee has an employee ID, full name, position, salary, date of hire, and 
contact information. 
●​ Employees are assigned to specific branches, and some may work shifts across 
multiple branches when needed. 
●​ Each branch also maintains shift schedules, recording which employees worked on 
specific dates and time slots. 
 
The restaurant offers a wide variety of menu items : 
●​ each identified by a unique item ID, name, description, price, and category (e.g., 
appetizer, main course, dessert, beverage). Some items may have optional add-ons 
or variations, such as extra cheese or large size, which should also be represented. 
●​ Menu items can appear in different branches, and each branch may have its own 
price adjustments or availability rules based on local preferences. 
 
Customers can dine in, order takeaway, or request delivery : 
●​ Each customer has a customer ID, full name, phone number, email, and loyalty points 
balance. Customers may visit multiple branches and place several orders over time. 
●​ An order is identified by an order ID and includes order type (dine-in, takeaway, 
delivery), date and time, total amount, payment method (cash, card, wallet), and 
status (pending, preparing, served, completed, canceled). 
●​ Orders are linked to a specific branch and handled by a responsible staff member 
(typically a waiter or cashier). 
●​ Each order contains one or more order items, representing the menu items 
purchased. For each order item, details such as quantity, unit price, special notes 
(e.g., “no onions”), and any selected add-ons should be stored. 
●​ Because the same menu item can appear in multiple orders, this relationship needs 
an associative entity. 
1
[P02] The restaurant also keeps records of inventory, where each branch maintains 
its stock of ingredients : 
●​ Each ingredient has an ingredient ID, name, unit (kg, liter, piece), and current 
quantity. 
●​ Menu items are prepared using multiple ingredients, and each ingredient can be 
used in several menu items. 
●​ Therefore, the recipe relationship between menu items and ingredients should 
include the required quantity of each ingredient per serving. 
 
Additionally, customers can leave feedback for orders they’ve completed : 
●​ Each feedback record includes a feedback ID, date, rating, comments, and references 
the corresponding customer and order. 
 
2

Aya Ali
21 Workshopes
select * from Patients

-- Offset -->> Skip
-- Fetch -->> Take

select *
from Patients
order by Id
offset 5 row
fetch next 5 rows only
-- Cant work without Order By


-- offset can work without fetch
select * from Patients
order by id
offset 0 row
fetch next 10 rows only


-- top

select top(10) *
from Patients


--------------------------------
-- Pagination

-- the first page [1 -> 5]  offset 0 fetch 5
-- the Second page [6 -> 10]  offset 5 fetch 5
-- the Third page [11 -> 15]  offset 10  fetch 5

-- Offset (PageNumber-1) * PageSize
-- Fetch PageSize

-- First Page
-- Offset (1-1)*5 -> 0
-- fetch -> 5

-- second Page
-- Offset (2-1)*5 -->
-- fetch 5

-- Q1 

select c.Name , c.Salary
from Consultants c
order by Salary  desc, id 
offset 0 row
fetch next 5 rows only

-- Q2

declare @PageNumber int = 3 ;
Declare @PageSize int= 10 ;

select *
from Patients p
order by id
offset (@PageNumber -1) *@PageSize row
fetch next @PageSize rows only


--Q3
select * from Consultants
order by Salary 


SELECT Name FROM Consultants
ORDER BY Salary 
OFFSET 2 ROWS FETCH NEXT 2 ROWS ONLY;
