--insert into

--insert into OldEmployees (col01 varchar(10) , col02 int , col03 varchar(10))
--select name(varchar(10)) , age int , address varchar(10)
--from employee
--where age > 50


create table HighSalaryNurses
(
id int primary key identity(10,10) ,
NurseName nvarchar(100) not null ,
salary decimal(18 ,0)

)

insert into HighSalaryNurses (NurseName , salary)
select Name , Salary
from Nurses
where Salary > 7000

-----------------------------------------------
-- Select Into


select name , Salary
into HighSalaryNursesv2
from Nurses
where Salary > 7000

drop table HighSalaryNursesv2

-- not copy with constraints or pk , fk

select Number , name , Salary
into HighSalaryNursesv3
from Nurses
where Salary > 7000


--  Insert Into vs Select Into

--Create ICUPatients (Id, Name, DOB), then copy into it all patients of the ward 'Intensive Care Unit (ICU)' (use a JOIN with Wards).

select p.Id , p.Name , p.DOB
into ICUPatients 
from Patients p join Wards w
on p.WardId = w.Id
where w.Name ='Intensive Care Unit (ICU)'

select * from ICUPatients

--Table WardSummary (WardName, PatientsCount) already exists. Fill it with the number of patients per ward.

create table WardSummary
(
 wardName nvarchar(100) ,
 patientCount int

)

insert into WardSummary
select w.Name , count(*) as 'Patiant count'
from Patients p join Wards w on p.WardId=w.Id
group by w.Name

select * from WardSummary

-- Q4 Fill NurseSalaryReport (NurseName, AnnualSalary) for all nurses using the existing function dbo.CalculateAnnualSalary().


create table NurseSalaryReport
(
 wardName nvarchar(100) ,
 AnnualSalary decimal(18,0)

)

create or alter function dbo.CalculateAnnualSalary(@NurseId int)
returns decimal(18,0)
as
begin
declare @AnnualSalary  decimal(18,0)
select @AnnualSalary = n.Salary*12
from Nurses n
where n.Number = @NurseId
return @AnnualSalary
end

go

insert into NurseSalaryReport 
select Name , dbo.CalculateAnnualSalary(number)
from Nurses

select * from NurseSalaryReport

-- Advanced DML

--Update

update e
set e.Salary = e.Salary+ 1000
from Employee e join Branch b on e.EmployeeId = b.ManagerId
where b.Name = 'Dokki'

-- Delete


delete b
from Employee e join Branch b on e.EmployeeId = b.ManagerId 
where e.FullName ='Hellana'


-- Merge 

--UPDATE with JOIN: raise the salary by 10% for nurses who serve in the ward 'Intensive Care Unit (ICU)'.


update n
set n.Salary = n.Salary *1.1  -- salary + salary *0.1
from Nurses n join Wards w on n.ServesInWardId = w.Id
where w.Name = 'Intensive Care Unit (ICU)'


--DELETE with JOIN: delete all DrugAdministrations of patients in the ward 'Emergency Department'. How many rows?

delete da
from DrugAdministrations da 
join patients p on p.Id=da.PatientId
join Wards w on p.WardId = w.Id
where w.Name = 'Emergency Department'



--Add 1000 to consultants with Salary < 12000 and use OUTPUT to show the name, old salary and new salary.

update c
set Salary = Salary + 1000
output
inserted.Name ,
deleted.Salary 'Old Salary' ,
inserted.Salary 'New Salary'
from Consultants c
where Salary< 12000

--NewWards = (4, 'Pediatrics & Neonatal'), (6, 'Oncology'). What is in Wards after this MERGE?

create table NewWards
(
 id int ,
 name nvarchar(100)
)

insert into NewWards values
 (4, 'Pediatrics & Neonatal'), (6, 'Oncology')


MERGE Wards t USING NewWards s ON t.Id = s.Id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.Name = s.Name
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT VALUES (s.Id, s.Name);

select * from Wards
select * from NewWards

[S03] OFFSET - FETCH
[S04] OFFSET - FETCH | OFFSET – FETCH | lets you | skip | a number of rows, then | return | a specific number of rows from a | sorted | result — the standard way to do | paging | in SQL Server. | SYNTAX | SELECT | column1, column2, ... | FROM | TableName | ORDER | BY | column1 | -- required | OFFSET | n | ROWS | -- rows to skip | FETCH | NEXT | m | ROWS | ONLY | ; | -- rows to return | i | Think of a | book | : ORDER BY numbers the pages, | OFFSET | = pages you flip past, | FETCH | = pages you actually read. | KEY POINTS | ✔ | ORDER BY | is mandatory — OFFSET-FETCH works on a | sorted | result. | ✔ | OFFSET n ROWS | = how many rows to | skip | (0 = skip nothing). | ✔ | FETCH NEXT m ROWS ONLY | = how many rows to | return | after skipping. | ✔ | OFFSET can be used | without FETCH | (skip n, return the rest) — but | FETCH needs OFFSET | . | ✔ | ROW / ROWS | and | FIRST / NEXT | mean the same thing. Available since | SQL Server 2012 | . | THE RULE IN ACTION | ✔ Correct | SELECT | * | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | OFFSET | 0 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 5 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | ✘ Error: OFFSET - FETCH without ORDER BY | SELECT | * | FROM | Products | OFFSET | 0 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 5 | ROWS | ONLY | ;
[S05] OFFSET - FETCH Example | Skip the | 2 most expensive | products, then return the | next 3 | — ordered by | Price DESC | . | Products | ordered by Price DESC · 8 rows | Id | ProductName | Price | Status | 1 | Laptop | 1000 | Skipped (OFFSET 2) | 6 | Desk | 300 | Skipped (OFFSET 2) | 4 | Monitor | 200 | ✔ Fetched | 5 | Chair | 150 | ✔ Fetched | 7 | Headphones | 80 | ✔ Fetched | 8 | Webcam | 60 | Not returned | 3 | Keyboard | 50 | Not returned | 2 | Mouse | 20 | Not returned | QUERY | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | OFFSET | 2 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Result | 3 rows | Id | ProductName | Price | 4 | Monitor | 200 | 5 | Chair | 150 | 7 | Headphones | 80 | i | OFFSET 2 | skipped Laptop and Desk  → | FETCH NEXT 3 | returned Monitor, Chair, Headphones  →  the remaining rows were | not returned | .
[S06] Paging with OFFSET - FETCH | OFFSET (PageNumber − 1) × PageSize ROWS   FETCH NEXT PageSize ROWS ONLY | QUERY — GET PAGE 2 | DECLARE | @PageNumber | INT | = | 2 | ; | DECLARE | @PageSize | INT | = | 3 | ; | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Id | OFFSET | ( | @PageNumber | - | 1 | ) * | @PageSize | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | @PageSize | ROWS | ONLY | ; | IN .NET — EF CORE TRANSLATES Skip / Take INTO OFFSET - FETCH | var page = context.Products | .OrderBy(p => p.Id) | .Skip((pageNumber - | 1 | ) * pageSize) | .Take(pageSize) | .ToList(); | PAGES  (PageSize = 3) | Page 1 | 1  Laptop | 2  Mouse | 3  Keyboard | Page 2 | 4  Monitor | 5  Chair | 6  Desk | Page 3 | 7  Headphones | 8  Webcam | @PageNumber | OFFSET | FETCH NEXT | Rows returned | 1 | 0 | 3 | Ids 1 – 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 | Ids 4 – 6 | 3 | 6 | 3 | Ids 7 – 8 | i | The | last page | may return | fewer rows | (page 3 → 2 rows). A page | after the end | returns | no rows | — not an error.
[S07] TOP vs OFFSET - FETCH | TOP  vs  OFFSET – FETCH | Feature | TOP | OFFSET – FETCH | Skip rows | ✘ No | ✔ Yes | ORDER BY | Optional | ✔ Required | Standard | T-SQL only | ANSI SQL standard | WITH TIES / PERCENT | ✔ Supported | ✘ Not supported | Best for | First N rows | Paging (page 1, 2, 3 …) | SAME RESULT, TWO WAYS | SELECT | TOP | ( | 3 | ) * | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | ; | -- is the same as | SELECT | * | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | OFFSET | 0 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | COMMON MISTAKE — UNSTABLE PAGES | ✘ Paging on a non-unique column | ORDER | BY | Price | OFFSET | 3 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Products with the | same price | may show up on | two pages | — or on | none | . | ✔ Add a unique tie-breaker column | ORDER | BY | Price, Id | OFFSET | 3 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | The order is now | always the same | → every row appears on | exactly one | page.
[S08] Paging with ROW_NUMBER() | Before SQL Server 2012 there was no OFFSET-FETCH — paging was done with | ROW_NUMBER() | . You'll still meet it in older projects. | QUERY — PAGE 2  (PageSize = 3) | SELECT | * | FROM | ( | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price, | ROW_NUMBER | () | OVER | ( | ORDER | BY | Id) | AS | RowNum | FROM | Products | ) | AS | t | WHERE | t. | RowNum | BETWEEN | 4 | AND | 6 | ; | -- page 2 | SAME RESULT WITH OFFSET - FETCH  (shorter & clearer) | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Id | OFFSET | 3 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Inner query (t) | RowNum 4 – 6 returned | Id | ProductName | Price | RowNum | 1 | Laptop | 1000 | 1 | 2 | Mouse | 20 | 2 | 3 | Keyboard | 50 | 3 | 4 | Monitor | 200 | 4 | 5 | Chair | 150 | 5 | 6 | Desk | 300 | 6 | 7 | Headphones | 80 | 7 | 8 | Webcam | 60 | 8 | ! | ROW_NUMBER() can't be used directly in | WHERE | — that's why we wrap it in a | subquery | (or a CTE).
[S09] OFFSET - FETCH — Practice | Use the | Hospital | database (restore | Hospital.bak | ) — tables | Consultants | and | Patients | . | Q1 | WRITE | Return the | 5 highest-paid consultants | (Name, Salary) using OFFSET - FETCH. | Q2 | WRITE | Show | page 3 | of the | Patients | list ordered by | Id | , with a page size of | 10 | . Which Ids appear? | Q3 | PREDICT | What does this query return? | SELECT | Name | FROM | Consultants | ORDER | BY | Salary | OFFSET | 2 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 2 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Q4 | FIX THE BUG | Paging consultants | 2 per page | : Dr. Amira El-Din sometimes shows on | two pages | . Why? Fix it. | SELECT | Name, Salary | FROM | Consultants | ORDER | BY | Salary | DESC | OFFSET | 2 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 2 | ROWS | ONLY | ;
[S10] Insert Based on Select
[S11] Insert Based on Select | INSERT INTO … SELECT | copies the result of a query into an | existing | table — instead of typing VALUES row by row, the rows come from a | SELECT | . | SYNTAX | INSERT | INTO | TargetTable | (col1, col2, ...) | SELECT | col1, col2, ... | FROM | SourceTable | WHERE | condition; | -- optional | i | Like copying rows from one Excel sheet and | pasting | them into another sheet that | already has its own headers | . | KEY POINTS | ✔ | The | target table must already exist | (unlike SELECT INTO). | ✔ | Columns must match in | number | and | order | , with | compatible data types | . | ✔ | Always write the | target column list | — safer and clearer. | ✔ | The SELECT can use | WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY | , expressions and constant values. | ✔ | Target | constraints | (PK, FK, CHECK, NOT NULL) are still checked — | IDENTITY | values are generated automatically. | THE RULE IN ACTION | ✔ Correct | INSERT | INTO | ArchivedEmployees (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | FROM | Employees; | ✘ Error: SELECT returns fewer columns than the insert list | INSERT | INTO | ArchivedEmployees (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName | FROM | Employees;
[S12] Insert Based on Select – Example | Copy the employees with | Salary > 20000 | into the | existing | table | HighSalaryEmployees | . | Employees | source table · 4 rows | EmployeeID | EmployeeName | DepartmentID | Salary | 1 | Ali Hassan | 1 | 25000 | 2 | Sara Mohamed | 2 | 18000 | 3 | Mona Ali | 1 | 22000 | 4 | Youssef Ibrahim | 3 | 16000 | HighSalaryEmployees | before · 1 row | Id (IDENTITY) | Name | Salary | 1 | Khaled Omar | 30000 | QUERY | INSERT | INTO | HighSalaryEmployees | (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | FROM | Employees | WHERE | Salary > | 20000 | ; | HighSalaryEmployees | after · (2 rows affected) | Id | Name | Salary | 1 | Khaled Omar | 30000 | existing | 2 | Ali Hassan | 25000 | ✔ inserted | 3 | Mona Ali | 22000 | ✔ inserted | i | The old row ( | Khaled Omar | ) is | kept | — INSERT … SELECT | adds | rows. | Id | is not in the column list because | IDENTITY | generates it.
[S13] Insert Select With JOIN & Expressions | Fill | EmployeeReport | with each employee's | department name | , | annual | salary and | today's date | . | QUERY | INSERT | INTO | EmployeeReport | (EmployeeName, DepartmentName, AnnualSalary, ReportDate) | SELECT | e.EmployeeName, | d.DepartmentName, | e.Salary * | 12 | , | -- expression | GETDATE | () | -- function value | FROM | Employees e | JOIN | Departments d | ON | e.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID; | COLUMN MAPPING (BY POSITION) | e.EmployeeName | EmployeeName | d.DepartmentName | DepartmentName | e.Salary * 12 | AnnualSalary | GETDATE() | ReportDate | EmployeeReport | (4 rows affected) | EmployeeName | DepartmentName | AnnualSalary | ReportDate | Ali Hassan | IT | 300000 | 2026-09-28 | Sara Mohamed | HR | 216000 | 2026-09-28 | Mona Ali | IT | 264000 | 2026-09-28 | Youssef Ibrahim | Sales | 192000 | 2026-09-28 | ! | Columns are matched by | position | , not by name — the 3rd SELECT item goes into the 3rd column ( | AnnualSalary | ).
[S14] SELECT INTO vs INSERT INTO … SELECT | SELECT INTO  (Session 06) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | INTO | NewEmployees | -- created now | FROM | Employees; | INSERT INTO … SELECT  (OldEmployees must exist) | INSERT | INTO | OldEmployees | (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | FROM | Employees; | SELECT INTO | INSERT INTO … SELECT | Target table | Created automatically — must NOT exist | Must already exist | Existing rows | — (brand-new table) | Kept — new rows are appended | PK / constraints / indexes | Not copied | The target's own constraints apply | Columns | Taken from the SELECT list | You choose the target columns | Error when… | The table already exists | Column count / data types don't match | Best for | Quick copy / backup of data | Loading data into a designed table | i | Rule of thumb: | New table? | → SELECT INTO. | Table already designed? | → INSERT INTO … SELECT.
[S15] Insert Based on Select — Practice | Use the | Hospital | database (restore | Hospital.bak | ) — tables | Patients | , | Wards | , | Consultants | , | Nurses | . | Q1 | WRITE | Create | ICUPatients | (Id, Name, DOB), then copy into it all patients of the ward | 'Intensive Care Unit (ICU)' | (use a JOIN with Wards). | Q2 | WRITE | Table | WardSummary | (WardName, PatientsCount) already exists. Fill it with the | number of patients per ward | . | Q3 | FIX THE BUG | Why does this INSERT fail? Fix it. | INSERT | INTO | HighPaidConsultants (Id, Name) | SELECT | Id, Name, Salary | FROM | Consultants | WHERE | Salary > | 20000 | ; | Q4 | WRITE | Fill | NurseSalaryReport | (NurseName, AnnualSalary) for all nurses using the existing function | dbo.CalculateAnnualSalary() | .
[S16] Advanced DML
[S17] UPDATE with JOIN | UPDATE … JOIN | changes rows in one table using data or conditions from | another table | . | SYNTAX | UPDATE | t | SET | t | .Column = s.Column | FROM | TargetTable | t | JOIN | SourceTable s | ON | t | .Key = s.Key | WHERE | condition; | -- optional | EXAMPLE — 10% RAISE FOR THE IT DEPARTMENT | UPDATE | e | SET | e | .Salary = | e | .Salary * | 1 | . | 10 | FROM | Employees | e | JOIN | Departments d | ON | e | .DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID | WHERE | d.DepartmentName = | 'IT' | ; | Employees | (2 rows affected) | EmployeeID | EmployeeName | Department | Salary (before) | Salary (after) | 1 | Ali Hassan | IT | 25000 | 27500  ✔ | 2 | Sara Mohamed | HR | 18000 | 18000  (no change) | 3 | Mona Ali | IT | 22000 | 24200  ✔ | 4 | Youssef Ibrahim | Sales | 16000 | 16000  (no change) | i | Safety tip: run it as a | SELECT | first (same FROM / JOIN / WHERE) to see | exactly which rows | will change — then turn it into UPDATE.
[S18] DELETE with JOIN | DELETE … JOIN | removes rows from one table based on data in | another table | . | SYNTAX | DELETE | t | FROM | TargetTable | t | JOIN | OtherTable o | ON | t | .Key = o.Key | WHERE | condition; | EXAMPLE — DELETE THE SALES EMPLOYEES | DELETE | e | FROM | Employees | e | JOIN | Departments d | ON | e | .DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID | WHERE | d.DepartmentName = | 'Sales' | ; | Employees | (1 row affected) | EmployeeID | EmployeeName | DepartmentID | Salary | 1 | Ali Hassan | 1 | 25000 | kept | 2 | Sara Mohamed | 2 | 18000 | kept | 3 | Mona Ali | 1 | 22000 | kept | 4 | Youssef Ibrahim | 3 | 16000 | ✘ deleted | i | The alias after | DELETE | ( | DELETE e | ) tells SQL Server | which table | to delete from — | Departments is not touched | .
[S19] MERGE | MERGE | compares a | source | with a | target | and — in | one statement | — updates matching rows, inserts new ones and (optionally) deletes missing ones. | SYNTAX | MERGE | TargetTable | AS | t | USING | SourceTable | AS | s | ON | t.Key = s.Key | WHEN | MATCHED | THEN | UPDATE | SET | t.Col = s.Col | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | TARGET | THEN | INSERT | (Key, Col) | VALUES | (s.Key, s.Col) | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | SOURCE | THEN | DELETE | ; | -- MERGE must end with ; | THE 3 CASES | WHEN MATCHED  →  UPDATE | The key exists in | both | tables → update the target row. | NOT MATCHED BY TARGET  →  INSERT | The row is | only in the source | → it's new, insert it. | NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE  →  DELETE | The row is | only in the target | → it's gone from the source, delete it (optional). | i | Real use: | sync | a table with fresh data — e.g. load today's price list into | Products | in one step instead of separate UPDATE + INSERT + DELETE.
[S20] MERGE – Example | Sync | Products | (target) with today's price list | NewPrices | (source). | Products | target · before | Id | ProductName | Price | 1 | Laptop | 1000 | 2 | Mouse | 20 | 3 | Keyboard | 50 | NewPrices | source | Id | ProductName | Price | 1 | Laptop | 950 | 3 | Keyboard | 55 | 4 | Monitor | 200 | Ids | 1, 3 | in both → | UPDATE | Id | 4 | only in source → | INSERT | Id | 2 | only in target → | DELETE | QUERY | MERGE | Products | AS | t | USING | NewPrices | AS | s | ON | t.Id = s.Id | WHEN | MATCHED | THEN | UPDATE | SET | t.Price = s.Price | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | TARGET | THEN | INSERT | (Id, ProductName, Price) | VALUES | (s.Id, s.ProductName, s.Price) | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | SOURCE | THEN | DELETE | ; | Products | after | Id | ProductName | Price | What happened | 1 | Laptop | 950 | UPDATE | 3 | Keyboard | 55 | UPDATE | 4 | Monitor | 200 | INSERT | 2 | Mouse | 20 | DELETE
[S21] Advanced DML — Practice | Use the | Hospital | database (restore | Hospital.bak | ) — tables | Nurses | , | Wards | , | Patients | , | DrugAdministrations | , | Consultants | . | Q1 | WRITE | UPDATE with JOIN: | raise the salary by | 10% | for nurses who | serve in | the ward | 'Intensive Care Unit (ICU)' | . | Q2 | WRITE | DELETE with JOIN: | delete all | DrugAdministrations | of patients in the ward | 'Emergency Department' | . How many rows? | Q3 | WRITE | Add | 1000 | to consultants with | Salary < 12000 | and use | OUTPUT | to show the name, old salary and new salary. | Q4 | PREDICT | NewWards = (4, 'Pediatrics & Neonatal'), (6, 'Oncology'). What is in | Wards | after this MERGE? | MERGE | Wards t | USING | NewWards s | ON | t.Id = s.Id | WHEN | MATCHED | THEN | UPDATE | SET | t.Name = s.Name | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | THEN | INSERT | VALUES | (s.Id, s.Name);
[S22] Temporary Tables
[S23] Temporary Tables | A | temporary table | is a real table stored in | tempdb | and deleted | automatically | — perfect for holding | intermediate results | while you work. | KEY POINTS | ✔ | Stored in the system database | tempdb | → System Databases → tempdb → Temporary Tables. | ✔ | The name starts with | # | (local) or | ## | (global). | ✔ | Works like a normal table: | INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, JOIN | , PK, constraints and | indexes | . | ✔ | Dropped | automatically | — or drop it yourself with | DROP TABLE #Name | . | i | Like a | whiteboard | in a meeting room: you use it during the meeting, and it's | wiped | when the meeting ends. | TYPES | # | Local Temp Table   #TableName | Visible | only | in the | session | (query window) that created it. Dropped when that session | closes | . | ## | Global Temp Table   ##TableName | Visible to | all sessions | . Dropped when the creating session closes | and | no other session is still using it.
[S24] Creating Temporary Tables | ①  CREATE TABLE  +  INSERT | CREATE | TABLE | #Students | ( | Id | INT | PRIMARY | KEY | , | Name | VARCHAR | ( | 50 | ), | Grade | INT | ); | INSERT | INTO | #Students | VALUES | ( | 1 | , | 'Ahmed' | , | 90 | ), ( | 2 | , | 'Mona' | , | 85 | ); | SELECT | * | FROM | #Students | ; | ④  DROP IT YOURSELF | DROP | TABLE | #Students | ; | -- drop now | DROP | TABLE | IF | EXISTS | #HighSalary | ; | -- 2016+ | ②  SELECT INTO  #Temp  (structure + data in one step) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | INTO | #HighSalary | FROM | Employees | WHERE | Salary > | 20000 | ; | SELECT | * | FROM | #HighSalary | ; | ③  GLOBAL TEMP TABLE  (two #) | CREATE | TABLE | ##Settings | ( | SettingKey | VARCHAR | ( | 50 | ), | SettingValue | VARCHAR | ( | 100 | ) | ); | i | Tip: start your script with | DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #Name | so you can | re-run | it without the error | "There is already an object named …" | .
[S25] Temporary Table – Real Use Case | Find the employees who earn | more than their department's average | salary. | STEP 1 · SAVE THE AVERAGES IN A TEMP TABLE | SELECT | DepartmentID, | AVG | (Salary) | AS | AvgSalary | INTO | #DeptAvg | FROM | Employees | GROUP | BY | DepartmentID; | #DeptAvg | TEMP | in tempdb | DepartmentID | AvgSalary | 1 | 23500 | 2 | 18000 | 3 | 16000 | STEP 3 · CLEAN UP (optional) | DROP | TABLE | #DeptAvg | ; | STEP 2 · USE IT IN ANOTHER QUERY | SELECT | e.EmployeeName, e.Salary, t.AvgSalary | FROM | Employees e | JOIN | #DeptAvg | t | ON | e.DepartmentID = t.DepartmentID | WHERE | e.Salary > t.AvgSalary; | Result | 1 row | EmployeeName | Salary | AvgSalary | Ali Hassan | 25000 | 23500 | i | Why a temp table? | The averages are calculated | once | and can be reused in | many queries | — and a big query becomes | small, readable steps | .
[S26] Local vs Global in Action | SQLQuery1.sql  —  Session 1 | CREATE | TABLE | #LocalTemp | (Id | INT | ); | CREATE | TABLE | ##GlobalTemp | (Id | INT | ); | SELECT | * | FROM | #LocalTemp | ; | -- works | SELECT | * | FROM | ##GlobalTemp | ; | -- works | SQLQuery2.sql  —  Session 2 | SELECT | * | FROM | #LocalTemp | ; | -- Error: Invalid object name '#LocalTemp'. | SELECT | * | FROM | ##GlobalTemp | ; | -- works | Local  #Temp | Global  ##Temp | Visible to | Only the session that created it | All sessions (every query window / user) | Dropped when | That session closes | The creator closes AND nobody else uses it | Same name in 2 sessions? | ✔ Yes — each session gets its own copy | ✘ No — only one table with that name | i | In tempdb, a local temp table gets a long | suffix | (e.g. | #LocalTemp_______00000000001A | ) — that's how two sessions can both have their | own | #LocalTemp | .
[S27] Temp Table vs Table Variable
[S28] Temp Table vs Table Variable | TABLE VARIABLE | DECLARE | @TopProducts | TABLE | ( | Id | INT | , | Name | VARCHAR | ( | 50 | ) | ); | INSERT | INTO | @TopProducts | SELECT | TOP | ( | 3 | ) Id, ProductName | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | ; | SELECT | * | FROM | @TopProducts | ; | ! | A table variable lives only for the | current batch | — run the DECLARE and the queries | together | ( | GO | ends the batch). | #Temp Table  vs  @Table Variable | #Temp Table | @Table Variable | Create | CREATE TABLE #T (…) | DECLARE @T TABLE (…) | Scope | Session (until closed / dropped) | Current batch / procedure only | Stored in | tempdb | tempdb too (not only memory!) | Indexes | PK, UNIQUE + CREATE INDEX later | Only inside the DECLARE | Statistics | ✔ Yes → good for large data | ✘ No → best for small data | ROLLBACK | Changes are rolled back | Data is NOT rolled back | ALTER / SELECT INTO | ✔ Allowed | ✘ Not allowed | i | Quick rule: | small data, simple use | → @Table variable. | Large data, needs indexes, or used across batches | → #Temp table.
[S29] CTE
[S30] CTE (Common Table Expression) | A | CTE | (Common Table Expression) is a | named temporary result | written with | WITH | — it exists | only for the statement right after it | . | SYNTAX | WITH | CteName | AS | ( | SELECT | ... | ) | SELECT | * | FROM | CteName | ; | ✔ | Not stored | anywhere — it's just a named query (unlike #Temp in tempdb). | ✔ | Used | only | by the next statement — then it's gone. | ✔ | The statement | before | WITH must end with | ; | . | ✔ | Makes long queries | readable | — a cleaner way to write a derived table (Session 06). | SAME USE CASE AS #DeptAvg — WITHOUT A TEMP TABLE | WITH | DeptAvg | AS | ( | SELECT | DepartmentID, | AVG | (Salary) | AS | AvgSalary | FROM | Employees | GROUP | BY | DepartmentID | ) | SELECT | e.EmployeeName, e.Salary, d.AvgSalary | FROM | Employees e | JOIN | DeptAvg | d | ON | e.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID | WHERE | e.Salary > d.AvgSalary; | Result | 1 row | EmployeeName | Salary | AvgSalary | Ali Hassan | 25000 | 23500
[S31] CTE vs Temp Table vs Table Variable | CTE  vs  #Temp  vs  @Table | CTE | #Temp Table | @Table Variable | Lives for | One statement | The session | The batch / procedure | Stored | Not stored (just a query) | tempdb | tempdb | Reuse in many queries | ✘ No | ✔ Yes | ✔ Yes (same batch) | Indexes | ✘ No | ✔ Yes | Only inside DECLARE | Best for | Readable one-time queries | Big results reused many times | Small data in a batch / procedure | COMMON MISTAKE — USING A CTE TWICE | WITH | DeptAvg | AS | ( | SELECT | DepartmentID, | AVG | (Salary) | AS | AvgSalary | FROM | Employees | GROUP | BY | DepartmentID ) | SELECT | * | FROM | DeptAvg; | -- works | SELECT | * | FROM | DeptAvg; | -- Error: Invalid object name 'DeptAvg'. | HOW TO CHOOSE | Need it once, just for readability? | CTE | Big data, reused in many queries? | #Temp Table | Small data inside a batch / procedure? | @Table Variable
[S32] Temp Tables & CTE — Practice | Use the | Hospital | database (restore | Hospital.bak | ) — tables | DrugAdministrations | , | Patients | , | Nurses | , | Wards | . | Q1 | WRITE | Save each patient's | total drug Quantity | in | #PatientDrugTotals | , then show the | top 5 | patients by name. | Q2 | PREDICT | Session 1 runs the two SELECT INTO below. In | Session 2 | : | SELECT * FROM #ICU | and | SELECT * FROM ##ICU | → what happens? | SELECT | * | INTO | #ICU | FROM | Patients | WHERE | WardId = | 2 | ; | SELECT | * | INTO | ##ICU | FROM | Patients | WHERE | WardId = | 2 | ; | Q3 | WRITE | Using a | CTE | , show each | ward name | with the | number of nurses serving in it | — only wards with | more than 6 | nurses. | Q4 | CHOOSE | CTE, #Temp or @Table? | (a) Drug totals reused in | 5 reports | , needs an | index | . | (b) | 3 ward Ids | inside a stored procedure. | (c) Make | one long query | easier to read.
[S33] Thank You | See You Next Session

| DECLARE | @PageSize | INT | = | 3 | ; | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Id | OFFSET | ( | @PageNumber | - | 1 | ) * | @PageSize | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | @PageSize | ROWS | ONLY | ; | IN .NET — EF CORE TRANSLATES Skip / Take INTO OFFSET - FETCH | var page = context.Products | .OrderBy(p => p.Id) | .Skip((pageNumber - | 1 | ) * pageSize) | .Take(pageSize) | .ToList(); | PAGES  (PageSize = 3) | Page 1 | 1  Laptop | 2  Mouse | 3  Keyboard | Page 2 | 4  Monitor | 5  Chair | 6  Desk | Page 3 | 7  Headphones | 8  Webcam | @PageNumber | OFFSET | FETCH NEXT | Rows returned | 1 | 0 | 3 | Ids 1 – 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 | Ids 4 – 6 | 3 | 6 | 3 | Ids 7 – 8 | i | The | last page | may return | fewer rows | (page 3 → 2 rows). A page | after the end | returns | no rows | — not an error."}, {"label": "Slide 07", "t": 7, "text": "TOP vs OFFSET - FETCH | TOP  vs  OFFSET – FETCH | Feature | TOP | OFFSET – FETCH | Skip rows | ✘ No | ✔ Yes | ORDER BY | Optional | ✔ Required | Standard | T-SQL only | ANSI SQL standard | WITH TIES / PERCENT | ✔ Supported | ✘ Not supported | Best for | First N rows | Paging (page 1, 2, 3 …) | SAME RESULT, TWO WAYS | SELECT | TOP | ( | 3 | ) * | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | ; | -- is the same as | SELECT | * | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | OFFSET | 0 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | COMMON MISTAKE — UNSTABLE PAGES | ✘ Paging on a non-unique column | ORDER | BY | Price | OFFSET | 3 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Products with the | same price | may show up on | two pages | — or on | none | . | ✔ Add a unique tie-breaker column | ORDER | BY | Price, Id | OFFSET | 3 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | The order is now | always the same | → every row appears on | exactly one | page."}, {"label": "Slide 08", "t": 8, "text": "Paging with ROW_NUMBER() | Before SQL Server 2012 there was no OFFSET-FETCH — paging was done with | ROW_NUMBER() | . You'll still meet it in older projects. | QUERY — PAGE 2  (PageSize = 3) | SELECT | * | FROM | ( | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price, | ROW_NUMBER | () | OVER | ( | ORDER | BY | Id) | AS | RowNum | FROM | Products | ) | AS | t | WHERE | t. | RowNum | BETWEEN | 4 | AND | 6 | ; | -- page 2 | SAME RESULT WITH OFFSET - FETCH  (shorter & clearer) | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Id | OFFSET | 3 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Inner query (t) | RowNum 4 – 6 returned | Id | ProductName | Price | RowNum | 1 | Laptop | 1000 | 1 | 2 | Mouse | 20 | 2 | 3 | Keyboard | 50 | 3 | 4 | Monitor | 200 | 4 | 5 | Chair | 150 | 5 | 6 | Desk | 300 | 6 | 7 | Headphones | 80 | 7 | 8 | Webcam | 60 | 8 | ! | ROW_NUMBER() can't be used directly in | WHERE | — that's why we wrap it in a | subquery | (or a CTE)."}, {"label": "Slide 09", "t": 9, "text": "OFFSET - FETCH — Practice | Use the | Hospital | database (restore | Hospital.bak | ) — tables | Consultants | and | Patients | . | Q1 | WRITE | Return the | 5 highest-paid consultants | (Name, Salary) using OFFSET - FETCH. | Q2 | WRITE | Show | page 3 | of the | Patients | list ordered by | Id | , with a page size of | 10 | . Which Ids appear? | Q3 | PREDICT | What does this query return? | SELECT | Name | FROM | Consultants | ORDER | BY | Salary | OFFSET | 2 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 2 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Q4 | FIX THE BUG | Paging consultants | 2 per page | : Dr. Amira El-Din sometimes shows on | two pages | . Why? Fix it. | SELECT | Name, Salary | FROM | Consultants | ORDER | BY | Salary | DESC | OFFSET | 2 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 2 | ROWS | ONLY | ;"}, {"label": "Slide 10", "t": 10, "text": "Insert Based on Select"}, {"label": "Slide 11", "t": 11, "text": "Insert Based on Select | INSERT INTO … SELECT | copies the result of a query into an | existing | table — instead of typing VALUES row by row, the rows come from a | SELECT | . | SYNTAX | INSERT | INTO | TargetTable | (col1, col2, ...) | SELECT | col1, col2, ... | FROM | SourceTable | WHERE | condition; | -- optional | i | Like copying rows from one Excel sheet and | pasting | them into another sheet that | already has its own headers | . | KEY POINTS | ✔ | The | target table must already exist | (unlike SELECT INTO). | ✔ | Columns must match in | number | and | order | , with | compatible data types | . | ✔ | Always write the | target column list | — safer and clearer. | ✔ | The SELECT can use | WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY | , expressions and constant values. | ✔ | Target | constraints | (PK, FK, CHECK, NOT NULL) are still checked — | IDENTITY | values are generated automatically. | THE RULE IN ACTION | ✔ Correct | INSERT | INTO | ArchivedEmployees (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | FROM | Employees; | ✘ Error: SELECT returns fewer columns than the insert list | INSERT | INTO | ArchivedEmployees (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName | FROM | Employees;"}, {"label": "Slide 12", "t": 12, "text": "Insert Based on Select – Example | Copy the employees with | Salary > 20000 | into the | existing | table | HighSalaryEmployees | . | Employees | source table · 4 rows | EmployeeID | EmployeeName | DepartmentID | Salary | 1 | Ali Hassan | 1 | 25000 | 2 | Sara Mohamed | 2 | 18000 | 3 | Mona Ali | 1 | 22000 | 4 | Youssef Ibrahim | 3 | 16000 | HighSalaryEmployees | before · 1 row | Id (IDENTITY) | Name | Salary | 1 | Khaled Omar | 30000 | QUERY | INSERT | INTO | HighSalaryEmployees | (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | FROM | Employees | WHERE | Salary > | 20000 | ; | HighSalaryEmployees | after · (2 rows affected) | Id | Name | Salary | 1 | Khaled Omar | 30000 | existing | 2 | Ali Hassan | 25000 | ✔ inserted | 3 | Mona Ali | 22000 | ✔ inserted | i | The old row ( | Khaled Omar | ) is | kept | — INSERT … SELECT | adds | rows. | Id | is not in the column list because | IDENTITY | generates it."}, {"label": "Slide 13", "t": 13, "text": "Insert Select With JOIN & Expressions | Fill | EmployeeReport | with each employee's | department name | , | annual | salary and | today's date | . | QUERY | INSERT | INTO | EmployeeReport | (EmployeeName, DepartmentName, AnnualSalary, ReportDate) | SELECT | e.EmployeeName, | d.DepartmentName, | e.Salary * | 12 | , | -- expression | GETDATE | () | -- function value | FROM | Employees e | JOIN | Departments d | ON | e.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID; | COLUMN MAPPING (BY POSITION) | e.EmployeeName | EmployeeName | d.DepartmentName | DepartmentName | e.Salary * 12 | AnnualSalary | GETDATE() | ReportDate | EmployeeReport | (4 rows affected) | EmployeeName | DepartmentName | AnnualSalary | ReportDate | Ali Hassan | IT | 300000 | 2026-09-28 | Sara Mohamed | HR | 216000 | 2026-09-28 | Mona Ali | IT | 264000 | 2026-09-28 | Youssef Ibrahim | Sales | 192000 | 2026-09-28 | ! | Columns are matched by | position | , not by name — the 3rd SELECT item goes into the 3rd column ( | AnnualSalary | )."}, {"label": "Slide 14", "t": 14, "text": "SELECT INTO vs INSERT INTO … SELECT | SELECT INTO  (Session 06) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | INTO | NewEmployees | -- created now | FROM | Employees; | INSERT INTO … SELECT  (OldEmployees must exist) | INSERT | INTO | OldEmployees | (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | FROM | Employees; | SELECT INTO | INSERT INTO … SELECT | Target table | Created automatically — must NOT exist | Must already exist | Existing rows | — (brand-new table) | Kept — new rows are appended | PK / constraints / indexes | Not copied | The target's own constraints apply | Columns | Taken from the SELECT list | You choose the target columns | Error when… | The table already exists | Column count / data types don't match | Best for | Quick copy / backup of data | Loading data into a designed table | i | Rule of thumb: | New table? | → SELECT INTO. | Table already designed? | → INSERT INTO … SELECT."}, {"label": "Slide 15", "t": 15, "text": "Insert Based on Select — Practice | Use the | Hospital | database (restore | Hospital.bak | ) — tables | Patients | , | Wards | , | Consultants | , | Nurses | . | Q1 | WRITE | Create | ICUPatients | (Id, Name, DOB), then copy into it all patients of the ward | 'Intensive Care Unit (ICU)' | (use a JOIN with Wards). | Q2 | WRITE | Table | WardSummary | (WardName, PatientsCount) already exists. Fill it with the | number of patients per ward | . | Q3 | FIX THE BUG | Why does this INSERT fail? Fix it. | INSERT | INTO | HighPaidConsultants (Id, Name) | SELECT | Id, Name, Salary | FROM | Consultants | WHERE | Salary > | 20000 | ; | Q4 | WRITE | Fill | NurseSalaryReport | (NurseName, AnnualSalary) for all nurses using the existing function | dbo.CalculateAnnualSalary() | ."}, {"label": "Slide 16", "t": 16, "text": "Advanced DML"}, {"label": "Slide 17", "t": 17, "text": "UPDATE with JOIN | UPDATE … JOIN | changes rows in one table using data or conditions from | another table | . | SYNTAX | UPDATE | t | SET | t | .Column = s.Column | FROM | TargetTable | t | JOIN | SourceTable s | ON | t | .Key = s.Key | WHERE | condition; | -- optional | EXAMPLE — 10% RAISE FOR THE IT DEPARTMENT | UPDATE | e | SET | e | .Salary = | e | .Salary * | 1 | . | 10 | FROM | Employees | e | JOIN | Departments d | ON | e | .DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID | WHERE | d.DepartmentName = | 'IT' | ; | Employees | (2 rows affected) | EmployeeID | EmployeeName | Department | Salary (before) | Salary (after) | 1 | Ali Hassan | IT | 25000 | 27500  ✔ | 2 | Sara Mohamed | HR | 18000 | 18000  (no change) | 3 | Mona Ali | IT | 22000 | 24200  ✔ | 4 | Youssef Ibrahim | Sales | 16000 | 16000  (no change) | i | Safety tip: run it as a | SELECT | first (same FROM / JOIN / WHERE) to see | exactly which rows | will change — then turn it into UPDATE."}, {"label": "Slide 18", "t": 18, "text": "DELETE with JOIN | DELETE … JOIN | removes rows from one table based on data in | another table | . | SYNTAX | DELETE | t | FROM | TargetTable | t | JOIN | OtherTable o | ON | t | .Key = o.Key | WHERE | condition; | EXAMPLE — DELETE THE SALES EMPLOYEES | DELETE | e | FROM | Employees | e | JOIN | Departments d | ON | e | .DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID | WHERE | d.DepartmentName = | 'Sales' | ; | Employees | (1 row affected) | EmployeeID | EmployeeName | DepartmentID | Salary | 1 | Ali Hassan | 1 | 25000 | kept | 2 | Sara Mohamed | 2 | 18000 | kept | 3 | Mona Ali | 1 | 22000 | kept | 4 | Youssef Ibrahim | 3 | 16000 | ✘ deleted | i | The alias after | DELETE | ( | DELETE e | ) tells SQL Server | which table | to delete from — | Departments is not touched | ."}, {"label": "Slide 19", "t": 19, "text": "MERGE | MERGE | compares a | source | with a | target | and — in | one statement | — updates matching rows, inserts new ones and (optionally) deletes missing ones. | SYNTAX | MERGE | TargetTable | AS | t | USING | SourceTable | AS | s | ON | t.Key = s.Key | WHEN | MATCHED | THEN | UPDATE | SET | t.Col = s.Col | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | TARGET | THEN | INSERT | (Key, Col) | VALUES | (s.Key, s.Col) | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | SOURCE | THEN | DELETE | ; | -- MERGE must end with ; | THE 3 CASES | WHEN MATCHED  →  UPDATE | The key exists in | both | tables → update the target row. | NOT MATCHED BY TARGET  →  INSERT | The row is | only in the source | → it's new, insert it. | NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE  →  DELETE | The row is | only in the target | → it's gone from the source, delete it (optional). | i | Real use: | sync | a table with fresh data — e.g. load today's price list into | Products | in one step instead of separate UPDATE + INSERT + DELETE."}, {"label": "Slide 20", "t": 20, "text": "MERGE – Example | Sync | Products | (target) with today's price list | NewPrices | (source). | Products | target · before | Id | ProductName | Price | 1 | Laptop | 1000 | 2 | Mouse | 20 | 3 | Keyboard | 50 | NewPrices | source | Id | ProductName | Price | 1 | Laptop | 950 | 3 | Keyboard | 55 | 4 | Monitor | 200 | Ids | 1, 3 | in both → | UPDATE | Id | 4 | only in source → | INSERT | Id | 2 | only in target → | DELETE | QUERY | MERGE | Products | AS | t | USING | NewPrices | AS | s | ON | t.Id = s.Id | WHEN | MATCHED | THEN | UPDATE | SET | t.Price = s.Price | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | TARGET | THEN | INSERT | (Id, ProductName, Price) | VALUES | (s.Id, s.ProductName, s.Price) | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | SOURCE | THEN | DELETE | ; | Products | after | Id | ProductName | Price | What happened | 1 | Laptop | 950 | UPDATE | 3 | Keyboard | 55 | UPDATE | 4 | Monitor | 200 | INSERT | 2 | Mouse | 20 | DELETE"}, {"label": "Slide 21", "t": 21, "text": "Advanced DML — Practice | Use the | Hospital | database (restore | Hospital.bak | ) — tables | Nurses | , | Wards | , | Patients | , | DrugAdministrations | , | Consultants | . | Q1 | WRITE | UPDATE with JOIN: | raise the salary by | 10% | for nurses who | serve in | the ward | 'Intensive Care Unit (ICU)' | . | Q2 | WRITE | DELETE with JOIN: | delete all | DrugAdministrations | of patients in the ward | 'Emergency Department' | . How many rows? | Q3 | WRITE | Add | 1000 | to consultants with | Salary < 12000 | and use | OUTPUT | to show the name, old salary and new salary. | Q4 | PREDICT | NewWards = (4, 'Pediatrics & Neonatal'), (6, 'Oncology'). What is in | Wards | after this MERGE? | MERGE | Wards t | USING | NewWards s | ON | t.Id = s.Id | WHEN | MATCHED | THEN | UPDATE | SET | t.Name = s.Name | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | THEN | INSERT | VALUES | (s.Id, s.Name);"}, {"label": "Slide 22", "t": 22, "text": "Temporary Tables"}, {"label": "Slide 23", "t": 23, "text": "Temporary Tables | A | temporary table | is a real table stored in | tempdb | and deleted | automatically | — perfect for holding | intermediate results | while you work. | KEY POINTS | ✔ | Stored in the system database | tempdb | → System Databases → tempdb → Temporary Tables. | ✔ | The name starts with | # | (local) or | ## | (global). | ✔ | Works like a normal table: | INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, JOIN | , PK, constraints and | indexes | . | ✔ | Dropped | automatically | — or drop it yourself with | DROP TABLE #Name | . | i | Like a | whiteboard | in a meeting room: you use it during the meeting, and it's | wiped | when the meeting ends. | TYPES | # | Local Temp Table   #TableName | Visible | only | in the | session | (query window) that created it. Dropped when that session | closes | . | ## | Global Temp Table   ##TableName | Visible to | all sessions | . Dropped when the creating session closes | and | no other session is still using it."}, {"label": "Slide 24", "t": 24, "text": "Creating Temporary Tables | ①  CREATE TABLE  +  INSERT | CREATE | TABLE | #Students | ( | Id | INT | PRIMARY | KEY | , | Name | VARCHAR | ( | 50 | ), | Grade | INT | ); | INSERT | INTO | #Students | VALUES | ( | 1 | , | 'Ahmed' | , | 90 | ), ( | 2 | , | 'Mona' | , | 85 | ); | SELECT | * | FROM | #Students | ; | ④  DROP IT YOURSELF | DROP | TABLE | #Students | ; | -- drop now | DROP | TABLE | IF | EXISTS | #HighSalary | ; | -- 2016+ | ②  SELECT INTO  #Temp  (structure + data in one step) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | INTO | #HighSalary | FROM | Employees | WHERE | Salary > | 20000 | ; | SELECT | * | FROM | #HighSalary | ; | ③  GLOBAL TEMP TABLE  (two #) | CREATE | TABLE | ##Settings | ( | SettingKey | VARCHAR | ( | 50 | ), | SettingValue | VARCHAR | ( | 100 | ) | ); | i | Tip: start your script with | DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #Name | so you can | re-run | it without the error | \"There is already an object named …\" | ."}, {"label": "Slide 25", "t": 25, "text": "Temporary Table – Real Use Case | Find the employees who earn | more than their department's average | salary. | STEP 1 · SAVE THE AVERAGES IN A TEMP TABLE | SELECT | DepartmentID, | AVG | (Salary) | AS | AvgSalary | INTO | #DeptAvg | FROM | Employees | GROUP | BY | DepartmentID; | #DeptAvg | TEMP | in tempdb | DepartmentID | AvgSalary | 1 | 23500 | 2 | 18000 | 3 | 16000 | STEP 3 · CLEAN UP (optional) | DROP | TABLE | #DeptAvg | ; | STEP 2 · USE IT IN ANOTHER QUERY | SELECT | e.EmployeeName, e.Salary, t.AvgSalary | FROM | Employees e | JOIN | #DeptAvg | t | ON | e.DepartmentID = t.DepartmentID | WHERE | e.Salary > t.AvgSalary; | Result | 1 row | EmployeeName | Salary | AvgSalary | Ali Hassan | 25000 | 23500 | i | Why a temp table? | The averages are calculated | once | and can be reused in | many queries | — and a big query becomes | small, readable steps | ."}, {"label": "Slide 26", "t": 26, "text": "Local vs Global in Action | SQLQuery1.sql  —  Session 1 | CREATE | TABLE | #LocalTemp | (Id | INT | ); | CREATE | TABLE | ##GlobalTemp | (Id | INT | ); | SELECT | * | FROM | #LocalTemp | ; | -- works | SELECT | * | FROM | ##GlobalTemp | ; | -- works | SQLQuery2.sql  —  Session 2 | SELECT | * | FROM | #LocalTemp | ; | -- Error: Invalid object name '#LocalTemp'. | SELECT | * | FROM | ##GlobalTemp | ; | -- works | Local  #Temp | Global  ##Temp | Visible to | Only the session that created it | All sessions (every query window / user) | Dropped when | That session closes | The creator closes AND nobody else uses it | Same name in 2 sessions? | ✔ Yes — each session gets its own copy | ✘ No — only one table with that name | i | In tempdb, a local temp table gets a long | suffix | (e.g. | #LocalTemp_______00000000001A | ) — that's how two sessions can both have their | own | #LocalTemp | ."}, {"label": "Slide 27", "t": 27, "text": "Temp Table vs Table Variable"}, {"label": "Slide 28", "t": 28, "text": "Temp Table vs Table Variable | TABLE VARIABLE | DECLARE | @TopProducts | TABLE | ( | Id | INT | , | Name | VARCHAR | ( | 50 | ) | ); | INSERT | INTO | @TopProducts | SELECT | TOP | ( | 3 | ) Id, ProductName | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | ; | SELECT | * | FROM | @TopProducts | ; | ! | A table variable lives only for the | current batch | — run the DECLARE and the queries | together | ( | GO | ends the batch). | #Temp Table  vs  @Table Variable | #Temp Table | @Table Variable | Create | CREATE TABLE #T (…) | DECLARE @T TABLE (…) | Scope | Session (until closed / dropped) | Current batch / procedure only | Stored in | tempdb | tempdb too (not only memory!) | Indexes | PK, UNIQUE + CREATE INDEX later | Only inside the DECLARE | Statistics | ✔ Yes → good for large data | ✘ No → best for small data | ROLLBACK | Changes are rolled back | Data is NOT rolled back | ALTER / SELECT INTO | ✔ Allowed | ✘ Not allowed | i | Quick rule: | small data, simple use | → @Table variable. | Large data, needs indexes, or used across batches | → #Temp table."}, {"label": "Slide 29", "t": 29, "text": "CTE"}, {"label": "Slide 30", "t": 30, "text": "CTE (Common Table Expression) | A | CTE | (Common Table Expression) is a | named temporary result | written with | WITH | — it exists | only for the statement right after it | . | SYNTAX | WITH | CteName | AS | ( | SELECT | ... | ) | SELECT | * | FROM | CteName | ; | ✔ | Not stored | anywhere — it's just a named query (unlike #Temp in tempdb). | ✔ | Used | only | by the next statement — then it's gone. | ✔ | The statement | before | WITH must end with | ; | . | ✔ | Makes long queries | readable | — a cleaner way to write a derived table (Session 06). | SAME USE CASE AS #DeptAvg — WITHOUT A TEMP TABLE | WITH | DeptAvg | AS | ( | SELECT | DepartmentID, | AVG | (Salary) | AS | AvgSalary | FROM | Employees | GROUP | BY | DepartmentID | ) | SELECT | e.EmployeeName, e.Salary, d.AvgSalary | FROM | Employees e | JOIN | DeptAvg | d | ON | e.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID | WHERE | e.Salary > d.AvgSalary; | Result | 1 row | EmployeeName | Salary | AvgSalary | Ali Hassan | 25000 | 23500"}, {"label": "Slide 31", "t": 31, "text": "CTE vs Temp Table vs Table Variable | CTE  vs  #Temp  vs  @Table | CTE | #Temp Table | @Table Variable | Lives for | One statement | The session | The batch / procedure | Stored | Not stored (just a query) | tempdb | tempdb | Reuse in many queries | ✘ No | ✔ Yes | ✔ Yes (same batch) | Indexes | ✘ No | ✔ Yes | Only inside DECLARE | Best for | Readable one-time queries | Big results reused many times | Small data in a batch / procedure | COMMON MISTAKE — USING A CTE TWICE | WITH | DeptAvg | AS | ( | SELECT | DepartmentID, | AVG | (Salary) | AS | AvgSalary | FROM | Employees | GROUP | BY | DepartmentID ) | SELECT | * | FROM | DeptAvg; | -- works | SELECT | * | FROM | DeptAvg; | -- Error: Invalid object name 'DeptAvg'. | HOW TO CHOOSE | Need it once, just for readability? | CTE | Big data, reused in many queries? | #Temp Table | Small data inside a batch / procedure? | @Table Variable"}, {"label": "Slide 32", "t": 32, "text": "Temp Tables & CTE — Practice | Use the | Hospital | database (restore | Hospital.bak | ) — tables | DrugAdministrations | , | Patients | , | Nurses | , | Wards | . | Q1 | WRITE | Save each patient's | total drug Quantity | in | #PatientDrugTotals | , then show the | top 5 | patients by name. | Q2 | PREDICT | Session 1 runs the two SELECT INTO below. In | Session 2 | : | SELECT * FROM #ICU | and | SELECT * FROM ##ICU | → what happens? | SELECT | * | INTO | #ICU | FROM | Patients | WHERE | WardId = | 2 | ; | SELECT | * | INTO | ##ICU | FROM | Patients | WHERE | WardId = | 2 | ; | Q3 | WRITE | Using a | CTE | , show each | ward name | with the | number of nurses serving in it | — only wards with | more than 6 | nurses. | Q4 | CHOOSE | CTE, #Temp or @Table? | (a) Drug totals reused in | 5 reports | , needs an | index | . | (b) | 3 ward Ids | inside a stored procedure. | (c) Make | one long query | easier to read."}, {"label": "Slide 33", "t": 33, "text": "Thank You | See You Next Session"}]

[@10:30|t=630] ROUTE OFFSET - FETCH OFFSET — FETCH lets you skip a number of rows, then return a specific number of rows from a sorted result — the standard way to do paging in SQL Server. SYNTAX SELECT columnl, column2, FROM TableName ORDER BY columnl OFFSET n ROWS FETCH NEXT m ROWS ONLY; - required rows to skip - rows to return Think of a book: ORDER BY numbers the pages, OFFSET O past, FETCH = pages you actually read. THE RULE IN ACTION = pages you flip Correct SELECT * ORDER BY OFFSET e .NET Track FROM Products Price ROWS FETCH NEXT 5 ROWS ONLY; KEY POINTS ORDER BY is mandatory — OFFSET-FETCH works on a sorted result. OF SET n ROWS = how many rows to skip (O = skip nothing). FETCH NEXT m ROWS ONLY = how many rows to return after skipping. OFFSET can be used without FETCH (skip n, return the rest) — but FETCH needs OFFSET. ROW I ROWS and FIRST I NEXT mean the same thing. Available since SQL Server 2012. X Error: OFFSET - FETCH Without ORDER BY SELECT * FROM products OFFSET e ROWS FETCH NEXT 5 ROWS ONLY;

Route - What's New in C# - Week 1 What's New in C# Versions Week 1: Cleaner Code & Modern Syntax "Write Less, Express More" C# 9 C# 10 C# 11 C# 12 C# 13 C# 14 The C# Evolution: A Quick Timeline C# has evolved dramatically since version 7. Each version focuses on making code shorter , safer , and more expressive . Version .NET Year Theme C# 9 .NET 5 2020 Records, Top-level statements, Pattern matching C# 10 .NET 6 2021 File-scoped namespaces, Global usings C# 11 .NET 7 2022 Raw string literals, List patterns C# 12 .NET 8 2023 Primary constructors, Collection expressions C# 13 .NET 9 2024 params collections, Partial properties, Lock type C# 14 .NET 10 2025 Extension members, Null-conditional assignment, field keyword Today's focus: Syntax features from C# 9–14 that make everyday code cleaner — no new OOP concepts required! 👆 Click to reveal Today's Agenda Section 01 — Project-Level Top-level statements File-scoped namespaces Global & implicit usings Section 02 — Expression-Level Target-typed new() Constant interpolated strings Default lambda parameters Alias any type Null-conditional assignment ?.= Section 03 — Strings & Interpolation Raw string literals """ Improved interpolation $$""" Newlines in interpolation After today you'll recognize old patterns and confidently refactor them to modern C#. No behavior changes — just cleaner code! 👆 Click to reveal Discussion: Old vs. Modern C# Look at these two versions of the same program . What differences do you notice? ❌ Classic C# (Before) using System; using System.Collections.Generic; namespace MyApp { class Program { static void Main ( string [] args) { List < string > names = new List < string >(); names. Add ( "Alice" ); Console . WriteLine (names[ 0 ]); } } } 15 lines ✅ Modern C# (After) List < string > names = new (); names. Add ( "Alice" ); Console . WriteLine (names[ 0 ]); 3 lines — same output! What changed? Each line that disappeared is a modern C# feature doing the work for you: Top-level statements Removed class + Main() File-scoped namespace Removed namespace { } Implicit usings Removed using System; Target-typed new Shorter new() syntax Output (both versions): Alice — Same result, 80% less code! 👆 Click to reveal Top-Level Statements C# 9 Top-level statements let you write code directly in Program.cs — no class , no Main() method, no ceremony. Before (C# 8 and earlier) using System; namespace MyApp { class Program { static void Main ( string [] args) { Console . WriteLine ( "Hello!" ); } } } After (C# 9+) Console . WriteLine ( "Hello!" ); One line instead of 11. The compiler generates the rest. Behind the scenes — What the compiler generates: // The compiler wraps your code in this: internal class Program { static void <Main>$ ( string [] args) { Console . WriteLine ( "Hello!" ); } } Note: You can still access args directly in top-level code — the compiler provides it for you! // args is available automatically if (args. Length > 0 ) Console . WriteLine ( $"Hello, {args[ 0 ]} !" ); else Console . WriteLine ( "Hello, World!" ); Common Mistake: Using top-level statements in more than one file // File1.cs Console . WriteLine ( "Hello" ); // File2.cs Console . WriteLine ( "World" ); // CS8802: Only one compilation unit // can have top-level statements. Rule: Only one file per project can have top-level statements. 👆 Click to reveal File-Scoped Namespaces C# 10 Replace the block-scoped namespace with a simple declaration . Saves one level of indentation across the entire file. Before namespace MyApp.Models { public class Student { public string Name { get ; set ; } public int Age { get ; set ; } } } After namespace MyApp.Models ; public class Student { public string Name { get ; set ; } public int Age { get ; set ; } } Key insight: The semicolon ; after the namespace means "this namespace applies to the entire file ." Limitation: File-scoped namespace allows only one namespace per file . You cannot declare multiple namespaces — if you need that (rare), use the old block syntax. 👆 Click to reveal Global & Implicit Usings C# 10 Global Usings Write global using once , available in every file . // GlobalUsings.cs global using System; global using System.Collections.Generic; global using System.Text; Implicit Usings .NET 6+ automatically adds common usings (hidden in obj/ folder). // Auto-generated for Console apps: global using System; global using System.IO; global using System.Linq; global using System.Collections.Generic; global using System.Threading.Tasks; Where are they hidden? Check obj/Debug/net10.0/YourProject.GlobalUsings.g.cs Best practice: Create a single GlobalUsings.cs file for your project-wide usings. Before vs After — File headers across your project: Before (repeated in every file) // StudentService.cs using System; using System.Linq; using System.Collections.Generic; using MyApp.Models; public class StudentService { ... } // CourseService.cs using System; using System.Linq; using System.Collections.Generic; using MyApp.Models; public class CourseService { ... } After (clean files!) // GlobalUsings.cs (one file) global using MyApp.Models; // StudentService.cs public class StudentService { ... } // CourseService.cs public class CourseService { ... } // No repeated usings! Enable / Disable implicit usings in .csproj: <!-- In your .csproj file --> <PropertyGroup> <!-- Enable (default in .NET 6+) --> <ImplicitUsings> enable </ImplicitUsings> <!-- Disable completely --> <ImplicitUsings> disable </ImplicitUsings> </PropertyGroup> Remove a specific implicit using: <!-- In your .csproj file --> <ItemGroup> <!-- Remove System.Net.Http from implicit usings --> <Using Remove= "System.Net.Http" /> </ItemGroup> 👆 Click to reveal Spot the Bug! Each snippet has one error . Can you find it? Bug #1 // File1.cs Console . WriteLine ( "Hello" ); // File2.cs Console . WriteLine ( "World" ); Hint: How many files can have top-level statements? CS8802: Only ONE file per project can have top-level statements! Hint Show Answer Bug #2 namespace MyApp ; { public class Student { } } Hint: What does the semicolon ; mean for file-scoped namespaces? CS8955: File-scoped namespace uses ; — remove the { } braces! Hint Show Answer Bug #3 namespace MyApp ; public class Helper { global using System.Text; } Hint: Where should global using be placed in a file? CS8915: global using must be at the TOP of the file, before any namespace! Hint Show Answer Bug #4 using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using System.Linq; List < int > nums = new () { 1 , 2 , 3 }; Console . WriteLine (nums. Sum ()); Hint: Are these usings really needed in .NET 6+? IDE0005: These usings are unnecessary — they're already included as implicit usings in .NET 6+. Remove them! Hint Show Answer 👆 Click to reveal next bug Target-Typed new() C# 9 When the compiler already knows the type from the left side, you can omit the type name from new . Before List < string > names = new List < string >(); Dictionary < string , int > scores = new Dictionary < string , int >(); StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder (); After List < string > names = new (); Dictionary < string , int > scores = new (); StringBuilder sb = new (); Works everywhere the type is known: // Field declaration private List < string > _names = new (); // Method parameter with default void Print ( List < string > items = new ()) { } // Return statement List < int > GetNumbers () => new (); Works with constructor parameters too: List < string > names = new ( 10 ); // capacity = 10 HttpClient client = new ( new HttpClientHandler { AllowAutoRedirect = false }); Common Mistake — does NOT work with var : var names = new (); // CS8754: new() type cannot be inferred var sb = new (); // CS8754: same error! // Fix: specify the type on the left side List < string > names = new (); // ✅ 👆 Click to reveal Constant Interpolated Strings C# 10 In C# 10, you can use $"" interpolation with const strings — as long as all parts are also constant . Before (C# 9) const string scheme = "https" ; const string domain = "route.com" ; // ERROR! Can't use $ with const const string url = $"{scheme}://{domain}" ; // Had to use concatenation: const string url = scheme + "://" + domain; After (C# 10+) const string scheme = "https" ; const string domain = "route.com" ; // ✅ Now works! const string url = $"{scheme}://{domain}" ; // Result: "https://route.com" Why it matters: Cleaner code for API endpoints, connection strings, and configuration constants. Common Mistake — all parts must be const : const string baseUrl = "https://api.route.com" ; string version = "v2" ; // NOT const! const string endpoint = $"{baseUrl}/{version}" ; // CS0133: not constant! // Fix: make ALL parts const const string version2 = "v2" ; // ✅ const const string endpoint2 = $"{baseUrl}/{version2}" ; // ✅ works! 👆 Click to reveal Default Lambda Parameters C# 12 Just like methods, lambda expressions can now have default parameter values . Before (C# 11) // No defaults in lambdas! var discount = ( decimal price, decimal rate) => price * rate; // Always need both args: discount( 100m , 0.1m ); // discount(100m); ← ERROR! After (C# 12) // Default values work! var discount = ( decimal price, decimal rate = 0.1m ) => price * rate; // Both work now: discount( 100m , 0.2m ); // 20 discount( 100m ); // 10 Useful for: Callbacks, event handlers, LINQ-style operations with configurable behavior. Same behavior as method defaults: Method default void Log ( string msg, string level = "INFO" ) { Console . WriteLine ( $"[{level}]{msg}" ); } Lambda default (same!) var log = ( string msg, string level = "INFO" ) => Console . WriteLine ( $"[{level}]{msg}" ); Bonus — params works in lambdas too (C# 12): var sum = ( params int [] numbers) => numbers. Sum (); sum( 1 , 2 , 3 ); // 6 sum( 10 , 20 ); // 30 sum(); // 0 👆 Click to reveal Alias Any Type C# 12 The using directive can now create aliases for any type — not just named types. Includes tuples, arrays, and pointers! // Alias a tuple type — much more readable! using Point = ( double X, double Y); using StudentScore = ( string Name, int Score); Point origin = ( 0 , 0 ); Point target = ( 3.5 , 7.2 ); StudentScore best = ( "Alice" , 98 ); Console . WriteLine ( $"Best student: {best.Name}" ); Before (C# 11) — named types only // ✅ Only named types worked using MyList = System.Collections.Generic. List < string >; // ❌ Tuples? NO // using Point = (double X, double Y); // ❌ Arrays? NO // using Matrix = int[][]; After (C# 12) — any type! // ✅ Named types (still works) using MyList = System.Collections.Generic. List < string >; // ✅ Tuples using Point = ( double X, double Y); // ✅ Arrays using Matrix = int [][]; More examples — arrays & nullable types: // Alias for arrays using Row = int []; using Grid = int [][]; // Alias for nullable using OptionalName = string ?; using MaybeInt = int ?; OptionalName nickname = null ; // no warning! Grid board = new int [ 3 ][]; Note: Type aliases are file-scoped by default. To make them available across the project, combine with global using : // GlobalUsings.cs global using Point = ( double X, double Y); // ✅ available everywhere Quick preview: We'll use this more in Week 2 when we explore records and data modeling. For now, just know that using aliases are much more powerful in C# 12. 👆 Click to reveal Null-Conditional Assignment C# 14 You already know ?. for reading through null safely. C# 14 finally lets you use ?. for writing too! ❌ Before (C# 13 and earlier) // The old null-check-then-assign pattern if (order is not null ) { order.Status = "Processed" ; order.UpdatedAt = DateTime .UtcNow; } // Nested? Even more verbose! if (customer is not null ) { if (customer.Address is not null ) { customer.Address.City = "Cairo" ; } } ✅ After (C# 14) // Clean null-conditional assignment order ?. Status = "Processed" ; order ?. UpdatedAt = DateTime .UtcNow; // Chaining works too! customer ?. Address ?. City = "Cairo" ; // Combine with ??= config ?. Settings ??= new Settings (); Key behavior: If the left side is null , the right side never executes — no wasted work, no side effects. Also works with += , -= , and ??= . Also works with +=, -= operators: // Events — safe subscribe/unsubscribe button ?. Click += OnClick; button ?. Click -= OnClick; // Counters logger ?. ErrorCount += 1 ; // Collections order ?. Items ?. Count += quantity; ?. evolution — reading vs writing: C# 6 — Read only // ✅ Safe reading var city = customer ?. Address ?. City; // ❌ Safe writing? NO! // customer?.Address?.City = "Cairo"; C# 14 — Read + Write // ✅ Safe reading (same) var city = customer ?. Address ?. City; // ✅ Safe writing (NEW!) customer ?. Address ?. City = "Cairo" ; 👆 Click to reveal The String Escaping Problem Before C# 11, writing strings with special characters was painful. Especially for JSON, SQL, HTML, and regex patterns. Try writing this JSON as a C# string: // What we WANT: { "name": "Alice", "age": 25 } // What we had to WRITE in C#: string json = "{ \"name\": \"Alice\", \"age\": 25 }" ; // Or with verbatim strings (@): string json = @"{ ""name"": ""Alice"", ""age"": 25 }" ; The pain: Every " needs escaping. Every { in interpolation needs doubling. Multi-line strings lose their formatting. It gets worse with SQL, Regex, and file paths: // SQL string sql = "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = \"Alice\"" ; // Regex — almost unreadable string pattern = "\\d{3}-\\d{3}-\\d{4}" ; // File paths string path = "C:\\Users\\Alice\\Documents\\file.txt" ; 👆 Click to reveal Raw String Literals C# 11 Use three or more quotes """ to create a raw string. No escaping needed! The string contains exactly what you type. Before (escaped mess) string json = @"{ ""name"": ""Alice"", ""age"": 25, ""active"": true }" ; After (clean!) string json = """ { "name": "Alice", "age": 25, "active": true } """ ; Works beautifully with SQL, Regex, and HTML: // SQL — no escaping quotes! string sql = """ SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = "Alice" AND Role = "Admin" """ ; // Regex — backslashes stay as-is! string pattern = """\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}""" ; // HTML — just paste it in! string html = """ <div class="card"> <h1>Hello "World"</h1> </div> """ ; Interpolation with raw strings — use $""" string name = "Alice" ; int age = 25 ; string json = $""" {{ "name": "{name}", "age": {age} }} """ ; // Need literal { } ? Use {{ }} // Need literal {name}? Use $$ with {{name}} 👆 Click to reveal Raw String Interpolation C# 11 Problem: JSON uses { and } , which conflict with interpolation {expression} . Solution: Use $$""" — then interpolation requires {{expression}} (double braces), and single { } are treated as literal text! string name = "Alice" ; int age = 25 ; string json = $$""" { "name": "{{name}}", "age": {{age}}, "generated": "{{DateTime.Now:yyyy-MM-dd}}" } """ ; // Output: // { // "name": "Alice", // "age": 25, // "generated": "2024-12-15" // } Real-world: HTML template with $$""" string title = "Dashboard" ; string user = "Alice" ; string page = $$""" <html> <head><title>{{title}}</title></head> <body> <h1>Welcome, {{user}}</h1> <style> .card { border: 1px solid #ccc; } </style> </body> </html> """ ; Common Mistake — using $ instead of $$ with JSON: // ❌ WRONG: $ treats { as interpolation start string json = $""" { "name": "{name}" } """ ; // CS1733: Expected expression // ✅ FIX: Use $$ so single { } are literal string json = $$""" { "name": "{{name}}" } """ ; // Works! 👆 Click to reveal Newlines in Interpolation C# 11 Before C# 11, interpolation expressions {...} had to be on a single line . Now you can spread them across multiple lines for readability. Before (crammed) int a = 10 , b = 20 , c = 30 ; // Crammed on one line! string msg = $"Result: {(a > b ? a * c : b * c)}" ; // ✅ Works but hard to read on one line After (readable) int a = 10 , b = 20 , c = 30 ; // Multi-line — much more readable! string msg = $"Result: {( a > b ? a * c : b * c )}" ; // ✅ Parentheses needed for ternary inside interpolation Especially useful when combining with ternary operators, LINQ, or method calls inside interpolated strings. Switch expression inside interpolation: int score = 85 ; decimal price = 100m ; string result = $"Discount: {( score switch { >= 90 => price * 0.2m , >= 80 => price * 0.1m , >= 70 => price * 0.05m , _ => 0m } )}" ; // "Discount: 10.0" Note: This works with all interpolated strings — regular $"" , verbatim $@"" , and raw $""" . It's not limited to raw strings! 👆 Click to reveal What We Learned Today Feature Version What It Does Top-level statements C# 9 No class / Main ceremony in Program.cs Target-typed new() C# 9 Less type repetition File-scoped namespaces C# 10 One less indentation level per file Global usings C# 10 Write using once for entire project Implicit usings C# 10 Common namespaces auto-imported Const interpolation C# 10 $"" works with const Raw strings """ C# 11 No more escaping nightmares $$""" interpolation C# 11 JSON + interpolation = easy Newlines in interpolation C# 11 Multi-line expressions inside {} Alias any type C# 12 using aliases for tuples, arrays, etc. Default lambda params C# 12 Lambdas get default values Null-conditional assign C# 14 obj?.Prop = value — safe writes Key takeaway: None of these change program behavior — they only change how we write and read code. The compiler produces the same IL output! 👆 Click to reveal When to Use What? Feature ✅ Use When ❌ Avoid When Top-level statements Console apps, scripts, quick tools Large apps with complex startup File-scoped namespaces Always! Less indentation, no downside Multiple namespaces in one file (rare) Global usings Namespaces used in 5+ files Niche namespaces used once Target-typed new() Type is clear from left side Would make code less readable Raw strings """ JSON, SQL, HTML, regex, paths Simple one-line strings Const interpolation API endpoints, config constants Non-const values or method calls Alias any type Complex tuples, repeated generic types Simple well-known types Default lambda params Callbacks with optional config When a named method is clearer Null-conditional assign Optional updates, event handlers When null means a real error Set your C# version in .csproj: <!-- Use latest C# version --> < PropertyGroup > < LangVersion >latest</ LangVersion > </ PropertyGroup > <!-- Or specify exact version --> < PropertyGroup > < LangVersion >12.0</ LangVersion > </ PropertyGroup > 👆 Click to reveal Next Week: Modern Data Modeling Week 2: Records, Init, Required & More What's Coming Records — data-focused types Init-only setters — safe initialization Required members — compiler-enforced field keyword C# 14 — cleaner auto-properties Primary constructors — less boilerplate Collection expressions — [1, 2, 3] Homework Look at any class you've written in the main sessions. Could it be simpler? We'll connect these features directly to the OOP concepts you're learning. Great work today! 👆 Click to reveal ◀ Previous Next ▶ 1 / 20 📋 Menu 🔴 Laser ⛶ Slide Navigation ×

21 Workshopes
[S01] C# Basics
[S02] Session Agenda | 01 | Operators | 02 | Operators Priority & Associativity | 03 | Evolution of switch in C# | 04 | String Methods
[S03] Operators | ++ | -- | Logical | Unary | Binary | Assignment | Relational | Bitwise | Ternary | ? : | + | - | * | / | % | = | += | -= | *= | /= | %= | == | != | >= | <= | > | < | ! | && | || | | | & | ^ | ~ | << | >>
[S04] Operators Priority and Associativity | Priority | Operator | Associativity | 1 | ( ) (parentheses) | Left-to-right | 2 | ++, -- (post-increment, post-decrement) | Left-to-right | 3 | ++, -- (pre-increment, pre-decrement) | Right-to-left | 4 | !, ~ (logical NOT, bitwise NOT) | Right-to-left | 5 | *, /, % (multiplication, division, modulus) | Left-to-right | 6 | +, - (addition, subtraction) | Left-to-right | 7 | <<, >> (bitwise shift left, shift right) | Left-to-right | 8 | <, <=, >, >= (comparison operators) | Left-to-right | 9 | ==, != (equality operators) | Left-to-right | 10 | & , ^ , | ,  (bitwise AND , bitwise XOR , bitwise OR) | Left-to-right | 11 | && , || (logical AND, logical OR) | Left-to-right | 12 | ? : (ternary conditional) | Right-to-left | 13 | =, +=, -=, *=, /=, %= (assignment operators) | Right-to-left | Operator priority and associativity determine the order in which operators are evaluated in an expression.
[S05] Evolution of switch in C# | Initial Version (C# 1.0 - C# 6.0) | The switch statement was quite basic and worked only with integral types such as int, char, byte, short, long, or enumerations. | Only constant expressions are allowed in | case | labels. | It could only handle primitive types or enums
[S06] Evolution of switch in C# | C# 7 : | introduced pattern matching, making switch statements more flexible. | starting with C# 7 we can use | pattern matching | with switch cases and another feature that comes with pattern matching is | case guards. | the switch statement could perform pattern matching on types and values | The switch statement in C# has evolved significantly over time, becoming more powerful and expressive
[S07] Evolution of switch in C# | Switch expressions can be Constant pattern , Discard pattern , Property pattern | C#8 : | Came with a whole new exciting thing called “ | Switch Expressions | ” , Enhance Pattern matching to Work without alias name , can work with nullable types and  Limited support for relational Patterns [Partially]
[S08] Evolution of switch in C# | Relational patterns : | Allow you to use relational operators (<, >, <=, >=) directly in a pattern to match values based on comparisons instead of exact equality. | Logical | patterns : | Allow you to combine multiple patterns using the logical operators: (and , or , not) This enables more expressive and concise pattern matching | C# 9 extended the capabilities of | switch expressions | and | switch statements | by introducing new pattern matching features, including | Relational Patterns | , | Logical Patterns | , and enhanced | Property Patterns | . These additions make switch expressions more expressive, readable, and suitable for handling complex matching scenarios.
[S09] String Methods | String methods provide built-in functionality to manipulate, search, compare, format, and extract data from strings efficiently.
[S10] Thank You | See You Next Session
