[S02] Before You Start | .NET Track | Project structure | Console app  +  a separate Class Library named CSharpBasicsLib | Right-click the console project → Add → Project Reference | All user-defined types (struct, enum, class) live in the library | Access modifiers to use | public — types and members the console app calls | internal — helpers used only inside the library | private — fields and implementation details | Rules | No LINQ — loops, arrays and your own functions only | Every task must be written as a reusable method, not inline in Main | Validate input; never let the program crash on bad data | Q1 – 5  Arrays      ·      Q6 – 8  Functions & Parameters      ·      Q9 – 10  Null Safety | Q11 – 13  Enums & Struct      ·      Q14 – 1 | 8 | Passing by Value vs by Reference | Submit one solution folder containing both projects. Name each method exactly as written in the question.
[S03] 1. | Bubble Sort with Swap | Arrays | .NET Track | Read N, then read N integers into an array. Sort the array ascending using Bubble Sort. | The swap must be done by a separate method:  static void Swap(ref int a, ref int b) | Print the sorted array on one line, separated by spaces. | Example 1 | Input | 5 | 4 2 7 1 3 | Output | 1 2 3 4 7 | Example 2 | Input | 4 | 9 9 1 5 | Output | 1 5 9 9
[S04] 2. | Rotate an Array by K | Arrays | .NET Track | Read N, then N integers, then a number K. Rotate the array K positions to the LEFT and print it. | K may be larger than N — handle it without an out-of-range exception. | Do it in a method:  static int[] RotateLeft(int[] source, int k) | Example 1 | Input | 5 | 1 2 3 4 5 | 2 | Output | 3 4 5 1 2 | Example 2 | Input | 4 | 10 20 30 40 | 6 | Output | 30 40 10 20
[S05] 3. | Frequency Counter | Arrays | .NET Track | Read N, then N integers. Print every distinct value together with how many times it appears. | Keep the order of first appearance — do not sort. | No LINQ and no Dictionary. Arrays and loops only. | Example 1 | Input | 6 | 3 5 3 7 5 3 | Output | 3 -> 3 | 5 -> 2 | 7 -> 1 | Example 2 | Input | 4 | 8 8 8 8 | Output | 8 -> 4
[S06] 4. | Matrix Transpose & Diagonal Sum | Arrays | .NET Track | Read the number of rows R and columns C, then fill an R × C two-dimensional array. | Print the transpose of the matrix. | If the matrix is square, print the sum of its main diagonal; otherwise print  Not square. | Example 1 | Input | 2 3 | 1 2 3 | 4 5 6 | Output | 1 4 | 2 5 | 3 6 | Not square | Example 2 | Input | 2 2 | 1 2 | 3 4 | Output | 1 3 | 2 4 | Diagonal Sum = 5
[S07] 5. | Merge, Remove Duplicates & Sort | Arrays | .NET Track | Read two arrays (each preceded by its size). Merge them into one array, remove every duplicate, sort ascending and print the result. | Write it as:  static int[] MergeDistinct(int[] first, int[] second) | Example 1 | Input | 3 | 5 1 3 | 4 | 3 9 1 7 | Output | 1 3 5 7 9 | Example 2 | Input | 2 | 2 2 | 2 | 2 2 | Output | 2
[S08] 6. | Array Statistics with out | Functions | .NET Track | Write one method that returns four results through out parameters: | static void GetStats(int[] data, out int min, out int max, out int sum, out double avg) | Read the array, call the method once, then print all four values. | Example 1 | Input | 4 | 4 8 1 9 | Output | Min = 1 | Max = 9 | Sum = 22 | Avg = 5.5 | Example 2 | Input | 3 | 7 7 7 | Output | Min = 7 | Max = 7 | Sum = 21 | Avg = 7
[S09] 7. | params Calculator | Functions | .NET Track | Write  static int Sum(params int[] numbers)  and  static double Average(params int[] numbers). | Read one line of numbers separated by spaces, then print the sum and the average. | An empty line means the methods are called with no arguments — they must not crash. | Example 1 | Input | 3 6 9 12 | Output | Sum = 30 | Average = 7.5 | Example 2 | Input | (empty line) | Output | Sum = 0 | Average = 0
[S10] 8. | Binary Search — Two Ways | Functions | .NET Track | Read a sorted array and a target value, then search for it with BOTH implementations: | static int SearchIterative(int[] data, int target) | static int SearchRecursive(int[] data, int target, int low, int high) | Print the index each one returns, or -1 when the value is not found. | Example 1 | Input | 6 | 2 4 6 8 10 12 | 10 | Output | Iterative: 4 | Recursive: 4 | Example 2 | Input | 5 | 1 3 5 7 9 | 4 | Output | Iterative: -1 | Recursive: -1
[S11] 9. | Safe Divide with int? | Null Safety | .NET Track | Write  static int? SafeDivide(int a, int b)  that returns null instead of throwing when b is 0. | Read two integers, call the method, and print the result. | Use the null-coalescing operator for the message — no if statement is allowed when printing. | Example 1 | Input | 20 | 4 | Output | 5 | Example 2 | Input | 7 | 0 | Output | Cannot divide by zero
[S12] 10. | Null-Safe Name List | Null Safety | .NET Track | Read N names into a string?[]. The word null means a real null entry, not the text. | For each name print its length using ?. — print N/A when it is null. | Then replace every null with "Unknown" using ??= and print the final list. | Example 1 | Input | 3 | Ahmed | null | Sara | Output | Ahmed -> 5 | null -> N/A | Sara -> 4 | Final: Ahmed, Unknown, Sara | Example 2 | Input | 2 | null | null | Output | null -> N/A | null -> N/A | Final: Unknown, Unknown
[S13] 11. | Grade Calculator | Enums | .NET Track | Create  enum Grade { F, D, C, B, A }  and map a mark to a grade with a switch expression using relational patterns. | 90+ → A   ·   80+ → B   ·   70+ → C   ·   60+ → D   ·   below 60 → F | Print the grade name and its underlying integer value. Reject marks outside 0 – 100. | Example 1 | Input | 87 | Output | Grade = B | Value = 3 | Example 2 | Input | 45 | Output | Grade = F | Value = 0
[S14] 12. | [Flags] Permission System | Enums | .NET Track | Create  [Flags] enum Permission { None = 0, Read = 1, Write = 2, Delete = 4, Execute = 8 }. | Read a line of permission names to grant and combine them with the bitwise OR operator. | Then read one permission name and report whether it was granted, using HasFlag. | Example 1 | Input | Read Write Delete | Write | Output | Granted: Read, Write, Delete | Value: 7 | Has Write: True | Example 2 | Input | Read Execute | Delete | Output | Granted: Read, Execute | Value: 9 | Has Delete: False
[S15] 13. | Point Struct & Value Semantics | Struct | .NET Track | Create  struct Point  with public X and Y and a method  double DistanceTo(Point other). | Read two points and print the distance rounded to 2 decimals. | Then write  Point p3 = p1;  change p3.X to 100, and print p1.X to prove a struct is copied, not shared. | Example 1 | Input | 0 0 | 3 4 | Output | Distance = 5 | p1.X after changing p3.X = 0 | Example 2 | Input | 1 2 | 4 6 | Output | Distance = 5 | p1.X after changing p3.X = 1
[S16] 14. | Swap — by Value vs by Ref | Ref vs Value | .NET Track | Write two methods that both try to swap two integers: | static void SwapByValue(int a, int b)   and   static void SwapByRef(ref int a, ref int b) | Read two numbers, call each method on the SAME original pair, and print both values after each call. | Example 1 | Input | 5 9 | Output | After SwapByValue: 5 9 | After SwapByRef: 9 5 | Example 2 | Input | 100 -3 | Output | After SwapByValue: 100 -3 | After SwapByRef: -3 100
[S17] 15. | Change an Element vs Replace the Array | Ref vs Value | .NET Track | Write three methods that each receive an int[] : | ChangeElement(int[] data) sets data[0] = 999   ·   ReplaceArray(int[] data) does data = new int[] { 1, 1, 1 }   ·   ReplaceArrayByRef(ref int[] data) does the same assignment | Read the array, call the three methods in this order, and print the caller's array after each call. | Example 1 | Input | 3 | 10 20 30 | Output | ChangeElement: 999 20 30 | ReplaceArray: 999 20 30 | ReplaceArrayByRef: 1 1 1 | Example 2 | Input | 2 | 7 8 | Output | ChangeElement: 999 8 | ReplaceArray: 999 8 | ReplaceArrayByRef: 1 1 1
[S18] 16. | Struct vs Class in the Same Method | Ref vs Value | .NET Track | Create  struct Box { public int Value; }  and  class Bag { public int Value; }  — one public field each. | Write Modify(Box b), Modify(ref Box b) and Modify(Bag g). Every one of them sets Value = 100. | Read a starting value, put it in both objects, call the three methods and print each result. | Example 1 | Input | 5 | Output | Box (by value): 5 | Box (by ref):   100 | Bag (by value): 100 | Example 2 | Input | 42 | Output | Box (by value): 42 | Box (by ref):   100 | Bag (by value): 100
[S19] 17. | String — a Reference Type that Acts Like a Value | Ref vs Value | .NET Track | Write  ChangeText(string text)  and  ChangeTextByRef(ref string text) . Both do the same thing:  text = text.ToUpper(); | Read one line, call each method on the original string, and print the string after each call. | In a comment, explain why the first method fails even though string is a reference type. | Example 1 | Input | route | Output | After ChangeText: route | After ChangeTextByRef: ROUTE | Example 2 | Input | Hello World | Output | After ChangeText: Hello World | After ChangeTextByRef: HELLO WORLD
[S20] 18. | Running Min / Max with ref | Ref vs Value | .NET Track | Write  static void Track(int value, ref int min, ref int max, ref int count)  that updates the three variables for every new value it receives. | Read numbers one by one until 0 is entered — 0 ends the input and is not part of the data. | Call Track once per number, then print Min, Max and Count after the loop. | Example 1 | Input | 4 9 2 7 0 | Output | Min = 2 | Max = 9 | Count = 4 | Example 2 | Input | 5 0 | Output | Min = 5 | Max = 5 | Count = 1
[S21] Thank You | See You Next Session

Menna Elashary
21 Workshopes
[S01] Arrays & Enums | Workshop 03   |   Array Functions · Jagged Arrays · [Flags]
[S02] Session Agenda | .NET Track | 01 | Array Functions | Sort · Reverse · IndexOf · BinarySearch · Copy · Resize · Fill | 02 | More Array Examples | Traversal patterns and the classic algorithms, written by hand | 03 | Jagged Arrays | int[][] — rows with different lengths, and how they sit in memory | 04 | Enum Permission Example | [Flags] · combine · check · add · revoke
[S03] Array Functions — the ones you will actually use | .NET Track | Method | Returns | What it does | Array.Sort(arr) | void | Sorts ascending, in place — the original array changes | Array.Reverse(arr) | void | Flips the order, in place. Sort then Reverse = descending | Array.IndexOf(arr, value) | int | First position of the value, or -1 when it is not there | Array.LastIndexOf(arr, value) | int | Same search, starting from the end | Array.BinarySearch(arr, value) | int | Much faster — but only valid on a SORTED array | Array.Copy(src, dest, count) | void | Copies count elements into an existing array | Array.Resize(ref arr, size) | void | Builds a NEW array and re-points your variable | Array.Fill(arr, value) / Clear(arr) | void | Fill every slot / reset every slot to its default | Notice: | most of these return void because they change the array you handed them. Only the search methods give you a value back.
[S04] Array Functions in Action | .NET Track | Code | int[] marks = { 70, 40, 90, 55, 90 }; | Console.WriteLine(Array.IndexOf(marks, 90)); | Console.WriteLine(Array.LastIndexOf(marks, 90)); | Array.Sort(marks); | Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", marks)); | Console.WriteLine(Array.BinarySearch(marks, 55)); | Array.Reverse(marks); | Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", marks)); | Array.Resize(ref marks, 7); | Array.Fill(marks, -1, 5, 2); | Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", marks)); | Output | 2 | 4 | 40 55 70 90 90 | 1 | 90 90 70 55 40 | 90 90 70 55 40 -1 -1 | IndexOf finds the FIRST 90, LastIndexOf the last one. | BinarySearch only works because Sort ran first. | Resize needs ref — it hands you back a different array. | Fill can take a start index and a count.
[S05] Copy  ·  CopyTo  ·  Resize | .NET Track | Three ways to move values between arrays — and only one of them creates the array for you. | Array.Copy | int[] dest = new int[5]; | // the whole array | Array.Copy(src, dest, 3); | // a slice from the middle | Array.Copy(src, 2, dest, 0, 3); | Copies into an array you created yourself. The five-argument version is the only way to take a slice out of the middle. | src.CopyTo(dest, i) | int[] dest = new int[5]; | src.CopyTo(dest, 0); | // same result as | // Array.Copy(src, dest, src.Length) | The same job written the other way round, starting from the source. dest must already be big enough or it throws. | Array.Resize | int[] arr = { 1, 2, 3 }; | Array.Resize(ref arr, 5); | // arr.Length -> 5 | // 1 2 3 0 0 | Does not resize anything. It builds a new array, copies the old values in, and re-points your variable — which is exactly why it needs ref. | The catch: | Copy and CopyTo need a destination that already exists and is big enough. Resize makes the new array itself — and any other variable still points at the OLD one.
[S06] Walking an Array — for vs foreach | .NET Track | for  —  you control the index | for (int i = 0; i < data.Length; i++) | { | data[i] = data[i] * 2;   // works | Console.WriteLine($"{i}: {data[i]}"); | } | You can change elements | You know the position | You can walk backwards or skip | foreach  —  read-only, no index | foreach (int value in data) | { | // value = value * 2;   won't compile | Console.WriteLine(value); | } | The loop variable is read-only | No index available | Shorter and safer when you only read | Rule of thumb: | reading only → foreach.   Changing elements, or you need the index → for.
[S07] More Examples — writing it yourself | .NET Track | The Array class already does these. Writing them by hand is how you learn what it is doing. | Reverse in place | int left = 0; | int right = a.Length - 1; | while (left < right) | { | int t = a[left]; | a[left] = a[right]; | a[right] = t; | left++; | right--; | } | Two pointers walking toward each other. No second array needed. | Move every 0 to the end | int write = 0; | for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++) | { | if (a[i] != 0) | { | a[write] = a[i]; | write++; | } | } | while (write < a.Length) | a[write++] = 0; | One read index, one write index — the order of the other values is kept. | Max without Array.Sort | int max = a[0]; | for (int i = 1; i < a.Length; i++) | { | if (a[i] > max) | { | max = a[i]; | } | } | Start from a[0], never from 0 — otherwise an all-negative array returns the wrong answer.
[S08] Jagged Arrays — three ways to build one | .NET Track | 1 · Row by row | int[][] jag = new int[3][]; | jag[0] = new int[4]; | jag[1] = new int[2]; | jag[2] = new int[5]; | The outer array holds 3 empty references until you fill them. Forgetting a row leaves it null. | 2 · With values | int[][] jag = new int[3][]; | jag[0] = new int[] { 1, 2, 3, 4 }; | jag[1] = new int[] { 5, 6 }; | jag[2] = new int[] { 7, 8, 9 }; | Each row is created and filled in one statement. | 3 · All at once | int[][] jag = | { | new int[] { 1, 2, 3, 4 }, | new int[] { 5, 6 }, | new int[] { 7, 8, 9 } | }; | The shortest form. Note there is no size in the brackets. | Sizes: | jag.Length is the number of ROWS.   jag[i].Length is the length of that one row — every row can differ. | Null trap: | a row you never created is null, and jag[i].Length on it throws NullReferenceException.
[S09] Jagged vs 2D — how they sit in memory | .NET Track | int[3,4]  —  one single block | Heap | One object, allocated once | Every row must have the same length | Slightly faster and more compact | int[3][]  —  an array of arrays | ref | ref | ref | One outer array + one object per row | Rows can have any length, even null | Perfect for real data: marks per student, days per month | Access syntax: | 2D uses one pair of brackets — grid[1, 2].   Jagged uses two — jag[1][2].
[S10] Jagged Arrays in Practice — marks per student | .NET Track | Code | string[] names = { "Ahmed", "Sara", "Omar" }; | int[][] marks = | { | new int[] { 80, 90, 70 }, | new int[] { 95, 85 }, | new int[] { 60, 75, 88, 91 } | }; | for (int i = 0; i < marks.Length; i++) | { | int total = 0; | for (int j = 0; j < marks[i].Length; j++) | { | total += marks[i][j]; | } | double avg = (double)total / marks[i].Length; | Console.WriteLine($"{names[i]}: {avg:F2}"); | } | Output | Ahmed: 80.00 | Sara: 90.00 | Omar: 78.50 | The inner loop must use marks[i].Length, never marks.Length | This is the case a 2D array cannot handle — the rows are different sizes | A parallel string[] of names keeps the example simple; a class would be the real answer later
[S11] Enum Permission — give every member its own bit | .NET Track | The declaration | [Flags] | enum Permission | { | None    = 0, | Read    = 1, | Write   = 2, | Delete  = 4, | Execute = 8 | } | Values must be powers of two — 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 … | None = 0 is the empty state | [Flags] does not change the values — it changes ToString() | Why powers of two | Member              Value        Bits | None | 0 | 0000 | Read | 1 | 0001 | Write | 2 | 0010 | Delete | 4 | 0100 | Execute | 8 | 1000 | Read | Write   =   0001 | 0010   =   0011   =   3 | Each member owns a different bit, so combining them can never collide. That is the whole trick.
[S12] Permission — combine · check · add · revoke | .NET Track | Code | // combine  ->  bitwise OR | Permission user = Permission.Read | Permission.Write; | Console.WriteLine($"{user} ({(int)user})"); | // check  ->  HasFlag | Console.WriteLine(user.HasFlag(Permission.Write)); | Console.WriteLine(user.HasFlag(Permission.Delete)); | // add  ->  |= | user |= Permission.Delete; | Console.WriteLine($"{user} ({(int)user})"); | // revoke  ->  &= ~ | user &= ~Permission.Write; | Console.WriteLine($"{user} ({(int)user})"); | // list what is granted | foreach (Permission p in Enum.GetValues<Permission>()) | { | if (p != Permission.None && user.HasFlag(p)) | Console.WriteLine($"  granted: {p}"); | } | Output | Read, Write (3) | True | False | Read, Write, Delete (7) | Read, Delete (5) | granted: Read | granted: Delete | |  adds a bit   ·   &  tests a bit   ·   ~  flips every bit | &= ~X is the standard way to remove one flag | HasFlag(None) is always true — skip None when listing
[S13] Permission — one variable replaces four booleans | .NET Track | Role | Permissions | Bits | Value | Viewer | Read | 0001 | 1 | Editor | Read | Write | 0011 | 3 | Manager | Read | Write | Delete | 0111 | 7 | Admin | Read | Write | Delete | Execute | 1111 | 15 | Without [Flags] | bool canRead; | bool canWrite; | bool canDelete; | bool canExecute; | With [Flags] | Permission access; | // one field, one column | // in the database, one check
[S14] Thank You | See You Next Session

Name each method exactly as written in the question.
[S03] 1. | Array Toolbox | Array Functions | .NET Track | Read N, then N integers, then one value to search for. | Print Array.IndexOf and Array.LastIndexOf of that value in the ORIGINAL array. | Then sort the array with Array.Sort and print it, and print it again in descending order. | Example 1 | Input | 6 | 5 9 3 9 1 9 | 9 | Output | IndexOf: 1 | LastIndexOf: 5 | Sorted: 1 3 5 9 9 9 | Descending: 9 9 9 5 3 1 | Example 2 | Input | 4 | 2 4 6 8 | 5 | Output | IndexOf: -1 | LastIndexOf: -1 | Sorted: 2 4 6 8 | Descending: 8 6 4 2
[S04] 2. | Resize & Fill | Array Functions | .NET Track | Read N, then N integers, then a new size for the array. | Use Array.Resize to change the array to that size — remember it needs ref. | If the array grew, use Array.Fill to put -1 in the NEW slots only. Print the length before and after, then the final array. | Example 1 | Input | 3 | 10 20 30 | 5 | Output | Before: 3 | After: 5 | 10 20 30 -1 -1 | Example 2 | Input | 4 | 1 2 3 4 | 2 | Output | Before: 4 | After: 2 | 1 2
[S05] 3. | Array Slice with Copy | Array Functions | .NET Track | Read N, then N integers, then a start index and a count. | Use Array.Copy to extract exactly that slice into a new array, and print it. | If the range runs past the end of the array, print  Invalid range  instead — do not let it throw. | Example 1 | Input | 6 | 10 20 30 40 50 60 | 2 3 | Output | 30 40 50 | Example 2 | Input | 4 | 1 2 3 4 | 2 5 | Output | Invalid range
[S06] 4. | Write It Yourself | Array Examples | .NET Track | Read N and N integers. Without using ANY Array class method, write and call three methods of your own: | static void ReverseInPlace(int[] data)   ·   static int MaxValue(int[] data)   ·   static int SumAll(int[] data) | Print the reversed array, then the maximum, then the sum. | Example 1 | Input | 5 | 3 8 1 9 4 | Output | Reversed: 4 9 1 8 3 | Max: 9 | Sum: 25 | Example 2 | Input | 3 | -5 -1 -9 | Output | Reversed: -9 -1 -5 | Max: -1 | Sum: -15
[S07] 5. | Move Zeros to the End | Array Examples | .NET Track | Read N and N integers. Move every 0 to the end of the array while keeping the order of all the other values. | Work inside the SAME array — do not create a second one and do not sort. | Write it as:  static void MoveZerosToEnd(int[] data) | Example 1 | Input | 6 | 0 3 0 5 7 0 | Output | 3 5 7 0 0 0 | Example 2 | Input | 4 | 1 0 2 0 | Output | 1 2 0 0
[S08] 6. | Build & Print a Jagged Array | Jagged Arrays | .NET Track | Read R, the number of rows. Each of the next R lines starts with that row's length, followed by its values. | Store everything in an  int[][]  — every row has its own length. | Print each row with its length and its sum, then the grand total of all rows. | Example 1 | Input | 3 | 4 1 2 3 4 | 2 5 6 | 3 7 8 9 | Output | Row 0 (4): 1 2 3 4 | Sum = 10 | Row 1 (2): 5 6 | Sum = 11 | Row 2 (3): 7 8 9 | Sum = 24 | Total = 45 | Example 2 | Input | 2 | 1 100 | 3 1 1 1 | Output | Row 0 (1): 100 | Sum = 100 | Row 1 (3): 1 1 1 | Sum = 3 | Total = 103
[S09] 7. | Student Marks | Jagged Arrays | .NET Track | Read S, the number of students. Each of the next S lines has a name followed by that student's marks. | Store the names in a  string[]  and the marks in an  int[][]  with one row per student. | Print every student's average to 2 decimals, then the name of the student with the highest average. | Example 1 | Input | 2 | Ahmed 80 90 70 | Sara 95 85 | Output | Ahmed: 80.00 | Sara: 90.00 | Top: Sara | Example 2 | Input | 2 | Omar 50 60 | Mona 40 40 40 40 | Output | Omar: 55.00 | Mona: 40.00 | Top: Omar
[S10] 8. | Permission System | [Flags] Enum | .NET Track | Create  [Flags] enum Permission { None = 0, Read = 1, Write = 2, Delete = 4, Execute = 8 }  inside the library. | Read a line of permissions to grant, then one permission to add, then one to revoke. | Print the combined value and its number after every step, then list each permission that is still granted. | Example 1 | Input | Read Write | Delete | Write | Output | Granted: Read, Write (3) | Add Delete: Read, Write, Delete (7) | Revoke Write: Read, Delete (5) | Has: Read, Delete | Example 2 | Input | Execute | Read | Execute | Output | Granted: Execute (8) | Add Read: Read, Execute (9) | Revoke Execute: Read (1) | Has: Read
[S11] Thank You | See You Next Session

[S01] Relationships & Binding | Workshop 04   |   Class Relationships · Binding · File Local Types
[S02] Session Agenda | .NET Track | 01 | Relationships Between Classes | Association · Aggregation · Composition · Inheritance · Dependency | 02 | Static & Dynamic Binding | What the compiler decides, and what waits until runtime | 03 | File Local Types | The file modifier — a type that never leaves its own source file
[S03] Relationships Between Classes | .NET Track | Classes rarely live alone. The question is always: how tightly are these two tied together? | Relationship | Reads as | Example | What it really means | Inheritance | IS-A | Student is a Person | The strongest tie — the child gets everything | Composition | HAS-A  (strong) | Car has an Engine | The part is created inside, and dies with the whole | Aggregation | HAS-A  (weak) | Department has Employees | The part is passed in, and outlives the whole | Association | KNOWS-A | Doctor and Patient | Two independent objects that hold a reference | Dependency | USES-A | Report uses PdfWriter | The weakest — it exists only during one method call | Read the list top to bottom and the coupling gets looser. | Inheritance welds two classes together forever; a dependency lasts one method call. | Design rule: | always pick the loosest relationship that still does the job.
[S04] Association — two classes that know each other | .NET Track | Code | public class Patient | { | public string Name { get; set; } | public Doctor? TreatedBy { get; set; } | } | public class Doctor | { | public string Name { get; set; } | public Patient[] Patients { get; set; } | public void Treat(Patient p) | { | p.TreatedBy = this;   // both directions | } | } | // neither one creates the other | Doctor d = new Doctor(); | Patient p = new Patient(); | d.Treat(p); | What makes it association | Both objects are created outside, by someone else | Each keeps a reference to the other, nothing more | Delete the doctor and the patient is still a valid object | One-directional is also association — only one side needs the reference | Careful: | a two-way association is easy to get wrong — update one side and forget the other, and the two objects disagree.
[S05] Aggregation  vs  Composition | .NET Track | Both are HAS-A. The difference is one question: who creates the part, and what happens when the whole dies? | Aggregation  —  weak HAS-A | public class Department | { | public Employee[] Staff { get; } | // the parts come from OUTSIDE | public Department(Employee[] staff) | { | Staff = staff; | } | } | Employee[] team = { e1, e2 }; | Department d = new Department(team); | d = null;   // team is still alive | The employees existed before the department and keep existing after it. Close the department, the people stay. | Composition  —  strong HAS-A | public class Car | { | private Engine _engine; | // the part is created INSIDE | public Car(int cc) | { | _engine = new Engine(cc); | } | } | Car c = new Car(2000); | // nobody outside can reach the engine | c = null;   // the engine goes with it | The engine is born inside the car and has no life without it. Scrap the car and the engine is gone too.
[S06] Inheritance (IS-A)  and  Dependency (USES-A) | .NET Track | Inheritance  —  IS-A | public class Person | { | public string Name { get; set; } | public Person(string name) | { | Name = name; | Console.WriteLine("Person ctor"); | } | } | public class Student : Person | { | public string Grade { get; set; } | public Student(string name, string grade) | : base(name)      // runs FIRST | { | Grade = grade; | } | } | The base constructor always runs before the derived one | A Student can be used anywhere a Person is expected | Use it only when the sentence "a Student IS a Person" is really true | Dependency  —  USES-A | public class Report | { | // no field, no property | public void Save(PdfWriter writer) | { | writer.Write(_content); | } | } | // or created and dropped inside | public void Print() | { | Printer p = new Printer(); | p.Send(_content); | }   // p is gone here | The other class appears as a parameter or a local variable only | Nothing is stored — the link disappears when the method returns | The loosest relationship there is, and usually the one you want
[S07] Which One Do I Use? | .NET Track | Walk the questions from the top. The first Yes is your answer. | # | Ask yourself | Answer | In code | 1 | Is B really a kind of A? | Inheritance | class B : A | 2 | Does A create B inside itself, and B dies with A? | Composition | private B _b = new B(); | 3 | Does A hold a B that was created outside and outlives it? | Aggregation | public A(B b) { _b = b; } | 4 | Do A and B just hold a reference to each other? | Association | public B Partner { get; set; } | 5 | Does A only touch B inside one method? | Dependency | void Do(B b) { ... } | The classic mistake: | reaching for inheritance because two classes share a few fields. Shared fields are not IS-A. | If the sentence "a Car IS an Engine" sounds wrong, inheritance is wrong — that one is composition.
[S08] Binding — who decides which method runs? | .NET Track | Static Binding | Dynamic Binding | Decided at | Compile time | Runtime | Decided by | The reference TYPE | The actual OBJECT | Also called | Early binding | Late binding | You get it from | Overloading, static, private, sealed | virtual  +  override | Cost | A direct call — nothing to look up | One lookup in the method table | Can it change later? | No — it is burned into the IL | Yes — a new subclass changes the answer | One sentence to remember: | static binding looks at the type of the variable, dynamic binding looks at the object the variable is pointing at.
[S09] Static Binding — the compiler already knows | .NET Track | Overloading is resolved at compile time | void Print(int n)    => Log("int"); | void Print(long n)   => Log("long"); | void Print(double n) => Log("double"); | void Print(object o) => Log("object"); | Print(5);      // int | Print(5L);     // long | Print(5.0);    // double | Print('A');    // int   <- char widens to int | Print("hi");   // object | // now DELETE the int overload: | Print(5);      // long | // the call site never changed, | // but the IL now points somewhere else | How the compiler chooses | 1 | Exact type match | 2 | Widening conversion — the smallest step wins | 3 | object, as the last resort | Why it matters: | adding or removing an overload can silently change which method an existing call runs — with no error and no warning. That is static binding at work.
[S10] Dynamic Binding — the object decides | .NET Track | virtual  +  override | public class Shape | { | public virtual double Area() => 0; | } | public class Circle : Shape | { | public override double Area() | => Math.PI * R * R; | } | public class Square : Shape | { | public override double Area() => S * S; | } | // ONE array, one loop, one call site | Shape[] shapes = { new Circle(2), new Square(5) }; | foreach (Shape s in shapes) | Console.WriteLine(s.Area()); | Output | 12.566370614359172 | 25 | The variable s is a Shape — yet Circle.Area() ran | The compiler could not know which one; it emits callvirt and lets the runtime look it up | Add a Triangle tomorrow and this loop keeps working, untouched | Remove virtual or override and every line prints 0
[S11] override  vs  new  —  the classic trap | .NET Track | Same call, two different answers | public class Animal | { | public virtual void Speak() | => Console.WriteLine("generic sound"); | } | public class Dog : Animal | { | public override void Speak()   // REPLACES | => Console.WriteLine("Woof"); | } | public class Cat : Animal | { | public new void Speak()        // HIDES | => Console.WriteLine("Meow"); | } | Animal a1 = new Dog();   a1.Speak(); | Animal a2 = new Cat();   a2.Speak(); | Output | Dog d = new Dog(); | Woof | Animal a = new Dog(); | Woof | Cat c = new Cat(); | Meow | Animal a = new Cat(); | generic sound | override | replaces the method in the table — the object always wins. | new | only hides it behind a second method. The reference type decides, so a base-typed variable never sees it.
[S12] File Local Types — the file modifier | .NET Track | New in C# 11. A type marked file simply does not exist outside its own .cs file. | EmailRules.cs | namespace MyApp.Rules; | file class Validator      // only here | { | public bool IsValid(string v) | => v.Contains('@'); | } | public class EmailChecker | { | public bool Check(string v) | { | Validator r = new Validator(); | return r.IsValid(v); | } | } | PhoneRules.cs | namespace MyApp.Rules; | file class Validator      // SAME name! | { | public bool IsValid(string v) | => v.Length == 11; | } | public class PhoneChecker | { | public bool Check(string v) | { | Validator r = new Validator(); | return r.IsValid(v); | } | } | Two classes, same namespace, same name — and it compiles. | Each file sees only its own Validator. Referring to it from a third file is a compile error, not a name clash.
[S13] file  vs  private  ·  internal  ·  public | .NET Track | Modifier | Who can see the type | Reach for it when… | public | Everywhere, including other projects | Your real API | internal | Anywhere inside the same project | Helpers shared across the project | private | Only inside the type that declares it | A nested detail of one class | file | Only inside the one .cs file | A helper nobody else should ever see | The rules | Top-level types only — it cannot be nested | It cannot appear in anything more visible: no public method may return it | Needs C# 11 or later (.NET 7+) | Where it earns its place | Source generators — generated code cannot collide with your class names | A small helper that belongs to exactly one file and would only pollute IntelliSense
[S14] Thank You | See You Next Session

The first Yes is your answer. | # | Ask yourself | Answer | In code | 1 | Is B really a kind of A? | Inheritance | class B : A | 2 | Does A create B inside itself, and B dies with A? | Composition | private B _b = new B(); | 3 | Does A hold a B that was created outside and outlives it? | Aggregation | public A(B b) { _b = b; } | 4 | Do A and B just hold a reference to each other? | Association | public B Partner { get; set; } | 5 | Does A only touch B inside one method? | Dependency | void Do(B b) { ... } | The classic mistake: | reaching for inheritance because two classes share a few fields. Shared fields are not IS-A. | If the sentence \"a Car IS an Engine\" sounds wrong, inheritance is wrong — that one is composition."}, {"label": "Slide 08", "t": 8, "text": "Binding — who decides which method runs? | .NET Track | Static Binding | Dynamic Binding | Decided at | Compile time | Runtime | Decided by | The reference TYPE | The actual OBJECT | Also called | Early binding | Late binding | You get it from | Overloading, static, private, sealed | virtual  +  override | Cost | A direct call — nothing to look up | One lookup in the method table | Can it change later? | No — it is burned into the IL | Yes — a new subclass changes the answer | One sentence to remember: | static binding looks at the type of the variable, dynamic binding looks at the object the variable is pointing at."}, {"label": "Slide 09", "t": 9, "text": "Static Binding — the compiler already knows | .NET Track | Overloading is resolved at compile time | void Print(int n)    => Log(\"int\"); | void Print(long n)   => Log(\"long\"); | void Print(double n) => Log(\"double\"); | void Print(object o) => Log(\"object\"); | Print(5);      // int | Print(5L);     // long | Print(5.0);    // double | Print('A');    // int   <- char widens to int | Print(\"hi\");   // object | // now DELETE the int overload: | Print(5);      // long | // the call site never changed, | // but the IL now points somewhere else | How the compiler chooses | 1 | Exact type match | 2 | Widening conversion — the smallest step wins | 3 | object, as the last resort | Why it matters: | adding or removing an overload can silently change which method an existing call runs — with no error and no warning. That is static binding at work."}, {"label": "Slide 10", "t": 10, "text": "Dynamic Binding — the object decides | .NET Track | virtual  +  override | public class Shape | { | public virtual double Area() => 0; | } | public class Circle : Shape | { | public override double Area() | => Math.PI * R * R; | } | public class Square : Shape | { | public override double Area() => S * S; | } | // ONE array, one loop, one call site | Shape[] shapes = { new Circle(2), new Square(5) }; | foreach (Shape s in shapes) | Console.WriteLine(s.Area()); | Output | 12.566370614359172 | 25 | The variable s is a Shape — yet Circle.Area() ran | The compiler could not know which one; it emits callvirt and lets the runtime look it up | Add a Triangle tomorrow and this loop keeps working, untouched | Remove virtual or override and every line prints 0"}, {"label": "Slide 11", "t": 11, "text": "override  vs  new  —  the classic trap | .NET Track | Same call, two different answers | public class Animal | { | public virtual void Speak() | => Console.WriteLine(\"generic sound\"); | } | public class Dog : Animal | { | public override void Speak()   // REPLACES | => Console.WriteLine(\"Woof\"); | } | public class Cat : Animal | { | public new void Speak()        // HIDES | => Console.WriteLine(\"Meow\"); | } | Animal a1 = new Dog();   a1.Speak(); | Animal a2 = new Cat();   a2.Speak(); | Output | Dog d = new Dog(); | Woof | Animal a = new Dog(); | Woof | Cat c = new Cat(); | Meow | Animal a = new Cat(); | generic sound | override | replaces the method in the table — the object always wins. | new | only hides it behind a second method. The reference type decides, so a base-typed variable never sees it."}, {"label": "Slide 12", "t": 12, "text": "File Local Types — the file modifier | .NET Track | New in C# 11. A type marked file simply does not exist outside its own .cs file. | EmailRules.cs | namespace MyApp.Rules; | file class Validator      // only here | { | public bool IsValid(string v) | => v.Contains('@'); | } | public class EmailChecker | { | public bool Check(string v) | { | Validator r = new Validator(); | return r.IsValid(v); | } | } | PhoneRules.cs | namespace MyApp.Rules; | file class Validator      // SAME name! | { | public bool IsValid(string v) | => v.Length == 11; | } | public class PhoneChecker | { | public bool Check(string v) | { | Validator r = new Validator(); | return r.IsValid(v); | } | } | Two classes, same namespace, same name — and it compiles. | Each file sees only its own Validator. Referring to it from a third file is a compile error, not a name clash."}, {"label": "Slide 13", "t": 13, "text": "file  vs  private  ·  internal  ·  public | .NET Track | Modifier | Who can see the type | Reach for it when… | public | Everywhere, including other projects | Your real API | internal | Anywhere inside the same project | Helpers shared across the project | private | Only inside the type that declares it | A nested detail of one class | file | Only inside the one .cs file | A helper nobody else should ever see | The rules | Top-level types only — it cannot be nested | It cannot appear in anything more visible: no public method may return it | Needs C# 11 or later (.NET 7+) | Where it earns its place | Source generators — generated code cannot collide with your class names | A small helper that belongs to exactly one file and would only pollute IntelliSense"}, {"label": "Slide 14", "t": 14, "text": "Thank You | See You Next Session"}]

Name each class exactly as written in the question.
[S03] 1. | Association — Doctor & Patient | Relationships | .NET Track | Write class Doctor (Name, Patient[] Patients) and class Patient (Name, Doctor TreatedBy). | Neither class may create the other — both objects are made in Main and only linked together. | Read the doctor's name, then N, then N patient names. Call doctor.Treat(patient) for each one. | Print the doctor's patients, then print who treats each patient — proving the link works both ways. | Example 1 | Input | Dr. Hassan | 2 | Sara | Omar | Output | Dr. Hassan treats: Sara, Omar | Sara -> treated by Dr. Hassan | Omar -> treated by Dr. Hassan | Example 2 | Input | Dr. Mona | 1 | Ali | Output | Dr. Mona treats: Ali | Ali -> treated by Dr. Mona
[S04] 2. | Aggregation — Department & Employees | Relationships | .NET Track | Write class Employee (Name) and class Department (Title, Employee[] Staff). | Department must receive the staff array through its constructor — it may NOT create employees itself. | Read the title, then N, then N employee names. Build the array first, then the department. | Print the department and its staff, then set the department variable to null and prove the array is still usable. | Example 1 | Input | IT | 3 | Ahmed | Sara | Omar | Output | Department: IT | Staff: Ahmed, Sara, Omar | Department closed | Employees still alive: 3 (first = Ahmed) | Example 2 | Input | HR | 2 | Mona | Ali | Output | Department: HR | Staff: Mona, Ali | Department closed | Employees still alive: 2 (first = Mona)
[S05] 3. | Composition — Car & Engine | Relationships | .NET Track | Write class Engine (Capacity) and class Car (Model, private Engine field). | The Car constructor must create its own Engine — no Engine may be passed in from outside. | Each constructor prints a line when it runs, so the creation order is visible. | Read the model and the capacity, build the car, print the engine capacity through a method on Car. | Example 1 | Input | BMW | 2000 | Output | Engine 2000 cc created | Car BMW created | BMW engine: 2000 cc | Car scrapped -> the engine goes with it | Example 2 | Input | Fiat | 1600 | Output | Engine 1600 cc created | Car Fiat created | Fiat engine: 1600 cc | Car scrapped -> the engine goes with it
[S06] 4. | Inheritance — Person & Student | Relationships | .NET Track | Write class Person (Name, Age) and class Student : Person (adds Grade). Each constructor prints its own line. | Student's constructor must call the base constructor with : base(name, age) | Read the type first: the word Person followed by a name and an age, or Student followed by a name, an age and a grade. | Build the right object and print its details. Notice which constructor runs first. | Example 1 | Input | Student Sara 20 A | Output | Person constructor | Student constructor | Sara, 20, Grade A | Example 2 | Input | Person Omar 45 | Output | Person constructor | Omar, 45
[S07] 5. | Static Binding — which overload runs? | Binding | .NET Track | Write four methods with the same name in one class:  Print(int)  ·  Print(long)  ·  Print(double)  ·  Print(object). | Each one prints its own signature, e.g.  Print(int) | Call them in this exact order:  Print(5)  ·  Print(5L)  ·  Print(5.0)  ·  Print('A')  ·  Print("hi") | For Example 2: delete the Print(int) overload, change nothing else, and run the same five calls again. | Example 1 | Input | (no input — the five calls are fixed) | Output | Print(int) | Print(long) | Print(double) | Print(int) | Print(object) | Example 2 | Input | (no input — Print(int) deleted) | Output | Print(long) | Print(long) | Print(double) | Print(long) | Print(object)
[S08] 6. | Dynamic Binding — Shape hierarchy | Binding | .NET Track | Write class Shape with  public virtual double Area()  returning 0, then Circle, Rectangle and Square that each override it. | Read N, then N lines: a shape name followed by its measurements. | Store every object in ONE  Shape[]  array and loop over it with a single call to Area(). | Print each shape's area to 2 decimals, then the total. | Example 1 | Input | 3 | Circle 2 | Rectangle 3 4 | Square 5 | Output | Circle -> 12.57 | Rectangle -> 12.00 | Square -> 25.00 | Total = 49.57 | Example 2 | Input | 2 | Square 3 | Circle 1 | Output | Square -> 9.00 | Circle -> 3.14 | Total = 12.14
[S09] 7. | override vs new | Binding | .NET Track | Write class Animal with  public virtual void Speak()  printing  generic sound. | Dog : Animal uses  override  and prints Woof.   Cat : Animal uses  new  and prints Meow. | Call Speak() four times: through a Dog variable, an Animal holding a Dog, a Cat variable, and an Animal holding a Cat. | For Example 2: change Cat's  new  to  override  and run exactly the same four calls. | Example 1 | Input | (no input — the four calls are fixed) | Output | Dog as Dog     : Woof | Dog as Animal  : Woof | Cat as Cat     : Meow | Cat as Animal  : generic sound | Example 2 | Input | (no input — Cat uses override) | Output | Dog as Dog     : Woof | Dog as Animal  : Woof | Cat as Cat     : Meow | Cat as Animal  : Meow
[S10] 8. | File Local Types | File Local | .NET Track | Create TWO files in the library: EmailRules.cs and PhoneRules.cs. Each one declares  file class Validator  — the same name in both. | The email Validator accepts a value containing @ and a dot. The phone Validator accepts 11 digits starting with 0. | Each file also holds a public class (EmailChecker, PhoneChecker) that uses its own Validator. | Read an email and a phone number from the console and print whether each one is valid. | Example 1 | Input | ahmed@route.com | 01012345678 | Output | Email: Valid | Phone: Valid | Example 2 | Input | ahmed.route.com | 0100 | Output | Email: Invalid | Phone: Invalid
[S11] Thank You | See You Next Session

City Library System — Project Requirements 📚 City Library System · Project Requirements City Library System Complete requirements for a console-based library management system. Every feature, every screen, every rule — defined without ambiguity. 1 User Stories 2 Console Output 3 Acceptance Criteria 4 Validation Rules 5 Fine Calculation Section 01 User Stories 8 features. Each story defines who needs it, the exact screen output , and every success and failure case. Nothing is left to interpretation. Option 1 · Branch Info Option 2 · Show Users Option 3 · Available Books Option 4 · All Copies Option 5 · Borrow Option 6 · Return Option 7 · History Option 8 · Register Entry Point Main Menu Shown on startup. Re-displays after every action until the user enters 0 to exit. ════════════════════════════════════════ CITY LIBRARY — MAIN MENU ════════════════════════════════════════ 1. Branch Information 2. Show All Users 3. Show Available Books 4. Show All Book Copies 5. Borrow a Book 6. Return a Book 7. Member Borrowing History 8. Register New Member ──────────────────────────────────────── 0. Exit ════════════════════════════════════════ Enter your choice: ℹ️ Loop behavior Menu loops continuously until user enters 0 to exit the application. User Story 1 Branch Information · Read Only · Menu Option 1 👤 As a Librarian… I want to see all branch details on one screen so I can verify the branch information is correct at any time. ════════════════════════════════════════ LIBRARY BRANCH INFO ════════════════════════════════════════ ID : BR-01 Name : City Library — Nasr City Branch Address : 15 Nasr Road, Nasr City, Cairo Phone : 01012345678 Opening Hours : Sat–Thu: 09:00 AM – 09:00 PM Manager : Sara Ahmed Total Members : 3 Total Book Copies : 4 ✔ All details displayed ID, name, address, phone, opening hours, and manager shown correctly. ✔ Auto-counted totals Total members and book copies update automatically — no manual input needed. ℹ No input required Display only — no user input needed to view branch info. User Story 2 Show All Users · Read Only · Menu Option 2 👤 As a Librarian… I want to see all registered users — librarian and members — so I can get a full overview of who is in the system. ════════════════════════════════════════ All Registered Users ════════════════════════════════════════ ──────── LIBRARIAN PROFILE ──────── ID : LIB-01 Name : Sara Ahmed Phone : 01012345678 Salary : $8,500.00 Hired : 15/03/2019 ──────── MEMBER PROFILE ──────── ID : MEM-001 Name : Ahmed Kamal Joined : 20/01/2023 Phone : 01098765432 Email : [email protected] Borrows : 0 ──────── MEMBER PROFILE ──────── ID : MEM-002 Name : Nour Hassan Joined : 05/03/2024 Phone : 01155556677 Email : [email protected] Borrows : 0 ✔ Librarian first Librarian profile always shown first. Branch has exactly one librarian. ✔ Email fallback If email not provided → shows N/A . User Story 3 Show Available Books · Read Only · Menu Option 3 👤 As a Librarian… I want to see which copies can be borrowed right now so I can answer member requests without walking to the shelf. ════════════════════════════════════════ Available Book Copies: ════════════════════════════════════════ Copy [COPY-001] - Clean Code | Condition: Good | Available Copy [COPY-003] - The Pragmatic Programmer | Condition: Excellent | Available ✔ Available only Only Available copies shown — Borrowed, Damaged, and Reserved copies never appear here. ✔ Row format Copy [ID] - Title | Condition: X | Available ✘ No copies available Prints: No available book copies found. User Story 4 Show All Book Copies · Read Only · Menu Option 4 👤 As a Librarian… I want to see all book copies regardless of status so I can get a full inventory overview. ════════════════════════════════════════ All Book Copies ════════════════════════════════════════ Copy [COPY-001] - Clean Code | Condition: Good | Available Copy [COPY-002] - Clean Code | Condition: Fair | Borrowed Copy [COPY-003] - The Pragmatic Programmer | Condition: Excellent | Available Copy [COPY-004] - To Kill a Mockingbird | Condition: Poor | Damaged 💡 Difference from Option 3 Option 3 shows only Available . This option shows all statuses — Available, Borrowed, Damaged, and Reserved. ✔ All statuses shown Row format: Copy [ID] — Title | Condition: X | Status ✘ No copies in system Prints: No book copies found. User Story 5 Borrow a Book · Write · Menu Option 5 👤 As a Librarian… I want to process a borrow so a member can take a copy home and the system records who has it and when it is due. Enter Member ID: MEM-001 ════════════════════════════════════════ Available Book Copies ════════════════════════════════════════ Copy [COPY-001] - Clean Code | Condition: Good | Available Copy [COPY-003] - The Pragmatic Programmer | Condition: Excellent | Available Enter Copy ID to borrow: COPY-001 Copy [COPY-001] "Clean Code" borrowed by Ahmed Kamal. Due date: 20/03/2026 ✔ Member ID → available list After entering member ID, available copies display automatically. ✔ Success output Copy [ID] "Title" borrowed by Name. + Due date: dd/MM/yyyy ✘ Invalid Member ID Throws: Member not found. ✘ Invalid Copy ID Throws: Book copy not found. User Story 6 Return a Book · Write · Menu Option 6 👤 As a Librarian… I want to process a return so the copy becomes available again and any fine is shown clearly. ✅ ON-TIME RETURN Enter Copy ID: COPY-001 Copy [COPY-001]: Clean Code returned. Late return Prints: Late return fine: X.XX EGP ✘ Copy not borrowed Throws: Copy [ID] is not currently borrowed. ✘ No active transaction Throws: No active transaction for this copy. User Story 7 Member Borrowing History · Read Only · Menu Option 7 👤 As a Librarian… I want to see everything a member has ever borrowed so I can track activity and verify outstanding fines. How to Think in OOP — City Library System 📚 City Library System · OOP Design Guide How to Think Before You Code You already know OOP concepts. This guide teaches you how to start — how to read a problem, extract classes, and build a class diagram step by step. 1 Read the Problem 2 Find the Nouns 3 Find the Verbs 4 Define Relationships 5 Draw the Diagram Section 01 Why Do Students Get Stuck? You know what a class is. You know inheritance. But you don't know where to begin . ⚠️ The Real Problem Students jump to coding. They write class Book without a plan — get lost, delete, start over. 😵 I don't know what classes to create How do I turn English requirements into classes? 🤔 I don't know who owns what Should borrow() be in Member or Book ? 😰 I don't know the relationships Inheritance? Composition? Association? 🚀 I code first, think later Without a diagram, code always becomes messy. ✅ The Fix A class diagram is your blueprint. Don't build a program without one. Section 01 — The Fix Think First, Code Second A structured thinking process turns any requirements into a clean class diagram — every time. 🗺️ The solution is a 5-step process Read → Extract Nouns → Extract Verbs → Identify Relationships → Draw the Diagram. Follow this order every time, and you will always know where to start. 📖 Read Understand the full scope before touching the keyboard. 🔵 Find Classes Extract the nouns — real-world things with state. ⚡ Find Methods Extract the verbs — actions each class must do. 🔗 Connect IS-A? Belongs to? Uses? Draw the relationships. 🏗️ Diagram Build your map first — then write the code. ⏱️ Time well spent Every minute on the diagram saves ten minutes of debugging. We'll walk through each step in detail shortly. Section 02 The OOP Mindset Everything in an OOP system is either a thing , a characteristic , or an action . THE GOLDEN RULE 💡 Nouns → Classes  |  Adjectives → Attributes  |  Verbs → Methods Underline every noun (candidate classes), circle every verb (methods), highlight every descriptive detail (attributes). 🔵 Nouns → Classes Real-world things with identity and state. Librarian Member BookCopy 🟡 Verbs → Methods Actions a class can perform. borrow() return() register() 🟢 Details → Attributes Descriptive values a class stores. dueDate condition salary Section 02 — Apply It Apply the Mindset to a Real Sentence Take this sentence from the Library System and apply the golden rule directly. "A Librarian wants to process a borrow so a member can take a copy home and the system records who has it and when the due date is." WHAT THE GOLDEN RULE EXTRACTS FROM THIS SENTENCE Word / Phrase Category Becomes Note Librarian Noun Class Has data + behaviour — qualifies as a class member Noun Class Has data + behaviour — qualifies as a class copy Noun Class (BookCopy) Physical item — has copyId, condition, status process Verb Method: Borrow() Action → lives in BookCopy (owns the status) due date Detail Attribute: dueDate Plain value — goes inside BorrowTransaction 🎯 Not every noun becomes a class Multiple attributes AND behaviours? → class. Just a plain value? → attribute. "due date" is only data — it's not a class. Section 03 The 5-Step Thinking Process We will now walk through each step in depth — using the Library System as our example throughout. 🗺️ Your roadmap for this section Each step has its own slide with worked examples and a practice question. Follow along — by the end you'll have a complete class diagram built from scratch. 1 Read Everything First — Don't Code Yet Understand the full picture. Summarise the system in one sentence. 2 Extract the Nouns — Find Your Classes List every significant noun, then filter out plain data values. 3 Extract the Verbs — Find Your Methods Assign each action to the class that owns the data it needs. 4 Identify Relationships — Connect the Classes Inheritance? Composition? Association? Ask the three questions. 5 Draw the Diagram Incrementally Start with one class. Add one class at a time. Never all at once. → Step 1 starts on the next slide Section 03 — Step 1 Read Everything First — Don't Code Yet Read all requirements before writing a single line of code. 🎯 For the Library System After reading: branch, members, librarian, physical book copies, borrow/return rules, fine rules. That's your system summary. ✏️ PRACTICE QUESTION In one sentence, what does the Library System actually do? Show Answer The Library System manages a branch that allows a librarian to register members, track book copies, process borrow/return transactions, and calculate fines for late returns. ⏱️ Don't rush — spend 10–15 minutes reading first You cannot design what you don't understand. No diagram, no coding. Reading time is design time. Section 03 — Step 2 Extract the Nouns — Find Your Classes Not every noun becomes a class — filter out plain data values. Found a Noun Does it have multiple attributes or behaviours? YES NO ✓ It's a Class Just an Attribute e.g. Branch, Member, BookCopy, BorrowTransaction 🧠 Key Insight: Book vs BookCopy ONE book "Clean Code" but MULTIPLE copies (COPY-001, COPY-002). Title/author → Book . Condition/status/copyId → BookCopy . Section 03 — Step 2 · Filtering Filtering the Nouns: What Made It and What Didn't Applying the noun filter to the requirements. Noun Found Class? Reason Branch ✓ Class Has ID, name, address, phone, manager, hours Librarian ✓ Class Has name, salary, hireDate, system actions Member ✓ Class Has ID, name, email, joinDate, borrow history Book ✓ Class Has title, author — template for copies BookCopy ✓ Class Has copyId, condition, status — physical item BorrowTransaction ✓ Class Has borrowDate, dueDate, returnDate — an event Phone Number ✗ Attribute Just a string value on Member/Librarian Due Date ✗ Attribute Just a date value on BorrowTransaction ✅ Result: 6 Classes LibraryBranch Librarian Member Book BookCopy BorrowTransaction — all from requirements. No guessing. Section 03 — Step 3 Extract the Verbs — Find Your Methods The key question: which class owns this action? 🎯 Ask: Who is responsible? The method lives in the class that owns the data it needs. Need status ? → BookCopy . Need dueDate ? → BorrowTransaction . Verb Found Method Lives In Why? register a member RegisterMember() LibraryBranch Branch owns the member list borrow a copy Borrow() BookCopy BookCopy knows its own status return a copy Return() BookCopy BookCopy manages its own state calculate fine CalculateFine() BorrowTransaction Has dueDate + returnDate display info Display() Each class Every class displays its own data ✏️ PRACTICE QUESTION Where should GetBorrowingHistory() live — in Member or Branch ? Show Answer In Member. Member stores its own list of BorrowTransactions. Branch calls member.GetHistory() — it doesn't own the history itself. Section 03 — Step 4 Identify Relationships Between Classes How do these classes know about each other? Three main types. 🧩 Association A uses B — linked but neither owns the other. Member has BorrowTransactions A ─────── B 🏗️ Composition A owns B — B cannot exist without A. Branch contains BookCopy A ◆───── B 🔗 Inheritance B is a type of A — they share common fields. Librarian IS-A User A △───── B ✏️ PRACTICE QUESTION What is the relationship between LibraryBranch and Librarian ? Show Answer Composition. A Librarian only exists in the context of this branch. Branch owns the Librarian — if the branch is removed, so is the librarian record. Section 03 — Step 4 (continued) How to Decide Which Relationship to Use Ask these three questions in order — the first "yes" gives you the answer. Is B a type of A? (IS-A) YES Inherit NO Does B belong to A? Can't exist alone? YES Compose NO Does A just use/know about B? YES Associate Librarian → User IS-A → Inheritance Librarian shares id/name with User Branch → BookCopy Owns → Composition Copy can't exist outside a Branch Member → Transaction Uses → Association Transaction can exist without Member 💡 Key difference: Composition vs Association Ask: "If A is deleted, does B disappear too?" YES → Composition. NO → Association. Section 03 — Step 5 Draw the Diagram Incrementally Don't try to draw everything at once. Start central, expand outward. 🏆 The Incremental Approach 1 class → add attributes → add methods → add related class → draw relationship → repeat. 1 Start with User (abstract base) Both Librarian and Member share id/name/phone → extract upward. 2 Add Librarian + Member Each extends User and adds unique fields. 3 Add Book + BookCopy + CopyStatus The blueprint and the physical items. 4 Add BorrowTransaction Links Member and BookCopy — records the event. 5 Add Branch (the hub) Ties everything together. → We'll now build each stage step by step on the following slides Section 04 — Stage 1 Start with LibraryUser (abstract base) Both Librarian and Member share id, name, phone — extract to a parent class. 1 Common base: the LibraryUser class 💡 Both Librarian and Member share id, name, phone. Extracting to User avoids repetition — that's inheritance in action. From requirements: Librarian: Name, Phone Member: Name, Phone → Shared → goes in LibraryUser (IDs are class-specific, not shared) «abstract» LibraryUser ~ Name : string ~ Phone : string + ToDisplayString() : string 🎓 Abstract — cannot be instantiated directly You never create a generic "LibraryUser". Only a Librarian or Member. Abstract class exists to share code between subclasses. Section 04 — Stages 2 & 3 Add Librarian and Member Both inherit from User and add their own unique fields. 2 Librarian — adds salary + hireDate 💡 Librarian IS-A User. Adds salary and hireDate unique to librarians. ID: LIB-01 → LibrarianId : string Salary: 8,500 EGP → Salary : decimal Hired: 15/03/2019 → HireDate : DateOnly Librarian extends LibraryUser + LibrarianId : string + Salary : decimal + HireDate : DateOnly + ToDisplayString() : string 3 Member — adds email + borrow history 💡 Member IS-A LibraryUser. Adds MembershipId, email, MembershipDate, and owns borrowing history. ID → MembershipId : string (MEM-001…) Email → Email : string? Joined → MembershipDate : DateOnly History → _transactions : List Member extends LibraryUser + MembershipId : string + DateOfBirth : DateOnly? + Email : string? + MembershipDate : DateOnly − _transactions : List<BorrowTransaction> + AddTransaction(t) : void + GetHistoryDisplayString() : string + ToDisplayString() : string Section 04 — Stage 4 Add Book — The Template for Copies 4 Book — the template for copies 💡 "Clean Code" appears twice (COPY-001, COPY-002). Title belongs to Book — not BookCopy. Book is the blueprint; BookCopy is the physical item. "Clean Code" → ISBN, Title, AuthorName Category: Software Engineering → Category Year: 2008 → PublicationYear Multiple COPY-00X → those are BookCopy Book + ISBN : string + Title : string + AuthorName : string + Category : string + PublicationYear : int + ToDisplayString() : string 🧠 The Key Distinction 1 Book record for "Clean Code" — 3 BookCopy records (COPY-001, 002, 003). Book = definition. Copy = physical thing on the shelf. Section 04 — Stage 5 Add BookCopy + CopyStatus Enum 5 BookCopy + CopyStatus enum 💡 BookCopy is the physical item. Status has exactly 4 possible values → that's an enum. CopyId → CopyId : string Condition → Condition : string Status: 4 values → CopyStatus enum Return() returns decimal fine BookCopy + CopyId : string + Condition : string + Status : CopyStatus + Book : Book + ActiveTransaction : BorrowTransaction? + IsAvailable() : bool + Borrow(member, loanDays) : void + Return() : decimal + ToDisplayString() : string «enum» CopyStatus Available Borrowed Damaged Reserved Section 04 — Stage 6 Add BorrowTransaction 6 BorrowTransaction — records each borrow event 💡 Every borrow creates a transaction — stores who borrowed it, when, when it's due, when returned, and the fine. #1001 → TransactionId : int Borrowed → BorrowDate : DateOnly Due → DueDate : DateOnly Returned → ReturnDate : DateOnly? Fine: 10 EGP/day → CalculateFine() BorrowTransaction + TransactionId : int + Member : Member + BookCopy : BookCopy + BorrowDate : DateOnly + DueDate : DateOnly + ReturnDate : DateOnly? const FinePerDay = 10m + IsReturned() : bool + CalculateFine() : decimal + MarkReturned(date) : void + ToDisplayString() : string Section 04 — Stage 7 Add LibraryBranch — The Central Hub 7 LibraryBranch — holds everything together 💡 LibraryBranch is the entry point — holds all members, copies, and the librarian. The "manager" class that coordinates all operations. The class is called LibraryBranch . BranchId, BranchName, Address, Phone, OpeningHours → public properties Manager → Manager : Librarian _members, _copies → private lists FindMember + FindCopy are public (used by services) LibraryBranch + BranchId : string + BranchName : string + Address : string + Phone : string + OpeningHours : string + Manager : Librarian − _members : List<Member> − _copies : List<BookCopy> + RegisterMember() : Member + FindMember(id) : Member + FindCopy(id) : BookCopy + AddBookCopy(copy) : void + GetAvailableCopies() : List + ToDisplayString() : string Section 05 Connecting the Classes All relationships with types and multiplicities. Composition ◆ — A owns B · B cannot exist without A Association → — A uses/knows B · both can exist independently Inheritance △ — B is a type of A · shares attributes & methods From Relationship To Multiplicity Plain English LibraryBranch Composition ◆ Librarian 1 → 1 A branch has exactly one librarian LibraryBranch Composition ◆ Member 1 → 0..* A branch has zero or more members LibraryBranch Composition ◆ BookCopy 1 → 0..* A branch holds zero or more copies Librarian Inheritance △ LibraryUser — Librarian is a LibraryUser Member Inheritance △ LibraryUser — Member is a LibraryUser BookCopy Association → Book * → 1 Many copies refer to one book Member Association → BorrowTransaction 1 → 0..* A member has zero or more transactions BookCopy Association → BorrowTransaction 1 → 0..1 A copy has at most one active transaction Section 06 · Complete The Full Class Diagram 7 classes · 1 enum · 2 interfaces — matching the actual code exactly. Summary Your OOP Thinking Checklist Use this every time you get a new OOP problem. 📖 1 — Read everything first — don't code yet Get the full picture before touching the keyboard. 🔍 2 — Underline nouns → filter → candidate classes Multiple attributes AND behaviours? → it's a class. ⚡ 3 — Circle verbs → assign to the class that owns the data The method lives where the data lives. 🔗 4 — Draw relationships → IS-A? Belongs to? Uses? Inherit · Compose · Associate 🏗️ 5 — Build diagram incrementally, one class at a time Start central, expand outward. Never design everything at once. 🚀 Now apply it — right now Take the next OOP problem you're given. Open a blank document. Follow steps 1 → 5 in order. Do not write a single line of code until you have a class diagram. ← Previous 1 / 22 Next → SWIPE TO NAVIGATE 📋 Menu 🔴 Laser ⛶ Fullscreen Slide Navigation ×

21 Workshopes\Menna Elashary\03 ADVC#\Session_01(Threading)\1- Presentation\Week06_Basics.pptx
Menna Elashary
21 Workshopes
[S01] Threading | Workshop 05   |   Threads · Thread Pool · Synchronization
[S02] Session Agenda | .NET Track | 01 | Process vs Thread | What a thread really is, and what it costs | 02 | Creating & Controlling Threads | Start · Join · Sleep · passing data in | 03 | Foreground vs Background | The thread that quietly disappears | 04 | Thread Pool | Borrow a thread instead of building one | 05 | Race Conditions & lock | Why count++ is not one operation | 06 | Deadlock | Two threads, two locks, and nobody moves
[S03] Process  vs  Thread | .NET Track | Process | Thread | What it is | A running program | One path of execution inside a process | Memory | Its own private address space | Shares everything with its siblings | Cost to create | Heavy — milliseconds | Light — but still ~1 MB of stack each | Talking to each other | IPC: files, pipes, sockets | Just a shared variable | If one crashes | The others are untouched | The whole process goes down | How many | At least one thread inside it | Never alone — it needs a process | One line to hold on to: | threads share memory. That is the whole reason they are fast, and the whole reason they are dangerous.
[S04] When Threads Help — and When They Hurt | .NET Track | CPU-bound work | Resizing 500 images, hashing, heavy maths | Split across cores and the wall-clock time really drops | Ceiling = the number of cores you actually have | More threads than cores buys you nothing | I/O-bound work | Reading files, calling an API, querying a database | The thread is doing nothing but waiting | Overlap the waiting and the app stays responsive | This is where async/await beats raw threads | The price tag | About 1 MB of stack reserved for every thread | Context switching costs real CPU time | Shared state now needs locking, and locking needs care | A thread is not free — never start one "just in case" | Concurrency | = several things in progress. | Parallelism | = several things running at the same instant. One core gives you the first, never the second.
[S05] Creating a Thread — four ways to start one | .NET Track | Code | // 1 - a method with no parameters | Thread t1 = new Thread(DoWork); | // 2 - a lambda | Thread t2 = new Thread(() => Console.WriteLine("hi")); | // 3 - ParameterizedThreadStart: exactly one object | Thread t3 = new Thread(DoWorkWithData); | t3.Start(42);            // the argument goes here | static void DoWorkWithData(object? data) | { | int n = (int)data!;  // you must cast it back | } | // 4 - a lambda capturing locals (best for many values) | int id = 7; | Thread t4 = new Thread(() => Register(id, "Sara")); | t1.Start();  t2.Start();  t4.Start(); | Watch out for | new Thread(...) does nothing yet — Start() is what asks the OS for a thread | Calling Start() twice throws ThreadStateException | ParameterizedThreadStart takes exactly one object — everything gets cast | A lambda is type-safe and takes as many values as you like — prefer it | Capturing a for-loop variable shares ONE variable across every thread — copy it into a local first
[S06] The Thread Object — what you can read and set | .NET Track | Member | Access | What it gives you | Thread.CurrentThread | static | The thread running this very line | ManagedThreadId | read only | A unique number from the CLR — not the OS id | Name | write once | For you and the debugger only — set it, then leave it alone | IsAlive | read only | True from Start() until the method returns | IsBackground | get / set | Set it BEFORE Start(). See the next slide | Priority | get / set | A hint to the scheduler, nothing more — never a fix | ThreadState | read only | Unstarted → Running → WaitSleepJoin → Stopped | About Priority: | raising it does not make a slow thread fast — it only changes who the OS prefers when both are ready to run. | If your code needs a priority change to work correctly, the real bug is somewhere else.
[S07] Foreground  vs  Background Threads | .NET Track | The process stays alive while ANY foreground thread is still running. Background threads get no such promise. | Foreground  (the default) | Thread t = new Thread(Work); | // t.IsBackground is false | t.Start(); | Console.WriteLine("Main ends here"); | // Main returns... and the app waits | Main ends here | Worker 1 | Worker 2 | Worker 3 | Main finished long ago. The process is still alive only because this thread is. | Background | Thread t = new Thread(Work); | t.IsBackground = true;   // BEFORE Start | t.Start(); | Console.WriteLine("Main ends here"); | // Main returns... and the app dies | Main ends here | The worker is killed mid-sentence. No exception, no finally block, no warning.
[S08] Join and Sleep — making Main wait | .NET Track | Code | static void Work(string name) | { | Thread.Sleep(500);        // pretend to be busy | Console.WriteLine($"{name} done"); | } | Thread[] workers = new Thread[3]; | for (int i = 0; i < workers.Length; i++) | { | int copy = i;             // copy the loop variable! | workers[i] = new Thread(() => Work($"Worker {copy}")); | workers[i].Start(); | } | // wait for every one of them | foreach (Thread w in workers) | { | w.Join(); | } | Console.WriteLine("All workers finished"); | Output | Worker 1 done | Worker 0 done | Worker 2 done | All workers finished | The first three lines come out in any order — that is threading, not a bug | The last line is guaranteed last, because of Join() | Join() blocks the CALLING thread until the other one ends | Sleep(0) gives up the rest of your time slice; Sleep never means "exactly this long"
[S09] Thread Pool — borrow instead of build | .NET Track | Queue the work, forget the thread | using System.Threading; | CountdownEvent done = new CountdownEvent(5); | for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) | { | int copy = i; | ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(state => | { | Console.WriteLine($"item {copy}"); | done.Signal(); | }); | } | done.Wait();      // pool threads are background — | // without this they may never run | Console.WriteLine("all queued work finished"); | new Thread  vs  ThreadPool | Thread | Pool | Who creates it | You | The runtime | Reused after? | No | Yes | Background? | No | Always | Good for | Long work | Short work | Can you Join it? | Yes | No | The pool already has threads warmed up — queuing costs almost nothing | Never block a pool thread for a long time; you are starving everyone else | Task, async/await and Parallel.For all sit on top of this same pool
[S10] Race Condition — count++ is not one operation | .NET Track | The bug | int count = 0; | void Add() | { | for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) | { | count++;      // looks atomic. it is not. | } | } | // two threads, both calling Add() | Expected : 2000000 | Actual   : 1362548   <- different every run | Nothing here is random. The two threads simply overlapped in a different place each time. | What count++ really is | 1 | READ | load count into a register | 2 | ADD | add 1 inside the register | 3 | WRITE | store it back to memory | A reads 100 | B reads 100      <- before A wrote | A writes 101 | B writes 101     <- one increment lost | Three steps means two windows where another thread can cut in.
[S11] lock — one thread at a time | .NET Track | The fix | private static readonly object _gate = new object(); | private static int _count; | void Add() | { | for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) | { | lock (_gate) | { | _count++; | } | } | } | lock (x) { } | is syntax sugar: the compiler emits Monitor.Enter before your code and Monitor.Exit inside a finally — so the lock is released even if the body throws. | What to lock on | YES | a private readonly object, used for nothing else | NO | lock(this) — anyone holding your object can lock it too | NO | lock("key") — strings are interned and shared process-wide | NO | a public field, or typeof(X) | Keep it short: | every line inside a lock is a line the other threads spend waiting.
[S12] lock  ·  Interlocked  ·  Monitor | .NET Track | Tool | Protects | Why you would pick it | The catch | lock (obj) { } | Any block of code | Simple, and you cannot forget to release it | Blocks. No timeout, ever | Interlocked.Increment | One int or long | No blocking at all — a single CPU instruction | Only ++, --, Add, Exchange | Monitor.TryEnter | Any block of code | You can give up after a timeout | You must release it yourself, in a finally | Mutex | Across processes | Works between two running apps | Far slower — it goes through the OS | Start with lock. | Move to Interlocked only when the whole critical section is one counter — then it is both faster and shorter. | Reach for Monitor.TryEnter when waiting forever is not an acceptable outcome, and for Mutex only when two separate processes must agree.
[S13] Deadlock — two threads, two locks, nobody moves | .NET Track | How to write one by accident | // Thread 1 | lock (_lockA) | { | Thread.Sleep(100); | lock (_lockB) { Transfer(); } | } | // Thread 2  — the SAME two locks, reversed | lock (_lockB) | { | Thread.Sleep(100); | lock (_lockA) { Transfer(); } | } | T1 holds A and waits for B.
T2 holds B and waits for A. | Neither will ever let go. The app does not crash — it just stops. | How to avoid it | Always take locks in the SAME order everywhere — this one rule kills most deadlocks | Hold one lock at a time if you possibly can | Never call unknown code (an event, a callback) while holding a lock | Use Monitor.TryEnter with a timeout when you cannot guarantee the order | if (Monitor.TryEnter(_lockB, 500)) | { | try { Transfer(); } | finally { Monitor.Exit(_lockB); } | }
[S14] Which One Do I Actually Use? | .NET Track | Tool | Built for | Pick it when | new Thread(...) | Long-running or blocking work that must not touch the pool | You need Join, a name, or a foreground thread | ThreadPool | Short background jobs, fire and forget | You do not need a result and do not need to wait | Task | Almost everything else | You want a result, exceptions, or continuations | async / await | I/O — files, HTTP, database | The thread would only be sitting there waiting | Parallel.For | The same CPU work over a big collection | Data parallelism, split across cores | Everything below the first row runs on the same thread pool. | Understanding Thread is what makes Task make sense later — but in real code you will reach for Task first. | Rule of thumb: raw threads for control, Task for results, async/await for waiting.
[S15] Thank You | See You Next Session
