21 Workshopes
[S01] Questions Bank | Workshop 05   |   Threading   |   8 Questions
[S02] Before You Start | .NET Track | Project structure | Console app  +  a Class Library named ThreadingLib | Right-click the console project → Add → Project Reference | using System.Threading; at the top of every file that needs it | Threading rules | Set IsBackground and Name BEFORE calling Start() | Copy the loop variable into a local before capturing it in a lambda | Join every thread you start, unless the question says otherwise | About the expected output | Threaded output is not always in the same order | Where a question says "order may vary", only the lines matter, not their order | Q6 and Q7 print a different number on every run — that is the answer, not a bug | Q1 – 3  Creating & Controlling Threads      ·      Q4 – 5  Background Threads & the Pool      ·      Q6 – 8  Races, lock & Deadlock | Submit one solution folder containing both projects. Name each class and method exactly as written in the question.
[S03] 1. | Main Thread vs Worker Thread | Threads | .NET Track | Set the main thread's Name to Main. Read a name and create ONE worker thread with that name. | The worker sleeps 300 ms, then prints  <name> running. | Print IsAlive right after Start(), call Join(), print IsAlive again, then print Main finished. | For Example 2: comment out the Join() line and run it again. Change nothing else. | Example 1 | Input | Worker-1 | Output | Main thread name  : Main | IsAlive after Start: True | Worker-1 running | IsAlive after Join : False | Main finished | Example 2 | Input | Worker-1   (Join commented out) | Output | Main thread name  : Main | IsAlive after Start: True | IsAlive after Join : True | Main finished | Worker-1 running
[S04] 2. | Passing Data to a Thread | Threads | .NET Track | Read a number N and a count C. Start ONE thread that prints N's multiplication table up to C, then Join it and print Done. | You must use ParameterizedThreadStart — the lambda form is not accepted here. | It takes exactly one object, so pack both values into an int[] and cast them back inside the method. | Example 1 | Input | 5 | 3 | Output | 5 x 1 = 5 | 5 x 2 = 10 | 5 x 3 = 15 | Done | Example 2 | Input | 7 | 2 | Output | 7 x 1 = 7 | 7 x 2 = 14 | Done
[S05] 3. | Join — waiting for many workers | Threads | .NET Track | Read N, then N numbers. Create N threads: thread i doubles numbers[i] and stores the result in results[i]. | No lock is allowed. Each thread must write to its own slot and touch nothing else. | Join every thread, then print the results on one line and the total. | Copy the loop counter into a local before you capture it — otherwise all threads share one variable. | Example 1 | Input | 4 | 10 20 30 40 | Output | 20 40 60 80 | Total = 200 | Example 2 | Input | 3 | 1 2 3 | Output | 2 4 6 | Total = 12
[S06] 4. | Foreground vs Background | Background | .NET Track | Write a worker that loops three times: sleep 300 ms, then print  Worker 1,  Worker 2,  Worker 3. | Start the thread and immediately print  Main ends here.  Do NOT call Join. | Run it once with IsBackground left alone, and once with IsBackground = true. | IsBackground must be set BEFORE Start() — after Start() it is too late. | Example 1 | Input | (no input — IsBackground = false) | Output | Main ends here | Worker 1 | Worker 2 | Worker 3 | Example 2 | Input | (no input — IsBackground = true) | Output | Main ends here
[S07] 5. | Queue Work on the Thread Pool | Thread Pool | .NET Track | Read N. Queue N work items with ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem; item i writes i * i into results[i]. | Use a CountdownEvent(N) so Main waits for all of them — each item calls Signal() when it finishes. | After Wait(), print the results on one line, then print whether pool threads are background threads. | Example 1 | Input | 5 | Output | 0 1 4 9 16 | Pool threads are background: True | Example 2 | Input | 3 | Output | 0 1 4 | Pool threads are background: True
[S08] 6. | Race Condition — the lost updates | Race | .NET Track | Write a shared static int counter starting at 0, and a method that increments it 1,000,000 times in a plain for loop. | Start TWO threads running that method, Join both, then print Expected, Actual and Lost. | Use no lock, no Interlocked, nothing. The point is to see it break. | Run the program at least three times. Your numbers will not match the ones below — they should not. | Example 1 | Input | (no input — first run) | Output | Expected: 2000000 | Actual  : 1362548 | Lost    : 637452 | Example 2 | Input | (no input — second run) | Output | Expected: 2000000 | Actual  : 1857330 | Lost    : 142670
[S09] 7. | Fix It — lock and Interlocked | Race | .NET Track | Take the counter from Q6 and run the same 2 × 1,000,000 increments three separate times: | once with no protection   ·   once inside  lock (_gate)   ·   once with Interlocked.Increment | Reset the counter to 0 before each run and print all three results. | The lock object must be a private static readonly object used for nothing else. | Example 1 | Input | (no input — first run) | Output | No protection: 1481902 | lock         : 2000000 | Interlocked  : 2000000 | Example 2 | Input | (no input — second run) | Output | No protection: 1735640 | lock         : 2000000 | Interlocked  : 2000000
[S10] 8. | Deadlock — and how to avoid it | Deadlock | .NET Track | Create two lock objects, A and B. Thread 1 takes A, sleeps 200 ms, then wants B. Thread 2 takes B, sleeps 200 ms, then wants A. | For the SECOND lock use Monitor.TryEnter with a 1000 ms timeout, so the program reports failure instead of freezing forever. | Then write an ordered version where BOTH threads take A first and B second, and show that it finishes. | The two Thread lines may appear in either order. | Example 1 | Input | (no input — reversed lock order) | Output | Thread 1: got A, waiting for B | Thread 2: got B, waiting for A | Thread 1: could not get B -> deadlock | Thread 2: could not get A -> deadlock | Example 2 | Input | (no input — same lock order) | Output | Thread 1: got A, got B, done | Thread 2: got A, got B, done
[S11] Thank You | See You Next Session

[S01] Normalization & Denormalization | Designing databases that are correct, clean, and fast | .NET Track
[S02] Session Agenda | 01 | Normalization | 1NF, 2NF and 3NF — fixing redundancy step by step | 02 | Denormalization | When (and why) breaking the rules on purpose pays off | 03 | Normalize vs Denormalize | Choosing the right approach for the right system | By the end of this session, you'll design tables that avoid redundancy — and know exactly when breaking that rule on purpose is the right call.
[S03] Normalization
[S04] What is Normalization? | Normalization is the process of organizing tables to reduce data redundancy and avoid update anomalies — situations where the same fact is stored in more than one place and can go out of sync. | Goal: every piece of data should be stored in exactly one place. | Why it matters: updating one fact means updating it everywhere it repeats — miss one row, and the data is inconsistent. | Normalization happens in stages called Normal Forms — each one builds on the last: 1NF → 2NF → 3NF. | Tip: Think of each Normal Form as a stricter rule. A table can't reach 3NF without already satisfying 1NF and 2NF.
[S05] 1NF — First Normal Form (Atomic Values) | Rule: every column must hold a single, indivisible (atomic) value — no lists, no repeating groups. | ❌  Before — Student | StudentId | Name | PhoneNumbers | 1 | Ahmed | 011111, 022222 | 2 | Sara | 033333 | ✅  After — split into two tables | StudentId | Name | 1 | Ahmed | 2 | Sara | StudentId | Phone | 1 | 011111 | 1 | 022222 | 2 | 033333 | One cell holds two phone numbers — you'd need string parsing to query "who owns 022222"! | Another example: an Order table with Products = "Laptop, Mouse, Keyboard" needs an OrderItems(OrderId, ProductId) table instead. Reminder: each cell = one value, one meaning.
[S06] 2NF — Second Normal Form (Full Dependency) | Rule: for composite primary keys — every non-key attribute must depend on the whole key, not just part of it. | ❌  Before — CourseEnrollment (PK: StudentId+CourseId) | StudentId | CourseId | StudentName | Grade | 1 | C1 | Ahmed | A | 1 | C2 | Ahmed | B | 2 | C1 | Sara | A | ✅  After — split into two tables | StudentId | Name | 1 | Ahmed | 2 | Sara | StudentId | CourseId | Grade | 1 | C1 | A | 1 | C2 | B | 2 | C1 | A | StudentName depends only on StudentId — it repeats for every course. That's a partial dependency. | Tip: if part of a composite key alone determines a column, that's a partial dependency — pull it into its own table.
[S07] 3NF — Third Normal Form (No Transitive Dependency) | Rule: if A → B and B → C, then A → C should not exist in the same table. Every non-key column must depend directly on the key. | ❌  Before — Employee | EmpId | DeptId | DeptName | 101 | D1 | IT | 102 | D1 | IT | 103 | D2 | HR | ✅  After — split into two tables | EmpId | DeptId | 101 | D1 | 102 | D1 | 103 | D2 | DeptId | DeptName | D1 | IT | D2 | HR | DeptName depends on DeptId, not on EmpId directly — a transitive dependency. "IT" is now stored twice. | Another example: Book(BookId, PublisherId, PublisherCountry) has the same issue. Tip: every non-key column must describe the key — nothing else.
[S08] Quick Recap — 1NF vs 2NF vs 3NF | Form | Fixes | Rule in one line | 1NF | Repeating groups / multivalued cells | One value per cell — no lists | 2NF | Partial dependency | Non-key columns depend on the whole composite key | 3NF | Transitive dependency | Non-key columns depend only on the key | One-liner to remember: 1NF = atomic cells. 2NF = depend on the whole key. 3NF = depend on nothing but the key.
[S09] Quick Think — Spot the Violation | ✖  Problem | OrderId | ProductId | ProductName | Qty | 1 | P1 | Mouse | 2 | 1 | P2 | Keyboard | 1 | 2 | P1 | Mouse | 3 | Primary Key = (OrderId, ProductId) | Which Normal Form does this table violate? | ✓  Answer: Violates 2NF | ProductName depends only on ProductId — not on the whole composite key (OrderId, ProductId). That's a partial dependency. | Fix: move ProductName into its own Product(ProductId, ProductName) table, and keep OrderItem(OrderId, ProductId, Qty) for the rest.
[S10] Denormalization
[S11] What is Denormalization? | Denormalization is the intentional introduction of redundancy into a normalized design — on purpose, to improve read performance or simplify queries. | It's the opposite direction of everything we just did — and that's okay! | Normalization protects correctness. Denormalization buys speed. | ⚖  The Tradeoff | ⚡ Speed | 🔒 Data Consistency | You can't maximize both at once — every denormalization decision trades one for some of the other.
[S12] When to Denormalize | Frequent joins are slowing down reporting or analytics queries. | You need summary or pre-aggregated data (totals, counts). | You're optimizing read performance in large-scale, read-heavy systems. | Before — normalized (recalculate every time) | OrderId | CustomerId | Amount | 1 | C1 | 200 | 2 | C1 | 300 | 3 | C2 | 150 | After — Customer stores a cached total | CustomerId | Name | TotalOrderAmount | C1 | Ahmed | 500 | C2 | Sara | 150 | Reading Customer.TotalOrderAmount is instant — no SUM() over Orders needed. The cost: every new order must also update this column, or the number goes stale. | Tip: denormalize only for measured performance reasons — never just for convenience.
[S13] Real-World Case — A Reporting Table | Dashboards often read the same joined data thousands of times a day. Denormalizing that combination into one flat table avoids repeating the same expensive join over and over. | ❌  Normalized — needs a 3-table JOIN | Order  ⋈  Customer  ⋈  Product | ✅  Denormalized — OrderSummary | OrderId | CustomerName | ProductName | Total | 1 | Ahmed | Laptop | 25000 | 2 | Sara | Mouse | 300 | One flat table, zero joins, instant dashboard reads. CustomerName and ProductName are now redundant copies — that's the accepted tradeoff. | This table is rebuilt or refreshed on a schedule (or via triggers) — it's a reporting copy, not the source of truth.
[S14] Normalization vs Denormalization | 🧩  Normalization | ✅  Eliminates redundancy | ✅  Prevents update anomalies | ✅  Best for OLTP (transactional) systems | ❌  More joins needed to read data | ⚡  Denormalization | ✅  Fewer joins, faster reads | ✅  Great for reporting / OLAP / dashboards | ❌  Redundant data — risk of inconsistency | ❌  More work to keep copies in sync | Rule of thumb: normalize the system that writes the data. Denormalize the system that reads it a lot.
[S15] Quick Think — Normalize or Denormalize? | A banking system must record every transaction with zero tolerance for inconsistent balances. Which fits best? | ✅ Normalize — financial data demands a single source of truth with no redundant copies that could drift. Classic OLTP. | An executive dashboard shows total sales per region, refreshed hourly, read by hundreds daily. Which fits best? | ✅ Denormalize — read-heavy, tolerates slightly-stale data, avoids expensive repeated joins. Classic reporting/OLAP.
[S16] Key Takeaways | 1 | 1NF: Atomic values — no repeating groups. | 2 | 2NF: Non-key columns depend on the whole composite key. | 3 | 3NF: Non-key columns depend only on the key — no transitive dependencies. | 4 | Denormalization trades some consistency for read speed — deliberately, only where it's measured to matter. | 5 | Normalize your OLTP core. Denormalize your reporting/read layers. | Final tip: normalize for data integrity — denormalize only for performance and reporting efficiency.
[S17] Thank You! | Questions?

Tip: every non-key column must describe the key — nothing else."}, {"label": "Slide 08", "t": 8, "text": "Quick Recap — 1NF vs 2NF vs 3NF | Form | Fixes | Rule in one line | 1NF | Repeating groups / multivalued cells | One value per cell — no lists | 2NF | Partial dependency | Non-key columns depend on the whole composite key | 3NF | Transitive dependency | Non-key columns depend only on the key | One-liner to remember: 1NF = atomic cells. 2NF = depend on the whole key. 3NF = depend on nothing but the key."}, {"label": "Slide 09", "t": 9, "text": "Quick Think — Spot the Violation | ✖  Problem | OrderId | ProductId | ProductName | Qty | 1 | P1 | Mouse | 2 | 1 | P2 | Keyboard | 1 | 2 | P1 | Mouse | 3 | Primary Key = (OrderId, ProductId) | Which Normal Form does this table violate? | ✓  Answer: Violates 2NF | ProductName depends only on ProductId — not on the whole composite key (OrderId, ProductId). That's a partial dependency. | Fix: move ProductName into its own Product(ProductId, ProductName) table, and keep OrderItem(OrderId, ProductId, Qty) for the rest."}, {"label": "Slide 10", "t": 10, "text": "Denormalization"}, {"label": "Slide 11", "t": 11, "text": "What is Denormalization? | Denormalization is the intentional introduction of redundancy into a normalized design — on purpose, to improve read performance or simplify queries. | It's the opposite direction of everything we just did — and that's okay! | Normalization protects correctness. Denormalization buys speed. | ⚖  The Tradeoff | ⚡ Speed | 🔒 Data Consistency | You can't maximize both at once — every denormalization decision trades one for some of the other."}, {"label": "Slide 12", "t": 12, "text": "When to Denormalize | Frequent joins are slowing down reporting or analytics queries. | You need summary or pre-aggregated data (totals, counts). | You're optimizing read performance in large-scale, read-heavy systems. | Before — normalized (recalculate every time) | OrderId | CustomerId | Amount | 1 | C1 | 200 | 2 | C1 | 300 | 3 | C2 | 150 | After — Customer stores a cached total | CustomerId | Name | TotalOrderAmount | C1 | Ahmed | 500 | C2 | Sara | 150 | Reading Customer.TotalOrderAmount is instant — no SUM() over Orders needed. The cost: every new order must also update this column, or the number goes stale. | Tip: denormalize only for measured performance reasons — never just for convenience."}, {"label": "Slide 13", "t": 13, "text": "Real-World Case — A Reporting Table | Dashboards often read the same joined data thousands of times a day. Denormalizing that combination into one flat table avoids repeating the same expensive join over and over. | ❌  Normalized — needs a 3-table JOIN | Order  ⋈  Customer  ⋈  Product | ✅  Denormalized — OrderSummary | OrderId | CustomerName | ProductName | Total | 1 | Ahmed | Laptop | 25000 | 2 | Sara | Mouse | 300 | One flat table, zero joins, instant dashboard reads. CustomerName and ProductName are now redundant copies — that's the accepted tradeoff. | This table is rebuilt or refreshed on a schedule (or via triggers) — it's a reporting copy, not the source of truth."}, {"label": "Slide 14", "t": 14, "text": "Normalization vs Denormalization | 🧩  Normalization | ✅  Eliminates redundancy | ✅  Prevents update anomalies | ✅  Best for OLTP (transactional) systems | ❌  More joins needed to read data | ⚡  Denormalization | ✅  Fewer joins, faster reads | ✅  Great for reporting / OLAP / dashboards | ❌  Redundant data — risk of inconsistency | ❌  More work to keep copies in sync | Rule of thumb: normalize the system that writes the data. Denormalize the system that reads it a lot."}, {"label": "Slide 15", "t": 15, "text": "Quick Think — Normalize or Denormalize? | A banking system must record every transaction with zero tolerance for inconsistent balances. Which fits best? | ✅ Normalize — financial data demands a single source of truth with no redundant copies that could drift. Classic OLTP. | An executive dashboard shows total sales per region, refreshed hourly, read by hundreds daily. Which fits best? | ✅ Denormalize — read-heavy, tolerates slightly-stale data, avoids expensive repeated joins. Classic reporting/OLAP."}, {"label": "Slide 16", "t": 16, "text": "Key Takeaways | 1 | 1NF: Atomic values — no repeating groups. | 2 | 2NF: Non-key columns depend on the whole composite key. | 3 | 3NF: Non-key columns depend only on the key — no transitive dependencies. | 4 | Denormalization trades some consistency for read speed — deliberately, only where it's measured to matter. | 5 | Normalize your OLTP core. Denormalize your reporting/read layers. | Final tip: normalize for data integrity — denormalize only for performance and reporting efficiency."}, {"label": "Slide 17", "t": 17, "text": "Thank You! | Questions?"}]

You need summary or pre-aggregated data (totals, counts). You're optimizing read performance in large-scale, read-heavy systems. CREATE DATABASE Hotel_Reservation

USE Hotel_Reservation

CREATE TABLE Hotels
(
  HotelId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
  Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  Address VARCHAR(50), 
  City VARCHAR(50), 
  StarRating TINYINT ,
   ContactNumber VARCHAR(50), 

   ManagerId INT UNIQUE NOT NULL -- =====

)


CREATE TABLE Staff
(
  StaffId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
  FullName VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  Position VARCHAR(20) ,
  Salary DECIMAL(10 , 2) ,

  HotelId INT NOT NULL  FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Hotels(HotelId)

  --CONSTRAINT FK_Staff_ HotelId FOREIGN KEY ( HotelId) REFERENCES Hotels(HotelId

)

CREATE TABLE Rooms
(
  RoomNumber INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
  RoomType VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  Capacipy DECIMAL(10 , 2), 
  DailyRate TINYINT , 
  Availability VARCHAR(20)  ,
   ContactNumber VARCHAR(50), 

  HotelId INT NOT NULL  ,

  CONSTRAINT FK_Rooms_HotelId FOREIGN KEY ( HotelId) REFERENCES Hotels(HotelId)


)

CREATE TABLE Rooms_Amentities
(
   Amentity  VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL , 
   RoomNumber INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Rooms (RoomNumber)
   PRIMARY KEY (Amentity ,RoomNumber ) , 
)


CREATE TABLE Guests
(
  GuestId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
  FullName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  Nationality VARCHAR(50), 
 PassportNumber VARCHAR(30), 
 DateOfBirth Date 


)

CREATE TABLE Guest_ContactDetails
(
   Detail VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL , 
   GuestId INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Guests (GuestId)
   PRIMARY KEY (Detail ,GuestId ) 
)
CREATE TABLE Services
(
  ServiceId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
  ServiceName VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  Change DECIMAl(10 , 2), 
  RequestDate DATETIME, 
   StaffId INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Staff (StaffId)

)


CREATE TABLE Payments
(
  PaymentId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
  Method VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  Date DATETIME ,
  Amount DECIMAL(10 , 2 ),
  ConfirmationNumber VARCHAR(50), 

  
)

CREATE TABLE Reservation
(
  ReservationId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
  BookingDate DATETIME NOT NULL ,
  CheckinDate DATETIME  ,
  CheckOutDate DATETIME ,
  ReservationStatus VARCHAR(20),
  TotalPrice DECIMAL(10 , 2),
  NumberOfAdults INT ,
  NumberOfChildren  INT ,
)

CREATE TABLE Reservation_Services 
(
   ReservationId  INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Reservation (ReservationId), 
   ServiceId INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Services (ServiceId)
   PRIMARY KEY (ReservationId ,ServiceId ) , 
)

CREATE TABLE Reservation_Guests 
(
   ReservationId  INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Reservation (ReservationId), 
   GuestId INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Guests (GuestId)

CREATE DATABASE Online_Store

USE Online_Store

CREATE TABLE Suppliers
(
   SupplierId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
   Name VARCHAR(50),
   Country VARCHAR(50),
   Email VARCHAR(30),
   Address VARCHAR(30),
   ContactNumber VARCHAR(30),

)

CREATE TABLE Categories
(
   CategoryId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
   Name VARCHAR(30),
   Description VARCHAR(50),
    MainCategoryId INT FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Categories(CategoryId)

)

CREATE TABLE Products
(
   ProductId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
   Name VARCHAR(50),
   StockQuantity INT ,
   ASddedDate Date,
   Description VARCHAR(50),
   UnitPrice Decimal(10 , 2),
   CategoryId INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Categories(CategoryId)

)

CREATE TABLE Product_Suppliers
(
   ProductId  INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Products (ProductId), 
   SupplierId INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Suppliers (SupplierId),
   PRIMARY KEY (ProductId ,SupplierId ) 
)


CREATE TABLE StockTransactions
(
   TranId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
   TranDate DATETIME,
   QuantityCharge INT ,
   Type VARCHAR(30),
   Reference VARCHAR(30),
   ProductId INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Products(ProductId)

)

CREATE TABLE Customers
(
   CustomerId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
   FulName VARCHAR(30),
   PhoneNumber VARCHAR(30),
   Email VARCHAR(20),
   ShippingAddres VARCHAR(30),
   RegistrationDate DATETIME ,


)

CREATE TABLE Reviews
(
   ReviewId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
   Rating TINYINT,
   Date DATETIME ,
   Comment VARCHAR(100),

   ProductId INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Products(ProductId),

   CustomerId INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Customers(CustomerId)
)


CREATE TABLE Payments
(
   PaymentId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
   PaymentDate DATETIME ,
   Amount DECIMAL(10 , 2),
   Status  VARCHAR(30),
    Method  VARCHAR(30),

)


CREATE TABLE Orders
(
 OrderId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
 Status  VARCHAR(30),
 TotalAmount DECIMAL(10 , 2),
 OrderDate DATETIME ,
 CustomerId INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Customers(CustomerId)
 

)

CREATE TABLE Order_Payments
(
   OrderId  INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Orders (OrderId), 
   PaymentId INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Payments (PaymentId),
   PRIMARY KEY (OrderId ,PaymentId ) 
)



CREATE TABLE Shipments
(
   ShipmentId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
   ShipmentDate DATETIME ,
   Status  VARCHAR(30),
    DeliveryDate DATETIME ,
    CarrierName  VARCHAR(30),
    TrackingNumber VARCHAR(20),
    OrderId INT NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Orders(OrderId)

)



CREATE TABLE OrderItems
(
   OrderItemId INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY ,
   Quantity INT ,
   UnitPrice DECIMAL(10 , 2),

)

---Q_01  Create ICUPatients (Id, Name, DOB), then copy into it all patients of the ward 'Intensive Care Unit (ICU)' (use a JOIN with Wards).

CREATE TABLE ICUPatients
(
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(30),
  DOB DATE 
)
INSERT INTO ICUPatients (Id , Name , DOB)
SELECT 
      P.Id,
      P.Name,
      P.DOB
FROM Patients P
WHERE P.WardId = (
                      SELECT 
                       W.Id
                    FROM Wards W
                    WHERE W.Name = 'Intensive Care Unit (ICU)'

                 )
SELECT * FROM ICUPatients












  ---Q_02  Table WardSummary (WardName, PatientsCount) [Suppose] already exists. Fill it with the number of patients per ward.

  CREATE TABLE WardSummary
(
 
  WardName VARCHAR(30),
  PatientsCount INT  
)

INSERT INTO WardSummary (WardName , PatientsCount)
SELECT 
   W.Name ,
   COUNT(*) 'PatientsCount'
FROM Patients P
JOIN Wards W
ON P.WardId = W.Id
GROUP BY  W.Name 


 


 
   ---Q_04 Fill NurseSalaryReport (NurseName, AnnualSalary) for all nurses using the existing function dbo.CalculateAnnualSalary().

CREATE TABLE NurseSalaryReport
(
 
  NurseName VARCHAR(30),
  AnnualSalary DECIMAL (18 , 2)  
)

GO
CREATE FUNCTION  dbo.CalculateAnnualSalary( @NurseId INT)
RETURNS DECIMAL(18 , 2)
AS
  BEGIN 
      DECLARE @AnnualSalary DECIMAL(18 , 2)
    SELECT 
       @AnnualSalary =  N.Salary * 12
    FROM Nurses N 
    WHERE N.Number = @NurseId

    RETURN @AnnualSalary

  END 
 GO 


INSERT INTO NurseSalaryReport
SELECT 
   N.Name , 
   dbo.CalculateAnnualSalary(N.Number)
FROM Nurses N

--Q_01 UPDATE with JOIN: raise the salary by 10% for nurses who serve in the ward 'Intensive Care Unit (ICU)'.

SELECT * FROM Nurses

UPDATE N
  SET N.Salary = N.Salary * 1.10
FROM  Nurses N
JOIN Wards W
ON N.ServesInWardId = W.Id
WHERE W.Name = 'Intensive Care Unit (ICU)'

--Q_02 DELETE with JOIN: delete all DrugAdministrations of patients in the ward 'Emergency Department'. How many rows?

DELETE  DA
FROM DrugAdministrations DA
JOIN Patients P
   ON DA.PatientId = P.Id
JOIN Wards W
   ON P.WardId = W.Id
WHERE W.Name = 'Emergency Department'

[S03] OFFSET - FETCH
[S04] OFFSET - FETCH | OFFSET – FETCH | lets you | skip | a number of rows, then | return | a specific number of rows from a | sorted | result — the standard way to do | paging | in SQL Server. | SYNTAX | SELECT | column1, column2, ... | FROM | TableName | ORDER | BY | column1 | -- required | OFFSET | n | ROWS | -- rows to skip | FETCH | NEXT | m | ROWS | ONLY | ; | -- rows to return | i | Think of a | book | : ORDER BY numbers the pages, | OFFSET | = pages you flip past, | FETCH | = pages you actually read. | KEY POINTS | ✔ | ORDER BY | is mandatory — OFFSET-FETCH works on a | sorted | result. | ✔ | OFFSET n ROWS | = how many rows to | skip | (0 = skip nothing). | ✔ | FETCH NEXT m ROWS ONLY | = how many rows to | return | after skipping. | ✔ | OFFSET can be used | without FETCH | (skip n, return the rest) — but | FETCH needs OFFSET | . | ✔ | ROW / ROWS | and | FIRST / NEXT | mean the same thing. Available since | SQL Server 2012 | . | THE RULE IN ACTION | ✔ Correct | SELECT | * | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | OFFSET | 0 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 5 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | ✘ Error: OFFSET - FETCH without ORDER BY | SELECT | * | FROM | Products | OFFSET | 0 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 5 | ROWS | ONLY | ;
[S05] OFFSET - FETCH Example | Skip the | 2 most expensive | products, then return the | next 3 | — ordered by | Price DESC | . | Products | ordered by Price DESC · 8 rows | Id | ProductName | Price | Status | 1 | Laptop | 1000 | Skipped (OFFSET 2) | 6 | Desk | 300 | Skipped (OFFSET 2) | 4 | Monitor | 200 | ✔ Fetched | 5 | Chair | 150 | ✔ Fetched | 7 | Headphones | 80 | ✔ Fetched | 8 | Webcam | 60 | Not returned | 3 | Keyboard | 50 | Not returned | 2 | Mouse | 20 | Not returned | QUERY | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | OFFSET | 2 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Result | 3 rows | Id | ProductName | Price | 4 | Monitor | 200 | 5 | Chair | 150 | 7 | Headphones | 80 | i | OFFSET 2 | skipped Laptop and Desk  → | FETCH NEXT 3 | returned Monitor, Chair, Headphones  →  the remaining rows were | not returned | .
[S06] Paging with OFFSET - FETCH | OFFSET (PageNumber − 1) × PageSize ROWS   FETCH NEXT PageSize ROWS ONLY | QUERY — GET PAGE 2 | DECLARE | @PageNumber | INT | = | 2 | ; | DECLARE | @PageSize | INT | = | 3 | ; | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Id | OFFSET | ( | @PageNumber | - | 1 | ) * | @PageSize | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | @PageSize | ROWS | ONLY | ; | IN .NET — EF CORE TRANSLATES Skip / Take INTO OFFSET - FETCH | var page = context.Products | .OrderBy(p => p.Id) | .Skip((pageNumber - | 1 | ) * pageSize) | .Take(pageSize) | .ToList(); | PAGES  (PageSize = 3) | Page 1 | 1  Laptop | 2  Mouse | 3  Keyboard | Page 2 | 4  Monitor | 5  Chair | 6  Desk | Page 3 | 7  Headphones | 8  Webcam | @PageNumber | OFFSET | FETCH NEXT | Rows returned | 1 | 0 | 3 | Ids 1 – 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 | Ids 4 – 6 | 3 | 6 | 3 | Ids 7 – 8 | i | The | last page | may return | fewer rows | (page 3 → 2 rows). A page | after the end | returns | no rows | — not an error.
[S07] TOP vs OFFSET - FETCH | TOP  vs  OFFSET – FETCH | Feature | TOP | OFFSET – FETCH | Skip rows | ✘ No | ✔ Yes | ORDER BY | Optional | ✔ Required | Standard | T-SQL only | ANSI SQL standard | WITH TIES / PERCENT | ✔ Supported | ✘ Not supported | Best for | First N rows | Paging (page 1, 2, 3 …) | SAME RESULT, TWO WAYS | SELECT | TOP | ( | 3 | ) * | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | ; | -- is the same as | SELECT | * | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | OFFSET | 0 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | COMMON MISTAKE — UNSTABLE PAGES | ✘ Paging on a non-unique column | ORDER | BY | Price | OFFSET | 3 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Products with the | same price | may show up on | two pages | — or on | none | . | ✔ Add a unique tie-breaker column | ORDER | BY | Price, Id | OFFSET | 3 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | The order is now | always the same | → every row appears on | exactly one | page.
[S08] Paging with ROW_NUMBER() | Before SQL Server 2012 there was no OFFSET-FETCH — paging was done with | ROW_NUMBER() | . You'll still meet it in older projects. | QUERY — PAGE 2  (PageSize = 3) | SELECT | * | FROM | ( | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price, | ROW_NUMBER | () | OVER | ( | ORDER | BY | Id) | AS | RowNum | FROM | Products | ) | AS | t | WHERE | t. | RowNum | BETWEEN | 4 | AND | 6 | ; | -- page 2 | SAME RESULT WITH OFFSET - FETCH  (shorter & clearer) | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Id | OFFSET | 3 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Inner query (t) | RowNum 4 – 6 returned | Id | ProductName | Price | RowNum | 1 | Laptop | 1000 | 1 | 2 | Mouse | 20 | 2 | 3 | Keyboard | 50 | 3 | 4 | Monitor | 200 | 4 | 5 | Chair | 150 | 5 | 6 | Desk | 300 | 6 | 7 | Headphones | 80 | 7 | 8 | Webcam | 60 | 8 | ! | ROW_NUMBER() can't be used directly in | WHERE | — that's why we wrap it in a | subquery | (or a CTE).

[S10] Insert Based on Select
[S11] Insert Based on Select | INSERT INTO … SELECT | copies the result of a query into an | existing | table — instead of typing VALUES row by row, the rows come from a | SELECT | . | SYNTAX | INSERT | INTO | TargetTable | (col1, col2, ...) | SELECT | col1, col2, ... | FROM | SourceTable | WHERE | condition; | -- optional | i | Like copying rows from one Excel sheet and | pasting | them into another sheet that | already has its own headers | . | KEY POINTS | ✔ | The | target table must already exist | (unlike SELECT INTO). | ✔ | Columns must match in | number | and | order | , with | compatible data types | . | ✔ | Always write the | target column list | — safer and clearer. | ✔ | The SELECT can use | WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY | , expressions and constant values. | ✔ | Target | constraints | (PK, FK, CHECK, NOT NULL) are still checked — | IDENTITY | values are generated automatically. | THE RULE IN ACTION | ✔ Correct | INSERT | INTO | ArchivedEmployees (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | FROM | Employees; | ✘ Error: SELECT returns fewer columns than the insert list | INSERT | INTO | ArchivedEmployees (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName | FROM | Employees;

[S13] Insert Select With JOIN & Expressions | Fill | EmployeeReport | with each employee's | department name | , | annual | salary and | today's date | . | QUERY | INSERT | INTO | EmployeeReport | (EmployeeName, DepartmentName, AnnualSalary, ReportDate) | SELECT | e.EmployeeName, | d.DepartmentName, | e.Salary * | 12 | , | -- expression | GETDATE | () | -- function value | FROM | Employees e | JOIN | Departments d | ON | e.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID; | COLUMN MAPPING (BY POSITION) | e.EmployeeName | EmployeeName | d.DepartmentName | DepartmentName | e.Salary * 12 | AnnualSalary | GETDATE() | ReportDate | EmployeeReport | (4 rows affected) | EmployeeName | DepartmentName | AnnualSalary | ReportDate | Ali Hassan | IT | 300000 | 2026-09-28 | Sara Mohamed | HR | 216000 | 2026-09-28 | Mona Ali | IT | 264000 | 2026-09-28 | Youssef Ibrahim | Sales | 192000 | 2026-09-28 | ! | Columns are matched by | position | , not by name — the 3rd SELECT item goes into the 3rd column ( | AnnualSalary | ).
[S14] SELECT INTO vs INSERT INTO … SELECT | SELECT INTO  (Session 06) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | INTO | NewEmployees | -- created now | FROM | Employees; | INSERT INTO … SELECT  (OldEmployees must exist) | INSERT | INTO | OldEmployees | (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | FROM | Employees; | SELECT INTO | INSERT INTO … SELECT | Target table | Created automatically — must NOT exist | Must already exist | Existing rows | — (brand-new table) | Kept — new rows are appended | PK / constraints / indexes | Not copied | The target's own constraints apply | Columns | Taken from the SELECT list | You choose the target columns | Error when… | The table already exists | Column count / data types don't match | Best for | Quick copy / backup of data | Loading data into a designed table | i | Rule of thumb: | New table? | → SELECT INTO. | Table already designed? | → INSERT INTO … SELECT.

[S16] Advanced DML
[S17] UPDATE with JOIN | UPDATE … JOIN | changes rows in one table using data or conditions from | another table | . | SYNTAX | UPDATE | t | SET | t | .Column = s.Column | FROM | TargetTable | t | JOIN | SourceTable s | ON | t | .Key = s.Key | WHERE | condition; | -- optional | EXAMPLE — 10% RAISE FOR THE IT DEPARTMENT | UPDATE | e | SET | e | .Salary = | e | .Salary * | 1 | . | 10 | FROM | Employees | e | JOIN | Departments d | ON | e | .DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID | WHERE | d.DepartmentName = | 'IT' | ; | Employees | (2 rows affected) | EmployeeID | EmployeeName | Department | Salary (before) | Salary (after) | 1 | Ali Hassan | IT | 25000 | 27500  ✔ | 2 | Sara Mohamed | HR | 18000 | 18000  (no change) | 3 | Mona Ali | IT | 22000 | 24200  ✔ | 4 | Youssef Ibrahim | Sales | 16000 | 16000  (no change) | i | Safety tip: run it as a | SELECT | first (same FROM / JOIN / WHERE) to see | exactly which rows | will change — then turn it into UPDATE.
[S18] DELETE with JOIN | DELETE … JOIN | removes rows from one table based on data in | another table | . | SYNTAX | DELETE | t | FROM | TargetTable | t | JOIN | OtherTable o | ON | t | .Key = o.Key | WHERE | condition; | EXAMPLE — DELETE THE SALES EMPLOYEES | DELETE | e | FROM | Employees | e | JOIN | Departments d | ON | e | .DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID | WHERE | d.DepartmentName = | 'Sales' | ; | Employees | (1 row affected) | EmployeeID | EmployeeName | DepartmentID | Salary | 1 | Ali Hassan | 1 | 25000 | kept | 2 | Sara Mohamed | 2 | 18000 | kept | 3 | Mona Ali | 1 | 22000 | kept | 4 | Youssef Ibrahim | 3 | 16000 | ✘ deleted | i | The alias after | DELETE | ( | DELETE e | ) tells SQL Server | which table | to delete from — | Departments is not touched | . | TEST IT SAFELY | BEGIN | TRAN | ; | DELETE | e | FROM | Employees e ...; | SELECT | * | FROM | Employees; | -- check | ROLLBACK | ; | -- undo
[S19] MERGE | MERGE | compares a | source | with a | target | and — in | one statement | — updates matching rows, inserts new ones and (optionally) deletes missing ones. | SYNTAX | MERGE | TargetTable | AS | t | USING | SourceTable | AS | s | ON | t.Key = s.Key | WHEN | MATCHED | THEN | UPDATE | SET | t.Col = s.Col | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | TARGET | THEN | INSERT | (Key, Col) | VALUES | (s.Key, s.Col) | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | SOURCE | THEN | DELETE | ; | -- MERGE must end with ; | THE 3 CASES | WHEN MATCHED  →  UPDATE | The key exists in | both | tables → update the target row. | NOT MATCHED BY TARGET  →  INSERT | The row is | only in the source | → it's new, insert it. | NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE  →  DELETE | The row is | only in the target | → it's gone from the source, delete it (optional). | i | Real use: | sync | a table with fresh data — e.g. load today's price list into | Products | in one step instead of separate UPDATE + INSERT + DELETE.

[S22] Temporary Tables
[S23] Temporary Tables | A | temporary table | is a real table stored in | tempdb | and deleted | automatically | — perfect for holding | intermediate results | while you work. | KEY POINTS | ✔ | Stored in the system database | tempdb | → System Databases → tempdb → Temporary Tables. | ✔ | The name starts with | # | (local) or | ## | (global). | ✔ | Works like a normal table: | INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, JOIN | , PK, constraints and | indexes | . | ✔ | Dropped | automatically | — or drop it yourself with | DROP TABLE #Name | . | i | Like a | whiteboard | in a meeting room: you use it during the meeting, and it's | wiped | when the meeting ends. | TYPES | # | Local Temp Table   #TableName | Visible | only | in the | session | (query window) that created it. Dropped when that session | closes | . | ## | Global Temp Table   ##TableName | Visible to | all sessions | . Dropped when the creating session closes | and | no other session is still using it.
[S24] Creating Temporary Tables | ①  CREATE TABLE  +  INSERT | CREATE | TABLE | #Students | ( | Id | INT | PRIMARY | KEY | , | Name | VARCHAR | ( | 50 | ), | Grade | INT | ); | INSERT | INTO | #Students | VALUES | ( | 1 | , | 'Ahmed' | , | 90 | ), ( | 2 | , | 'Mona' | , | 85 | ); | SELECT | * | FROM | #Students | ; | ④  DROP IT YOURSELF | DROP | TABLE | #Students | ; | -- drop now | DROP | TABLE | IF | EXISTS | #HighSalary | ; | -- 2016+ | ②  SELECT INTO  #Temp  (structure + data in one step) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | INTO | #HighSalary | FROM | Employees | WHERE | Salary > | 20000 | ; | SELECT | * | FROM | #HighSalary | ; | ③  GLOBAL TEMP TABLE  (two #) | CREATE | TABLE | ##Settings | ( | SettingKey | VARCHAR | ( | 50 | ), | SettingValue | VARCHAR | ( | 100 | ) | ); | i | Tip: start your script with | DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #Name | so you can | re-run | it without the error | "There is already an object named …" | .
[S25] Temporary Table – Real Use Case | Find the employees who earn | more than their department's average | salary. | STEP 1 · SAVE THE AVERAGES IN A TEMP TABLE | SELECT | DepartmentID, | AVG | (Salary) | AS | AvgSalary | INTO | #DeptAvg | FROM | Employees | GROUP | BY | DepartmentID; | #DeptAvg | TEMP | in tempdb | DepartmentID | AvgSalary | 1 | 23500 | 2 | 18000 | 3 | 16000 | STEP 3 · CLEAN UP (optional) | DROP | TABLE | #DeptAvg | ; | STEP 2 · USE IT IN ANOTHER QUERY | SELECT | e.EmployeeName, e.Salary, t.AvgSalary | FROM | Employees e | JOIN | #DeptAvg | t | ON | e.DepartmentID = t.DepartmentID | WHERE | e.Salary > t.AvgSalary; | Result | 1 row | EmployeeName | Salary | AvgSalary | Ali Hassan | 25000 | 23500 | i | Why a temp table? | The averages are calculated | once | and can be reused in | many queries | — and a big query becomes | small, readable steps | .
[S26] Local vs Global in Action | SQLQuery1.sql  —  Session 1 | CREATE | TABLE | #LocalTemp | (Id | INT | ); | CREATE | TABLE | ##GlobalTemp | (Id | INT | ); | SELECT | * | FROM | #LocalTemp | ; | -- works | SELECT | * | FROM | ##GlobalTemp | ; | -- works | SQLQuery2.sql  —  Session 2 | SELECT | * | FROM | #LocalTemp | ; | -- Error: Invalid object name '#LocalTemp'. | SELECT | * | FROM | ##GlobalTemp | ; | -- works | Local  #Temp | Global  ##Temp | Visible to | Only the session that created it | All sessions (every query window / user) | Dropped when | That session closes | The creator closes AND nobody else uses it | Same name in 2 sessions? | ✔ Yes — each session gets its own copy | ✘ No — only one table with that name | i | In tempdb, a local temp table gets a long | suffix | (e.g. | #LocalTemp_______00000000001A | ) — that's how two sessions can both have their | own | #LocalTemp | .
[S27] Temp Table vs Table Variable
[S28] Temp Table vs Table Variable | TABLE VARIABLE | DECLARE | @TopProducts | TABLE | ( | Id | INT | , | Name | VARCHAR | ( | 50 | ) | ); | INSERT | INTO | @TopProducts | SELECT | TOP | ( | 3 | ) Id, ProductName | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | ; | SELECT | * | FROM | @TopProducts | ; | ! | A table variable lives only for the | current batch | — run the DECLARE and the queries | together | ( | GO | ends the batch). | #Temp Table  vs  @Table Variable | #Temp Table | @Table Variable | Create | CREATE TABLE #T (…) | DECLARE @T TABLE (…) | Scope | Session (until closed / dropped) | Current batch / procedure only | Stored in | tempdb | tempdb too (not only memory!) | Indexes | PK, UNIQUE + CREATE INDEX later | Only inside the DECLARE | Statistics | ✔ Yes → good for large data | ✘ No → best for small data | ROLLBACK | Changes are rolled back | Data is NOT rolled back | ALTER / SELECT INTO | ✔ Allowed | ✘ Not allowed | i | Quick rule: | small data, simple use | → @Table variable. | Large data, needs indexes, or used across batches | → #Temp table.

ASP.Net Course
Question 1 — Archive Patients With No Drug History
Copy into PatientsBackup every patient who has never received any drug, then delete those same patients from Patients. Use a subquery for the condition, not a hard-coded list of Ids.
Question 2 — Raise Salaries Above the Average Examination Count
Raise the salary of every consultant by 15% if the number of examinations they performed is greater than the average number of examinations per consultant.
Question 3 — Delete the Drug Administrations of One Ward
Delete every row in DrugAdministrations that belongs to a patient staying in the ward named 'Cardiology'. The ward name must be resolved inside a subquery.
Question 4 — Patients Above the Overall Average Quantity
Show the patient name, ward name, and the total quantity of drugs they received, but only for patients whose total is greater than the average total across all patients.
Question 5 — Nurses Serving in the Busiest Ward
List the nurses who serve in the ward that currently holds the largest number of patients, showing the nurse name and the ward name.
Question 6 — Examined Patients - Three Ways
Return the patients who have at least one row in PatientExaminations, together with their ward name. Write it three times: with IN, with EXISTS, and with JOIN. Then explain what differs between them.
Question 7 — Patients Who Never Received a Drug
Return the patients who have never received any drug, with their ward name. Write it with NOT IN, with NOT EXISTS, and with LEFT JOIN. Then answer: if DrugAdministrations.PatientId contained a single NULL row, which version would break and exactly why?
Question 8 — Patients Above Their Own Ward Average
Return every patient whose total administered quantity is greater than the average total of the patients in the SAME ward - not the overall average. Show the ward name next to each patient.
Question 9 — Most Administered Drug per Ward
For each ward, return the drug with the highest total administered quantity, showing the ward name, the drug name, and that total.
Question 10 — Wards Above the Average Patient Count
Return the wards holding more patients than the average number of patients per ward, showing the ward name and its patient count, sorted from the busiest down.
Question 11 — Consultants Assigned but Never Examining
A consultant can be assigned to a patient without ever examining him. Return every assignment where the consultant has never examined that same patient, showing the consultant name and the patient name.
Question 12 — Ward Summary With Scalar Subqueries
For every ward, show the ward name, how many patients it holds, and how many nurses serve in it. Use scalar subqueries in the SELECT list instead of joining and grouping.
Question 13 — Nurses Who Served the Cardiology Ward
Return the nurses who administered at least one drug to a patient staying in the ward named 'Cardiology'. Resolve the ward name inside a subquery.
Question 14 — Consultants Above Every Idle Consultant
Return the consultants whose salary is higher than the salary of EVERY consultant who has never examined a patient. Use ALL in your answer.
Question 15 — Assign Unassigned Patients to the Emptiest Ward
Every patient whose WardId is NULL must be moved into the ward that currently holds the fewest patients. Resolve that ward with a subquery, not with a hard-coded Id.

--========================================================================

(

)

(

(
    Id INT   ,

SELECT * FROM @VariableTable



--========================================================================
--   2-    CTE
--========================================================================
-- Nurser whose salary > avg salary of all nurses
-- display Nurse name , salary , Totalavgsalary  

SELECT 
   N.Name , 
   N.Salary ,
   (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Nurses) AS  TotalAvgSalary
FROM Nurses N     
WHERE N.Salary > (
                    SELECT AVG(Salary)
                    FROM Nurses
                  )
-- ----------same with CTE

;WITH TotalAvg AS
(
        SELECT AVG(Salary) AS AvgSalary
                    FROM Nurses
                    )

SELECT 
   N.Name , 
   N.Salary ,
   (SELECT AvgSalary FROM TotalAvg ) AS TotalAvg
FROM Nurses N     
WHERE N.Salary > (SELECT AvgSalary FROM TotalAvg )






--------------------- 2 CTE 

;WITH TotalAvg AS
(
        SELECT AVG(Salary) AS AvgSalary
         FROM Nurses
  ) , 
  TotalSum AS 
 (
      SELECT SUM(Salary) AS SUMSalary
         FROM Nurses
     
  )

SELECT 
   N.Name , 
   N.Salary ,
   (SELECT AvgSalary FROM TotalAvg ) AS TotalAvg ,
   (SELECT SUMSalary FROM TotalSum ) AS TotalSum
FROM Nurses N     
WHERE N.Salary > (SELECT AvgSalary FROM TotalAvg )


--SELECT AvgSalary FROM TotalAvg



--========================================================================
--   3-    CTE Practice
--========================================================================

--Q_1  Save each patient's total drug Quantity in #PatientDrugTotals, then show the top 5 patients [patient name , TotalQuantity]
--

SELECT 
   DA.PatientId , 
   SUM(Quantity) AS TotalQuantity
INTO #PatientDrugTotals
FROM DrugAdministrations DA 
GROUP BY DA.PatientId 


SELECT TOP 5  
  P.Name ,
  PT.TotalQuantity
FROM #PatientDrugTotals  PT
JOIN Patients P
 ON PT.PatientId = P.Id
ORDER BY TotalQuantity DESC 









--Q_03 Using a CTE, show each ward name with the number of nurses serving in it  only wards with more than 6 nurses.
   -- [ward name - NursesCount in each ward]


WITH TotalCount AS
(
   SELECT 
    N.ServesInWardId ,
    COUNT(*)  AS NumberOfNurses
   FROM Nurses N
   GROUP BY N.ServesInWardId
)

SELECT  
  W.Name,
  TC.NumberOfNurses
FROM Wards W
JOIN TotalCount TC
  ON W.Id = TC.ServesInWardId
WHERE TC.NumberOfNurses > 6



--========================================================================
--   4-   Questions 
--========================================================================

--Question 1  Archive Patients With No Drug History

--Copy into PatientsBackup every patient who has never received any drug, 
--then delete those same patients from Patients. 
--Use a subquery for the condition, not a hard-coded list of Ids.


SELECT  P.Id , P.Name , P.DOB , P.WardId
INTO #PatientsBackup
FROM Patients P
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
                     SELECT 1
                     FROM DrugAdministrations DA 
                     WHERE DA.PatientId = P.Id
                     ) 

DELETE P
FROM Patients P
WHERE  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM #PatientsBackup  B WHERE B.Id = P.Id  )



-- EXISTS (SELECT 1 )
-- NOT EXISTS () 









--Question 2  Raise Salaries Above the Average Examination Count
--Raise the salary of every consultant by 15% 
--if the number of examinations they performed is greater than the average number of examinations per consultant.




UPDATE Consultants 
SET Salary = Salary * 1.15
WHERE (
            SELECT 
            COUNT(*) 
            FROM PatientExaminations PE 
            WHERE PE.ConsultantId = Consultants.Id 
            )  >  (
                        SELECT 
                        AVG(X.PatientsCounts)

                        FROM (

                        SELECT 
                            COUNT(*) AS PatientsCounts
                        FROM PatientExaminations PE
                        GROUP BY PE.ConsultantId
                        ) X
                        )




--Question 3  Delete the Drug Administrations of One Ward

--Delete every row in DrugAdministrations that belongs to a patient staying in the ward named 'Cardiology'.
--The ward name must be resolved inside a subquery.
-- Use CTE

WITH CardiologyPatients AS 
(
 SELECT  
    P.Id
 FROM Patients P
 JOIN Wards W 
   ON P.WardId = W.Id
 WHERE W.Name = 'Cardiology'

)

DELETE D 
FROM DrugAdministrations D
WHERE D.PatientId IN (SELECT Id FROM CardiologyPatients )





--Question 4  Patients Above the Overall Average Quantity
--Show the patient name, ward name, and the total quantity of drugs they received,
--but only for patients whose total is greater than the average total across all patients.


select p.Name, w.Name, sum(da.Quantity) as totalDrug
from Patients p 
join DrugAdministrations da
on da.PatientId = p.Id
left join Wards w
on p.WardId = w.Id
group by p.Id, p.Name, w.Name
having sum(da.Quantity) > (
select avg (y)
from (select sum(Quantity) as y
from DrugAdministrations
group by PatientId) as x
)





--Question 5  Nurses Serving in the Busiest Ward
--List the nurses who serve in the ward that currently holds the largest number of patients,
--showing the nurse name and the ward name.


SELECT N.Name AS NurseName, W.Name AS WardName
FROM Nurses N INNER JOIN Wards W 
ON N.ServesInWardId = W.Id
WHERE W.Id IN (

SELECT TOP 1 WITH TIES P.WardId
FROM Patients P
GROUP BY P.WardId
HAVING COUNT(P.WardId) != 0
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC

)






--------- 

--Question 6  Examined Patients - Three Ways

--Return the patients who have at least one row in PatientExaminations,
--together with their ward name. 
--Write it three times: with IN, with EXISTS, and with JOIN. 
--Then explain what differs between them.

            
--(1) IN

SELECT 
  P.Name AS PatientName  ,
  W.Name  AS WardName 
FROM Patients P
JOIN Wards W 
  ON P.WardId = W.Id
WHERE P.Id IN 
(

 SELECT  PE.PatientId
 FROM PatientExaminations PE
 GROUP BY PE.PatientId

)



--(2)   EXISTS

SELECT 
  P.Name AS PatientName  ,
  W.Name  AS WardName 
FROM Patients P
JOIN Wards W 
  ON P.WardId = W.Id
WHERE EXISTS 
(
SELECT 1
FROM PatientExaminations PE 
WHERE PE.PatientId = P.Id


)





--(3)   JOIN


SELECT 
  DISTINCT
  P.Name AS PatientName  ,
  W.Name  AS WardName 
FROM Patients P
JOIN Wards W 
  ON P.WardId = W.Id
JOIN PatientExaminations PE 
  ON PE.PatientId = P.Id

[S02] Workshop Agenda | 01 | OFFSET - FETCH | 02 | Insert Based on Select | 03 | Advanced DML | 04 | Temporary Tables | 05 | Temp Table vs Table Variable | 06 | CTE (Common Table Expression)
[S03] OFFSET - FETCH
[S04] OFFSET - FETCH | OFFSET – FETCH | lets you | skip | a number of rows, then | return | a specific number of rows from a | sorted | result — the standard way to do | paging | in SQL Server. | SYNTAX | SELECT | column1, column2, ... | FROM | TableName | ORDER | BY | column1 | -- required | OFFSET | n | ROWS | -- rows to skip | FETCH | NEXT | m | ROWS | ONLY | ; | -- rows to return | i | Think of a | book | : ORDER BY numbers the pages, | OFFSET | = pages you flip past, | FETCH | = pages you actually read. | KEY POINTS | ✔ | ORDER BY | is mandatory — OFFSET-FETCH works on a | sorted | result. | ✔ | OFFSET n ROWS | = how many rows to | skip | (0 = skip nothing). | ✔ | FETCH NEXT m ROWS ONLY | = how many rows to | return | after skipping. | ✔ | OFFSET can be used | without FETCH | (skip n, return the rest) — but | FETCH needs OFFSET | . | ✔ | ROW / ROWS | and | FIRST / NEXT | mean the same thing. Available since | SQL Server 2012 | . | THE RULE IN ACTION | ✔ Correct | SELECT | * | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | OFFSET | 0 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 5 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | ✘ Error: OFFSET - FETCH without ORDER BY | SELECT | * | FROM | Products | OFFSET | 0 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 5 | ROWS | ONLY | ;
[S05] OFFSET - FETCH Example | Skip the | 2 most expensive | products, then return the | next 3 | — ordered by | Price DESC | . | Products | ordered by Price DESC · 8 rows | Id | ProductName | Price | Status | 1 | Laptop | 1000 | Skipped (OFFSET 2) | 6 | Desk | 300 | Skipped (OFFSET 2) | 4 | Monitor | 200 | ✔ Fetched | 5 | Chair | 150 | ✔ Fetched | 7 | Headphones | 80 | ✔ Fetched | 8 | Webcam | 60 | Not returned | 3 | Keyboard | 50 | Not returned | 2 | Mouse | 20 | Not returned | QUERY | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | OFFSET | 2 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Result | 3 rows | Id | ProductName | Price | 4 | Monitor | 200 | 5 | Chair | 150 | 7 | Headphones | 80 | i | OFFSET 2 | skipped Laptop and Desk  → | FETCH NEXT 3 | returned Monitor, Chair, Headphones  →  the remaining rows were | not returned | .
[S06] Paging with OFFSET - FETCH | OFFSET (PageNumber − 1) × PageSize ROWS   FETCH NEXT PageSize ROWS ONLY | QUERY — GET PAGE 2 | DECLARE | @PageNumber | INT | = | 2 | ; | DECLARE | @PageSize | INT | = | 3 | ; | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Id | OFFSET | ( | @PageNumber | - | 1 | ) * | @PageSize | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | @PageSize | ROWS | ONLY | ; | IN .NET — EF CORE TRANSLATES Skip / Take INTO OFFSET - FETCH | var page = context.Products | .OrderBy(p => p.Id) | .Skip((pageNumber - | 1 | ) * pageSize) | .Take(pageSize) | .ToList(); | PAGES  (PageSize = 3) | Page 1 | 1  Laptop | 2  Mouse | 3  Keyboard | Page 2 | 4  Monitor | 5  Chair | 6  Desk | Page 3 | 7  Headphones | 8  Webcam | @PageNumber | OFFSET | FETCH NEXT | Rows returned | 1 | 0 | 3 | Ids 1 – 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 | Ids 4 – 6 | 3 | 6 | 3 | Ids 7 – 8 | i | The | last page | may return | fewer rows | (page 3 → 2 rows). A page | after the end | returns | no rows | — not an error.
[S07] TOP vs OFFSET - FETCH | TOP  vs  OFFSET – FETCH | Feature | TOP | OFFSET – FETCH | Skip rows | ✘ No | ✔ Yes | ORDER BY | Optional | ✔ Required | Standard | T-SQL only | ANSI SQL standard | WITH TIES / PERCENT | ✔ Supported | ✘ Not supported | Best for | First N rows | Paging (page 1, 2, 3 …) | SAME RESULT, TWO WAYS | SELECT | TOP | ( | 3 | ) * | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | ; | -- is the same as | SELECT | * | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | OFFSET | 0 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | COMMON MISTAKE — UNSTABLE PAGES | ✘ Paging on a non-unique column | ORDER | BY | Price | OFFSET | 3 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Products with the | same price | may show up on | two pages | — or on | none | . | ✔ Add a unique tie-breaker column | ORDER | BY | Price, Id | OFFSET | 3 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | The order is now | always the same | → every row appears on | exactly one | page.
[S08] Paging with ROW_NUMBER() | Before SQL Server 2012 there was no OFFSET-FETCH — paging was done with | ROW_NUMBER() | . You'll still meet it in older projects. | QUERY — PAGE 2  (PageSize = 3) | SELECT | * | FROM | ( | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price, | ROW_NUMBER | () | OVER | ( | ORDER | BY | Id) | AS | RowNum | FROM | Products | ) | AS | t | WHERE | t. | RowNum | BETWEEN | 4 | AND | 6 | ; | -- page 2 | SAME RESULT WITH OFFSET - FETCH  (shorter & clearer) | SELECT | Id, ProductName, Price | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Id | OFFSET | 3 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 3 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Inner query (t) | RowNum 4 – 6 returned | Id | ProductName | Price | RowNum | 1 | Laptop | 1000 | 1 | 2 | Mouse | 20 | 2 | 3 | Keyboard | 50 | 3 | 4 | Monitor | 200 | 4 | 5 | Chair | 150 | 5 | 6 | Desk | 300 | 6 | 7 | Headphones | 80 | 7 | 8 | Webcam | 60 | 8 | ! | ROW_NUMBER() can't be used directly in | WHERE | — that's why we wrap it in a | subquery | (or a CTE).
[S09] OFFSET - FETCH — Practice | Use the | Hospital | database (restore | Hospital.bak | ) — tables | Consultants | and | Patients | . | Q1 | WRITE | Return the | 5 highest-paid consultants | (Name, Salary) using OFFSET - FETCH. | Q2 | WRITE | Show | page 3 | of the | Patients | list ordered by | Id | , with a page size of | 10 | . Which Ids appear? | Q3 | PREDICT | What does this query return? | SELECT | Name | FROM | Consultants | ORDER | BY | Salary | OFFSET | 2 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 2 | ROWS | ONLY | ; | Q4 | FIX THE BUG | Paging consultants | 2 per page | : Dr. Amira El-Din sometimes shows on | two pages | . Why? Fix it. | SELECT | Name, Salary | FROM | Consultants | ORDER | BY | Salary | DESC | OFFSET | 2 | ROWS | FETCH | NEXT | 2 | ROWS | ONLY | ;
[S10] Insert Based on Select
[S11] Insert Based on Select | INSERT INTO … SELECT | copies the result of a query into an | existing | table — instead of typing VALUES row by row, the rows come from a | SELECT | . | SYNTAX | INSERT | INTO | TargetTable | (col1, col2, ...) | SELECT | col1, col2, ... | FROM | SourceTable | WHERE | condition; | -- optional | i | Like copying rows from one Excel sheet and | pasting | them into another sheet that | already has its own headers | . | KEY POINTS | ✔ | The | target table must already exist | (unlike SELECT INTO). | ✔ | Columns must match in | number | and | order | , with | compatible data types | . | ✔ | Always write the | target column list | — safer and clearer. | ✔ | The SELECT can use | WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY | , expressions and constant values. | ✔ | Target | constraints | (PK, FK, CHECK, NOT NULL) are still checked — | IDENTITY | values are generated automatically. | THE RULE IN ACTION | ✔ Correct | INSERT | INTO | ArchivedEmployees (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | FROM | Employees; | ✘ Error: SELECT returns fewer columns than the insert list | INSERT | INTO | ArchivedEmployees (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName | FROM | Employees;
[S12] Insert Based on Select – Example | Copy the employees with | Salary > 20000 | into the | existing | table | HighSalaryEmployees | . | Employees | source table · 4 rows | EmployeeID | EmployeeName | DepartmentID | Salary | 1 | Ali Hassan | 1 | 25000 | 2 | Sara Mohamed | 2 | 18000 | 3 | Mona Ali | 1 | 22000 | 4 | Youssef Ibrahim | 3 | 16000 | HighSalaryEmployees | before · 1 row | Id (IDENTITY) | Name | Salary | 1 | Khaled Omar | 30000 | QUERY | INSERT | INTO | HighSalaryEmployees | (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | FROM | Employees | WHERE | Salary > | 20000 | ; | HighSalaryEmployees | after · (2 rows affected) | Id | Name | Salary | 1 | Khaled Omar | 30000 | existing | 2 | Ali Hassan | 25000 | ✔ inserted | 3 | Mona Ali | 22000 | ✔ inserted | i | The old row ( | Khaled Omar | ) is | kept | — INSERT … SELECT | adds | rows. | Id | is not in the column list because | IDENTITY | generates it.
[S13] Insert Select With JOIN & Expressions | Fill | EmployeeReport | with each employee's | department name | , | annual | salary and | today's date | . | QUERY | INSERT | INTO | EmployeeReport | (EmployeeName, DepartmentName, AnnualSalary, ReportDate) | SELECT | e.EmployeeName, | d.DepartmentName, | e.Salary * | 12 | , | -- expression | GETDATE | () | -- function value | FROM | Employees e | JOIN | Departments d | ON | e.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID; | COLUMN MAPPING (BY POSITION) | e.EmployeeName | EmployeeName | d.DepartmentName | DepartmentName | e.Salary * 12 | AnnualSalary | GETDATE() | ReportDate | EmployeeReport | (4 rows affected) | EmployeeName | DepartmentName | AnnualSalary | ReportDate | Ali Hassan | IT | 300000 | 2026-09-28 | Sara Mohamed | HR | 216000 | 2026-09-28 | Mona Ali | IT | 264000 | 2026-09-28 | Youssef Ibrahim | Sales | 192000 | 2026-09-28 | ! | Columns are matched by | position | , not by name — the 3rd SELECT item goes into the 3rd column ( | AnnualSalary | ).
[S14] SELECT INTO vs INSERT INTO … SELECT | SELECT INTO  (Session 06) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | INTO | NewEmployees | -- created now | FROM | Employees; | INSERT INTO … SELECT  (OldEmployees must exist) | INSERT | INTO | OldEmployees | (Name, Salary) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | FROM | Employees; | SELECT INTO | INSERT INTO … SELECT | Target table | Created automatically — must NOT exist | Must already exist | Existing rows | — (brand-new table) | Kept — new rows are appended | PK / constraints / indexes | Not copied | The target's own constraints apply | Columns | Taken from the SELECT list | You choose the target columns | Error when… | The table already exists | Column count / data types don't match | Best for | Quick copy / backup of data | Loading data into a designed table | i | Rule of thumb: | New table? | → SELECT INTO. | Table already designed? | → INSERT INTO … SELECT.
[S15] Insert Based on Select — Practice | Use the | Hospital | database (restore | Hospital.bak | ) — tables | Patients | , | Wards | , | Consultants | , | Nurses | . | Q1 | WRITE | Create | ICUPatients | (Id, Name, DOB), then copy into it all patients of the ward | 'Intensive Care Unit (ICU)' | (use a JOIN with Wards). | Q2 | WRITE | Table | WardSummary | (WardName, PatientsCount) already exists. Fill it with the | number of patients per ward | . | Q3 | FIX THE BUG | Why does this INSERT fail? [S16] Advanced DML
[S17] UPDATE with JOIN | UPDATE … JOIN | changes rows in one table using data or conditions from | another table | . | SYNTAX | UPDATE | t | SET | t | .Column = s.Column | FROM | TargetTable | t | JOIN | SourceTable s | ON | t | .Key = s.Key | WHERE | condition; | -- optional | EXAMPLE — 10% RAISE FOR THE IT DEPARTMENT | UPDATE | e | SET | e | .Salary = | e | .Salary * | 1 | . | 10 | FROM | Employees | e | JOIN | Departments d | ON | e | .DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID | WHERE | d.DepartmentName = | 'IT' | ; | Employees | (2 rows affected) | EmployeeID | EmployeeName | Department | Salary (before) | Salary (after) | 1 | Ali Hassan | IT | 25000 | 27500  ✔ | 2 | Sara Mohamed | HR | 18000 | 18000  (no change) | 3 | Mona Ali | IT | 22000 | 24200  ✔ | 4 | Youssef Ibrahim | Sales | 16000 | 16000  (no change) | i | Safety tip: run it as a | SELECT | first (same FROM / JOIN / WHERE) to see | exactly which rows | will change — then turn it into UPDATE.
[S18] DELETE with JOIN | DELETE … JOIN | removes rows from one table based on data in | another table | . | SYNTAX | DELETE | t | FROM | TargetTable | t | JOIN | OtherTable o | ON | t | .Key = o.Key | WHERE | condition; | EXAMPLE — DELETE THE SALES EMPLOYEES | DELETE | e | FROM | Employees | e | JOIN | Departments d | ON | e | .DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID | WHERE | d.DepartmentName = | 'Sales' | ; | Employees | (1 row affected) | EmployeeID | EmployeeName | DepartmentID | Salary | 1 | Ali Hassan | 1 | 25000 | kept | 2 | Sara Mohamed | 2 | 18000 | kept | 3 | Mona Ali | 1 | 22000 | kept | 4 | Youssef Ibrahim | 3 | 16000 | ✘ deleted | i | The alias after | DELETE | ( | DELETE e | ) tells SQL Server | which table | to delete from — | Departments is not touched | . | TEST IT SAFELY | BEGIN | TRAN | ; | DELETE | e | FROM | Employees e ...; | SELECT | * | FROM | Employees; | -- check | ROLLBACK | ; | -- undo
[S19] MERGE | MERGE | compares a | source | with a | target | and — in | one statement | — updates matching rows, inserts new ones and (optionally) deletes missing ones. | SYNTAX | MERGE | TargetTable | AS | t | USING | SourceTable | AS | s | ON | t.Key = s.Key | WHEN | MATCHED | THEN | UPDATE | SET | t.Col = s.Col | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | TARGET | THEN | INSERT | (Key, Col) | VALUES | (s.Key, s.Col) | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | SOURCE | THEN | DELETE | ; | -- MERGE must end with ; | THE 3 CASES | WHEN MATCHED  →  UPDATE | The key exists in | both | tables → update the target row. | NOT MATCHED BY TARGET  →  INSERT | The row is | only in the source | → it's new, insert it. | NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE  →  DELETE | The row is | only in the target | → it's gone from the source, delete it (optional). | i | Real use: | sync | a table with fresh data — e.g. load today's price list into | Products | in one step instead of separate UPDATE + INSERT + DELETE.
[S20] MERGE – Example | Sync | Products | (target) with today's price list | NewPrices | (source). | Products | target · before | Id | ProductName | Price | 1 | Laptop | 1000 | 2 | Mouse | 20 | 3 | Keyboard | 50 | NewPrices | source | Id | ProductName | Price | 1 | Laptop | 950 | 3 | Keyboard | 55 | 4 | Monitor | 200 | Ids | 1, 3 | in both → | UPDATE | Id | 4 | only in source → | INSERT | Id | 2 | only in target → | DELETE | QUERY | MERGE | Products | AS | t | USING | NewPrices | AS | s | ON | t.Id = s.Id | WHEN | MATCHED | THEN | UPDATE | SET | t.Price = s.Price | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | TARGET | THEN | INSERT | (Id, ProductName, Price) | VALUES | (s.Id, s.ProductName, s.Price) | WHEN | NOT | MATCHED | BY | SOURCE | THEN | DELETE | ; | Products | after | Id | ProductName | Price | What happened | 1 | Laptop | 950 | UPDATE | 3 | Keyboard | 55 | UPDATE | 4 | Monitor | 200 | INSERT | 2 | Mouse | 20 | DELETE

[S22] Temporary Tables
[S23] Temporary Tables | A | temporary table | is a real table stored in | tempdb | and deleted | automatically | — perfect for holding | intermediate results | while you work. | KEY POINTS | ✔ | Stored in the system database | tempdb | → System Databases → tempdb → Temporary Tables. | ✔ | The name starts with | # | (local) or | ## | (global). | ✔ | Works like a normal table: | INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, JOIN | , PK, constraints and | indexes | . | ✔ | Dropped | automatically | — or drop it yourself with | DROP TABLE #Name | . | i | Like a | whiteboard | in a meeting room: you use it during the meeting, and it's | wiped | when the meeting ends. | TYPES | # | Local Temp Table   #TableName | Visible | only | in the | session | (query window) that created it. Dropped when that session | closes | . | ## | Global Temp Table   ##TableName | Visible to | all sessions | . Dropped when the creating session closes | and | no other session is still using it.
[S24] Creating Temporary Tables | ①  CREATE TABLE  +  INSERT | CREATE | TABLE | #Students | ( | Id | INT | PRIMARY | KEY | , | Name | VARCHAR | ( | 50 | ), | Grade | INT | ); | INSERT | INTO | #Students | VALUES | ( | 1 | , | 'Ahmed' | , | 90 | ), ( | 2 | , | 'Mona' | , | 85 | ); | SELECT | * | FROM | #Students | ; | ④  DROP IT YOURSELF | DROP | TABLE | #Students | ; | -- drop now | DROP | TABLE | IF | EXISTS | #HighSalary | ; | -- 2016+ | ②  SELECT INTO  #Temp  (structure + data in one step) | SELECT | EmployeeName, Salary | INTO | #HighSalary | FROM | Employees | WHERE | Salary > | 20000 | ; | SELECT | * | FROM | #HighSalary | ; | ③  GLOBAL TEMP TABLE  (two #) | CREATE | TABLE | ##Settings | ( | SettingKey | VARCHAR | ( | 50 | ), | SettingValue | VARCHAR | ( | 100 | ) | ); | i | Tip: start your script with | DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #Name | so you can | re-run | it without the error | "There is already an object named …" | .
[S25] Temporary Table – Real Use Case | Find the employees who earn | more than their department's average | salary. | STEP 1 · SAVE THE AVERAGES IN A TEMP TABLE | SELECT | DepartmentID, | AVG | (Salary) | AS | AvgSalary | INTO | #DeptAvg | FROM | Employees | GROUP | BY | DepartmentID; | #DeptAvg | TEMP | in tempdb | DepartmentID | AvgSalary | 1 | 23500 | 2 | 18000 | 3 | 16000 | STEP 3 · CLEAN UP (optional) | DROP | TABLE | #DeptAvg | ; | STEP 2 · USE IT IN ANOTHER QUERY | SELECT | e.EmployeeName, e.Salary, t.AvgSalary | FROM | Employees e | JOIN | #DeptAvg | t | ON | e.DepartmentID = t.DepartmentID | WHERE | e.Salary > t.AvgSalary; | Result | 1 row | EmployeeName | Salary | AvgSalary | Ali Hassan | 25000 | 23500 | i | Why a temp table? | The averages are calculated | once | and can be reused in | many queries | — and a big query becomes | small, readable steps | .
[S26] Local vs Global in Action | SQLQuery1.sql  —  Session 1 | CREATE | TABLE | #LocalTemp | (Id | INT | ); | CREATE | TABLE | ##GlobalTemp | (Id | INT | ); | SELECT | * | FROM | #LocalTemp | ; | -- works | SELECT | * | FROM | ##GlobalTemp | ; | -- works | SQLQuery2.sql  —  Session 2 | SELECT | * | FROM | #LocalTemp | ; | -- Error: Invalid object name '#LocalTemp'. | SELECT | * | FROM | ##GlobalTemp | ; | -- works | Local  #Temp | Global  ##Temp | Visible to | Only the session that created it | All sessions (every query window / user) | Dropped when | That session closes | The creator closes AND nobody else uses it | Same name in 2 sessions? | ✔ Yes — each session gets its own copy | ✘ No — only one table with that name | i | In tempdb, a local temp table gets a long | suffix | (e.g. | #LocalTemp_______00000000001A | ) — that's how two sessions can both have their | own | #LocalTemp | .
[S27] Temp Table vs Table Variable
[S28] Temp Table vs Table Variable | TABLE VARIABLE | DECLARE | @TopProducts | TABLE | ( | Id | INT | , | Name | VARCHAR | ( | 50 | ) | ); | INSERT | INTO | @TopProducts | SELECT | TOP | ( | 3 | ) Id, ProductName | FROM | Products | ORDER | BY | Price | DESC | ; | SELECT | * | FROM | @TopProducts | ; | ! | A table variable lives only for the | current batch | — run the DECLARE and the queries | together | ( | GO | ends the batch). | #Temp Table  vs  @Table Variable | #Temp Table | @Table Variable | Create | CREATE TABLE #T (…) | DECLARE @T TABLE (…) | Scope | Session (until closed / dropped) | Current batch / procedure only | Stored in | tempdb | tempdb too (not only memory!) | Indexes | PK, UNIQUE + CREATE INDEX later | Only inside the DECLARE | Statistics | ✔ Yes → good for large data | ✘ No → best for small data | ROLLBACK | Changes are rolled back | Data is NOT rolled back | ALTER / SELECT INTO | ✔ Allowed | ✘ Not allowed | i | Quick rule: | small data, simple use | → @Table variable. | Large data, needs indexes, or used across batches | → #Temp table.
[S29] CTE
[S30] CTE (Common Table Expression) | A | CTE | (Common Table Expression) is a | named temporary result | written with | WITH | — it exists | only for the statement right after it | . | SYNTAX | WITH | CteName | AS | ( | SELECT | ... | ) | SELECT | * | FROM | CteName | ; | ✔ | Not stored | anywhere — it's just a named query (unlike #Temp in tempdb). | ✔ | Used | only | by the next statement — then it's gone. | ✔ | The statement | before | WITH must end with | ; | . | ✔ | Makes long queries | readable | — a cleaner way to write a derived table (Session 06). | SAME USE CASE AS #DeptAvg — WITHOUT A TEMP TABLE | WITH | DeptAvg | AS | ( | SELECT | DepartmentID, | AVG | (Salary) | AS | AvgSalary | FROM | Employees | GROUP | BY | DepartmentID | ) | SELECT | e.EmployeeName, e.Salary, d.AvgSalary | FROM | Employees e | JOIN | DeptAvg | d | ON | e.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID | WHERE | e.Salary > d.AvgSalary; | Result | 1 row | EmployeeName | Salary | AvgSalary | Ali Hassan | 25000 | 23500
[S31] CTE vs Temp Table vs Table Variable | CTE  vs  #Temp  vs  @Table | CTE | #Temp Table | @Table Variable | Lives for | One statement | The session | The batch / procedure | Stored | Not stored (just a query) | tempdb | tempdb | Reuse in many queries | ✘ No | ✔ Yes | ✔ Yes (same batch) | Indexes | ✘ No | ✔ Yes | Only inside DECLARE | Best for | Readable one-time queries | Big results reused many times | Small data in a batch / procedure | COMMON MISTAKE — USING A CTE TWICE | WITH | DeptAvg | AS | ( | SELECT | DepartmentID, | AVG | (Salary) | AS | AvgSalary | FROM | Employees | GROUP | BY | DepartmentID ) | SELECT | * | FROM | DeptAvg; | -- works | SELECT | * | FROM | DeptAvg; | -- Error: Invalid object name 'DeptAvg'. | HOW TO CHOOSE | Need it once, just for readability? | CTE | Big data, reused in many queries? | #Temp Table | Small data inside a batch / procedure? | @Table Variable

LINQ Challenge: Which Countries Still Buy From Us? 🌍 LINQ Challenge: Which Countries Still Buy From Us? A real business problem. Let's help the boss! 1 The Story 👩‍💼 "Hi! We sell food to shops all around the world. I want to know which countries bought from us in 1997 and are still buying in 1998 . Can you make me a report?" Think about it like this: a country is a happy market if shops there bought in both years. If a country bought in 1997 but stopped in 1998, the boss is worried. 😟 Country A Country B Country C 1997 1998 Country C has no green bar. It stopped buying. The boss does not want it in the report. 2 Your Data 🧑‍🍳 Customer CompanyName Country Orders Every customer lives in one country and has a list of orders. 🧾 Order OrderDate Total Each order has a date and money amount. You will use Source.CustomerList . 3 Your Mission For each country , show these 3 things: Total sales in 1997 💰 Total sales in 1998 💰 How many customers bought in 1998 🙋 Two more rules: ✅ Show only countries that bought in both years. ✅ Put the country with the biggest 1997 sales on top. 4 What Your Report Looks Like The numbers below are fake. They only show the shape of the table. Country Sales 1997 Sales 1998 Customers in 1998 Country A $ ? ? ? $ ? ? ? ? Country B $ ? ? ? $ ? ? ? ? Country D $ ? ? ? $ ? ? ? ? 5 Stuck? Open a Hint Hint 1: How do I start? Put customers in one group for each country. Think about which LINQ method makes groups. Hint 2: Orders are inside customers! A country has many customers, and each customer has many orders. How can you put all the orders of one country in one flat list? Hint 3: How do I split by year? Filter the orders by year. Then add up the totals. Do it once for each year. Think about it after you finish Look at the last order date in the data. Is it fair to compare 1997 and 1998? Why or why not? 🚀 "Every big query starts as one small step. Keep going, you are closer than you think!" your mentor : Menna Elashry 💜

1. Overview
The Library Management System (LMS) is designed to manage books, categories, authors, members, loans, and fines in an efficient and structured way.
It provides:
A structured way to organize books by categories and authors.
Easy registration and tracking of members.
Automated borrowing and returning of books.
Fine calculation for overdue or damaged items.
System Behavior:
The system should allow members to search books by title, author, or category.
When borrowing, the system should assign a due date (e.g., 14 days from loan date).
If the book is returned on time, no fine is applied.
If the book is overdue or damaged, the system should automatically calculate and issue a fine when the book is returned.
If fines remain unpaid, the member’s account status may be set to Suspended.
2. Entities & Their Details
2.1 Book ( Represents a book in the library )
Attributes:
 Id  – Unique identifier
Title – Title of the book
Price - the Book Price
 PublicationYear – Year of publication
AvailableCopies – Number of available copies
TotalCopies – Total number of copies in the library
Relationships:
One book → One author
One book → Many loans
One book → One Category (Each book must belong to one category)
2.2 Category ( Represents a category for books )
Attributes:
Id – Unique identifier
Title - Name of the category
Description - Category details
Relationships:
One Category → Many books (Each Book Must Belong To One Category)
2.3 Author ( Represents a writer of one or more books )
Attributes:
Id – Unique identifier
FirstName
LastName
DateOfBirth
Relationships:
One author → Many books (Each Book Must Belong To One Author)
2.4 Member ( Represents a registered library member )
Attributes:
Id – Unique identifier
Name
Email
PhoneNumber
Address
MembershipDate
Status (Active, Suspended)
Relationships:
One member → Many loans (One Member Can Loan Many Books)
2.5 Loan ( Represents a borrowing/returning transaction)
Attributes:
Id – Unique identifier
LoanDate – Date when book was borrowed
Status (Borrowed, Returned, Overdue)
Relationships:
When a member borrows a book, the system should store the following data :
DueDate – Expected return date
ReturnDate –  Actual return date
One Fine → One Loan (if the member exceeds the due date )
2.6 Fine ( Represents the money charged for overdue or damaged books )
Attributes:
Id – Unique identifier
Amount – the fine amount
IssuedDate – Date when fine was issued
PaidDate – Date when fine was paid
Status ( Pending, Paid)
Relationships:
One Fine → One Loan
