Resources.SearchableText: MVC-Session03.pptx 08 MVC\Hossam mostafa\Session 04\Presentation\MVC-Session03.pptx Hossam Mostafa Session 04 [S01] SESSION 03 ASP.NET Core MVC Repository, Dependency Injection, Plan Edit, ViewModels & Service Layer .NET Track [S02] Agenda MVC · Session 03 01 Repository Pattern SOLID's S & D · all data access in one place 02 Dependency Injection Ask for objects — don’t create them 03 Plan Edit — GET Tag Helpers · ViewData · ViewBag · TempData 04 Plan Edit — POST ViewModels · ModelState · PRG [S03] SECTION 01 Repository Pattern Move every database call out of the controller into one dedicated class 01 [S04] The Fat Controller MVC · Repository Pattern Look at what PlanController does right now — too many jobs for one class: 1 Repeated queries Plans. ToListAsync () copied into many actions and controllers. 2 Knows EF Core Controller depends on DbContext, DbSet, SaveChanges. 3 Hard to test Testing one action needs a real database. 4 Hard to change New data source → rewrite every controller. [S05] SOLID — Five Principles MVC · Repository Pattern SOLID = five design principles for code that is easy to change. We'll name each letter when it fixes a real problem. S Single Responsibility A class has one job — one reason to change. O Open / Closed Open for extension, closed for modification. L Liskov Substitution A subtype can replace its base type without breaking anything. I Interface Segregation Many small interfaces beat one fat interface. D Dependency Inversion Depend on abstractions, not on implementations. 💡 The fat controller breaks two of them: the S (too many jobs) and the D (tied to concrete classes). Let's fix them one by one. [S06] The S — One Class, One Job MVC · Repository Pattern Single Responsibility: a class should have one reason to change . PlanController has two. ❌ One class, two jobs PlanController HTTP read the request · pick the view · redirect Data access queries · Find · Add · Update · SaveChanges split ✅ One class, one job PlanController HTTP only changes when the UI flow changes PlanRepository data access only changes when a query or the database changes 💡 Changing a query should not mean opening the controller — and changing a view should not touch the database code. [S07] The Repository Idea MVC · Repository Pattern A repository hides how data is stored. The rest of the app asks it for data — it never sees EF Core. 1 One place for data code Every query on Plans lives in one class . 2 One per entity PlanRepository, MemberRepository…not one fat one [S08] The D — Depend on Abstractions, Not Implementations MVC · Repository Pattern Before we write PlanRepository, one more rule: the controller should not be tied to it directly. 1 High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both depend on abstractions. 2 Abstractions should not depend on details. Details depend on abstractions. ❌ Depend on the class PlanController high-level PlanRepository low-level · concrete depends on the implementation HIGH-LEVEL LOW-LEVEL ✅ Depend on the abstraction PlanController high-level IPlanRepository abstraction PlanRepository low-level · EF Core depends on ↓ implements ↑ (arrow inverted) 💡 That is why our repository comes as a pair: the interface IPlanRepository and the class PlanRepository . [S09] Why Depend on an Interface? MVC · Repository Pattern Dependency Inversion : high-level code (controllers) depends on abstractions , not on concrete classes. 1 Loose coupling The controller only knows the contract . The class behind it can change freely. 2 Swap the class EF Core → Dapper → in-memory: the controller keeps using the same interface. 3 Easy testing Give the controller a fake repository that returns test data — no database. 4 Clear boundaries Each layer has one job and one way in. IPlanRepository planRepository = new PlanRepository (); // today IPlanRepository planRepository = new CachedPlanRepository (); // tomorrow — same interface [S10] One Socket, Many Plugs MVC · Repository Pattern The controller is plugged into a contract . The class behind it can be swapped. PlanController only knows the interface depends on INTERFACE IPlanRepository the contract PlanRepository EF Core ● plugged in · today CachedPlanRepository adds caching tomorrow FakePlanRepository returns test data unit tests implements O · Open / Closed — add a new plug as a new class; the controller is never edited. L · Liskov — every plug must behave the way IPlanRepository promises. Right now the controller picks the plug itself → private readonly IPlanRepository _planRepository = new PlanRepository (); ⚠️ The controller still creates the class with new — the next section fixes exactly this. [S11] Quick Check MVC · Repository Pattern [S12] Quick Check MVC · Repository Pattern [S13] Quick Check MVC · Repository Pattern [S14] Quick Check MVC · Repository Pattern [S15] SECTION 02 Dependency Injection Stop writing new — let ASP.NET Core create and hand you what you need 02 [S16] Where We Stopped — The Repository MVC · Dependency Injection The repository moved the data code out — but the controller still creates it with new, and the repository creates the DbContext the same way. // PlanController.cs public class PlanController : Controller { // the controller builds its own repository private readonly IPlanRepository _planRepository = new PlanRepository (); } // PlanRepository.cs public class PlanRepository : IPlanRepository { // the repository builds its own DbContext private readonly GymDbContext _dbContext = new GymDbContext (); } // GymDbContext.cs protected override void OnConfiguring( DbContextOptionsBuilder optionsBuilder) => optionsBuilder.UseSqlServer( "Server=.;Database=GymDb;..." ); 1 Tight coupling Each class is glued to the concrete class it creates. 2 Hard to test You can’t hand the controller a fake repository. 3 Hard-coded settings Connection string lives inside C# code. 4 Who cleans up? Nobody controls when the context is disposed. [S17] Problem 1 — Tight Coupling MVC · Dependency Injection PlanController depends on IPlanRepository — but still creates PlanRepository with new, so it is glued to that class. ❌ Right now public class PlanController : Controller { // ❌ the controller picks the concrete class itself private readonly IPlanRepository _planRepository = new PlanRepository (); } // Tomorrow we want CachedPlanRepository: // ❌ edit "new PlanRepository()" in every // controller that uses it 💡 The controller should only say what it needs. Which class it gets is decided in one place: Program.cs. [S18] Problem 2 — Hard to Test MVC · Dependency Injection We built IPlanRepository so a test could use a fake — but the controller gives us no way to hand one in. ❌ Right now // Unit test public void Index_ReturnsAllPlans() { var controller = new PlanController (); var result = controller.Index(); // ❌ new PlanController() → new PlanRepository() // → new GymDbContext() // ❌ hits the real GymDb on SQL Server // ❌ no way to pass a FakePlanRepository in } [S19] Problem 3 — Hard-Coded Settings MVC · Dependency Injection The connection string is compiled into C# — every server or database change means editing code. ❌ Right now // GymDbContext.cs protected override void OnConfiguring( DbContextOptionsBuilder optionsBuilder) { optionsBuilder.UseSqlServer( "Server=.;Database=GymDb;..." ); } // ❌ new server or database → edit C#, rebuild, redeploy // ❌ the same string on every machine and environment // ❌ secrets end up in source control [S20] Problem 4 — Who Cleans Up? MVC · Dependency Injection Whoever calls new owns the object — and must remember to Dispose() it. ❌ Right now public class PlanRepository : IPlanRepository { private readonly GymDbContext _dbContext = new GymDbContext (); // ❌ nobody ever calls _dbContext.Dispose() } // The manual fix — repeated in every method: public Plan ? GetById(int id) { using var dbContext = new GymDbContext (); return dbContext.Plans.Find(id); } // ❌ easy to forget, and still tightly coupled [S21] DIP · IoC · DI · Container MVC · Dependency Injection Four words that sound alike — each one answers a different question. WHAT DIP Dependency Inversion Principle the principle Depend on abstractions, not on implementations. WHO IoC Inversion of Control the idea The class stops creating its own dependencies — someone else does. HOW DI Dependency Injection the technique Dependencies are handed in from outside, usually through the constructor. WITH WHAT Container IServiceProvider the tool Built into ASP.NET Core: creates, injects and disposes for you. principle → idea → technique → tool ✅ DIP and DI work together. From the Repository section, DIP decided what PlanController depends on: IPlanRepository . In this section, DI decides who creates it: the container. [S22] The Fix — DI in Action MVC · Dependency Injection Same classes — but now nobody writes new . They only ask, and the container does the rest. appsettings.json the connection string lives here Program.cs registers IPlanRepository and GymDbContext DI Container creates · injects · disposes PlanController constructor asks for IPlanRepository 3 4 1 2 Tight coupling ✓ The controller asks for IPlanRepository — it never picks the class. fixed in: PlanController 1 Hard to test ✓ A test passes a FakePlanRepository in through the constructor. fixed in: PlanController 2 Hard-coded settings ✓ The connection string moves out of C# into appsettings.json. fixed in: appsettings.json 3 Who cleans up? ✓ The container disposes the DbContext when the request ends. fixed in: DI Container 4 [S23] What Is Dependency Injection? MVC · Dependency Injection A class should not create the objects it needs. It asks for them in its constructor, and the DI container hands them over. D Dependency Any object your class needs to do its job. PlanController needs IPlanRepository. I Injection Passing that object in from outside — usually through the constructor . C DI Container Built into ASP.NET Core ( IServiceProvider ). It creates , injects and disposes objects for you. 💡 Think of a restaurant: you order a meal, you don’t walk into the kitchen and cook it. The controller orders IPlanRepository — the container cooks it. Without DI With DI new PlanRepository() inside the class IPlanRepository comes through the constructor Change the class → edit every controller Change one line in Program.cs [S24] How the DI Container Works MVC · Dependency Injection Two moments: you register services once at startup — the container resolves them on every request. Register Program.cs AddDbContext<>() → Request GET /Plan → Resolve needs PlanController → needs IPlanRepository → Inject new PlanController(repo) → Dispose end of request dbContext.Dispose() 1 Registration builder.Services.Add...() tells the container what to create and how long it lives. 2 Resolution When MVC needs a controller, it reads the constructor and builds every parameter — recursively. 3 Disposal Objects created for a request are disposed automatically when the request ends. Controllers are created by the container too — that’s why their constructor parameters “just arrive”. ⚠️ Forgot to register a service? You get: Unable to resolve service for type ... while attempting to activate PlanController . [S25] Resolving the Whole Chain MVC · Dependency Injection The container reads each constructor, then the constructor of everything that needs — all the way down. ① Resolve: read constructors left → right PlanController GET /Plan needs it IPlanRepository → PlanRepository GymDbContext registered by AddDbContext DbContextOptions connection string from appsettings.json needs needs needs ② Build: create objects right → left, then inject each one into the next built 4th built 3rd built 2nd built 1st 💡 You write zero new — the container builds all four objects for every request. ⚠️ One missing registration anywhere in the chain → Unable to resolve service for type … Add more classes later and the chain just grows — the container builds it the same way. [S26] Service Lifetimes MVC · Dependency Injection When you register a service you also choose how long each created object lives. Method New object created… Shared? Typical use AddSingleton() Once — for the whole app lifetime By everyone, every request Configuration, caches, stateless helpers AddScoped() Once per HTTP request Inside the same request DbContext, repositories AddTransient() Every time it is requested Never Light, stateless utilities S Singleton Must be thread-safe — many requests use it at the same time. S Scoped The safe default for anything that touches the database. T Transient Cheap to create; never holds shared state. [S27] Lifetimes MVC · Dependency Injection Two requests arrive. Inside each, PlanRepository and then MemberRepository ask for GymDbContext. Request 1 Request 2 PlanRepository MemberRepository PlanRepository MemberRepository Singleton one object for the whole app ctx #1 ctx #1 ctx #1 ctx #1 Same everywhere Scoped one object per request ctx #1 ctx #1 ctx #2 ctx #2 Same per request Transient a new object every time ctx #1 ctx #2 ctx #3 ctx #4 Always new request 1 ends → its Scoped objects are disposed faded bar = how long each object lives [S28] Lifetime Rules of Thumb MVC · Dependency Injection 1 DbContext is Scoped AddDbContext already registers it as Scoped — one unit of work per request. 2 Scoped → Scoped Repositories that use the DbContext should be Scoped too. 3 Never Scoped inside Singleton A singleton would keep one DbContext forever → captive dependency . Rule: a service can only depend on services that live as long or longer than itself. Singleton can use → Singleton Scoped can use → Scoped, Singleton Transient can use → anything [S29] Quick Check MVC · Dependency Injection [S30] Quick Check MVC · Dependency Injection [S31] Quick Check MVC · Dependency Injection [S32] Quick Check MVC · Dependency Injection [S33] Quick Check MVC · Dependency Injection [S34] Quick Check MVC · Dependency Injection [S35] Quick Check MVC · Dependency Injection [S36] Quick Check MVC · Dependency Injection [S37] Quick Check MVC · Dependency Injection [S38] Quick Check MVC · Dependency Injection [S39] Quick Check MVC · Dependency Injection [S40] Quick Check MVC · Dependency Injection [S41] SECTION 03 Plan Edit — GET Open an edit form filled with the plan’s data, and learn the ways a controller passes data to a view 03 [S42] The Goal MVC · Plan Edit (GET) Click Edit on a plan card → open /Plan/Edit/3 → see a form already filled with that plan’s data. Edit button on the plan card → GET /Plan/Edit/3 browser → PlanController Edit(int id) → Find(3) plan or NotFound() → View(plan) filled form [S43] Edit — GET Action MVC · Plan Edit (GET) [S44] Edit — GET Flow MVC · Plan Edit (GET) Every path ends with a proper response — the action never crashes on a bad id. GET /Plan/Edit/3 id > 0 ? Find(id) search by primary key found ? View(plan) Model = plan Filled form user sees it yes yes no no Stop early an id ≤ 0 can never exist NotFound() 404 — no crash on null 1 2 3 4 1 Validate the input An id of 0 or less can never exist. 2 Find(id) Searches by primary key. Returns null if not found. 3 Handle “not found” Return NotFound() — never crash with a null. 4 Pass the model View(plan) → the view gets it as Model . [S45] Passing Data: Controller → View MVC · Plan Edit (GET) The Model carries the main data. For small extras there are three more containers: M Model Strongly typed — View(plan) + @model Plan . IntelliSense and compile-time checks. V ViewData A dictionary: ViewData["Title"] = "Edit" . Key = string, value = object. B ViewBag A dynamic wrapper over ViewData: ViewBag.Title = "Edit" . T TempData Survives one redirect . Perfect for “Saved successfully” messages. 💡 Rule: the main data of a page always goes in the Model. ViewData/ViewBag are for small extras : page title, a dropdown list, a flag. Scenario Use The plan being edited Model The page ViewData / ViewBag “Plan updated” after redirect TempData [S46] ViewData vs ViewBag MVC · Plan Edit (GET) Controller public IActionResult Edit( int id) { ViewData[ "Title" ] = "Edit Plan" ; ViewBag.MaxDays = 365 ; ... return View(plan); } View <h2> @ViewData [ "Title" ] </h2> <h2> @ViewBag .Title </h2> @* same value! *@ <small> Max: @ViewBag .MaxDays days </small> ViewData ViewBag Syntax ViewData["Key"] ViewBag.Key Type ViewDataDictionary dynamic Casting for objects Needed: (List<Plan>)ViewData["Plans"] Not needed Typo in the key null at runtime null at runtime They share the same storage : ViewBag.Title reads ViewData["Title"] . Both live for one request only . [S47] TempData — Data Across a Redirect MVC · Plan Edit (GET) After a redirect the browser makes a new request → ViewData/ViewBag are empty. TempData survives that jump. POST /Plan/Edit/3 save changes → TempData[...] = "Plan updated" → 302 Redirect to /Plan → GET /Plan reads TempData → Removed after it is read Method Effect TempData["Key"] Read → marked for deletion TempData.Peek("Key") Read without deleting TempData.Keep("Key") Keep it one more request 💡 TempData is stored in a cookie by default — keep it small (strings, numbers). Use \u0022\u0022 as the key for a ModelOnly error."},{"label":"Slide 60","t":60,"text":"Post / Redirect / Get (PRG) MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST) After a successful POST, always redirect \u2014 never return a view directly. \u274C POST \u2192 return View() Browser stays on the POST URL User presses F5 \u2192 \u201CResend form data?\u201D The same update runs again Bad for Create \u2192 duplicate rows \u2705 POST \u2192 Redirect \u2192 GET Server answers 302 \u002B new URL Browser makes a fresh GET /Plan F5 only repeats the harmless GET TempData carries the success message POST /Plan/Edit/3 \u2192 SaveChanges() \u2192 302 \u2192 /Plan \u2192 GET /Plan"},{"label":"Slide 61","t":61,"text":"Why Not Post the Entity Directly? MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST) If the POST action receives Plan itself, model binding fills every property the browser sends \u2014 even ones you never put in the form. // \u274C binds the whole entity [HttpPost] public IActionResult Edit( Plan plan) { _planRepository.Update(plan); return RedirectToAction( \u0022Index\u0022 ); } \u003C!-- attacker adds in DevTools: --\u003E \u003Cinput name= \u0022Name\u0022 value= \u0022Free Plan\u0022 /\u003E \u003Cinput name= \u0022IsActive\u0022 value= \u0022true\u0022 /\u003E \u003Cinput name= \u0022CreatedAt\u0022 value= \u00222000-01-01\u0022 /\u003E 1 Overposting Users can change fields that aren\u2019t even on the form. 2 Wrong shape The form needs 4 fields \u2014 the entity has 8. 3 Mixed rules UI messages end up on the database class."},{"label":"Slide 62","t":62,"text":"Overposting \u2014 What Really Gets Sent MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST) The form shows a few fields \u2014 but the browser can send anything . Model binding fills whatever matches. WHAT THE USER SEES Edit plan Name (display only) Basic Plan Description Access to gym equipment DurationDays 30 Price 300 Save plan submit WHAT THE SERVER RECEIVES (form data) Description = Access to gym equipment DurationDays = 30 Price = 300 __RequestVerificationToken = CfDJ8N\u2026 Name = Free Plan IsActive = true CreatedAt = 2000-01-01 added in DevTools Edit(Plan plan) \u274C Name, IsActive and CreatedAt are bound too \u2192 saved to the database. Edit(UpdatePlanViewModel model) \u2705 The ViewModel has no such properties \u2192 the extra values are ignored."},{"label":"Slide 63","t":63,"text":"What Is a ViewModel? MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST) A ViewModel is a class shaped for one view : only the data that view needs, plus that view\u2019s validation rules. Plan  (Entity \u2192 table) Id Name Description DurationDays Price IsActive CreatedAt UpdatedAt \u2192 UpdatePlanViewModel  (Form) PlanName display only Description [Required] DurationDays [Range(1, 365)] Price [Range] \uD83D\uDCA1 Entity = shape of the table . ViewModel = shape of the screen . One entity can have many ViewModels: Index, Details, Update\u2026"},{"label":"Slide 64","t":64,"text":"Anti-Forgery Token MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST) CSRF[Cross-Site Request Forgery ] : a bad site tricks a logged-in user\u2019s browser into posting to *your* site. The anti-forgery token blocks it. You write \u003Cform asp-action = \u0022Edit\u0022 method= \u0022post\u0022 \u003E ... \u003C/form\u003E Browser receives \u003Cform action= \u0022/Plan/Edit/3\u0022 method= \u0022post\u0022 \u003E \u003Cinput name= \u0022__RequestVerificationToken\u0022 type= \u0022hidden\u0022 value= \u0022CfDJ8N...\u0022 /\u003E 1 Form Tag Helper \u003Cform asp-action\u003E adds the hidden token automatically. 2 [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] Checks the token on the POST. Missing / wrong \u2192 400 . 3 Why it works Another site can\u2019t read your page, so it can\u2019t know the token. \uD83D\uDCA1 Put [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] on every POST action that changes data."},{"label":"Slide 65","t":65,"text":"Edit \u2014 POST Flow MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST) One POST, three possible endings: rejected, sent back with errors, or saved and redirected. POST /Plan/Edit/3 token valid ? Model binding form \u2192 ViewModel id \u2190 route ModelState valid ? Find \u002B copy only allowed fields SaveChanges \u002B TempData message 302 Redirect \u2192 GET /Plan yes yes no no 400 request rejected return View(model) same form \u002B error messages user fixes the errors \u0026 resubmits 1 2 3 4 5 [HttpPost] \u002B [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] guard the door before any of your code runs. Numbers match the five steps on \u201CEdit \u2014 POST Action\u201D."},{"label":"Slide 66","t":66,"text":"The Full Edit Cycle MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST) Browser PlanController Database SECTION 02 GET half SECTION 03 POST half GET /Plan/Edit/3 Find(3) plan  (null \u2192 NotFound) View(plan) \u2192 form already filled POST /Plan/Edit/3  \u002B token invalid \u2192 View(model) \u002B errors  (user fixes \u0026 resubmits) SaveChanges() 302 \u2192 /Plan   \u002B TempData \u0022Plan updated\u0022 GET /Plan Index page \u002B \u0022Plan updated\u0022 message \u2713"},{"label":"Slide 67","t":67,"text":"Quick Check MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST)"},{"label":"Slide 68","t":68,"text":"Quick Check MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST)"},{"label":"Slide 69","t":69,"text":"Quick Check MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST)"},{"label":"Slide 70","t":70,"text":"Quick Check MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST)"},{"label":"Slide 71","t":71,"text":"Quick Check MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST)"},{"label":"Slide 72","t":72,"text":"Quick Check MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST)"},{"label":"Slide 73","t":73,"text":"Quick Check MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST)"},{"label":"Slide 74","t":74,"text":"Quick Check MVC \u00B7 Plan Edit (POST)"},{"label":"Slide 75","t":75,"text":"QUESTIONS?
